def: A box in the corner of the sheet with the part name, drawing number, revision, scale, material, and general tolerance.
expand: Title Block in the bottom-right corner (ISO 7200): part name, drawing number, Revision, scale, material, finish, general tolerance (ISO 2768-mK), weight, drawn/checked/approved by + dates. The material and general tolerance fields are the most-read in production!

def: A table listing every part in an assembly: item number, part number, description, quantity, and material.
expand: BOM/Parts List: item number (matches the balloon!), part number, description, quantity, material/note. Rules: standard parts get a full designation (DIN 912 M8×30-8.8), sorted by number, quantities per single assembly unit. The BOM feeds purchasing and ERP — an error here means a wrong order.

def: A number/letter indicating the current drawing revision, documented in the revision table.
expand: Revision: every released drawing change gets a new letter (A→B→C, skipping I, O, Q). The revision table lists: change description, date, approver, and sometimes a revision cloud on the drawing. Iron rule: manufacture only to the Rev on the order! A part per an old Rev is a reject even if perfect.

def: The ratio between drawing size and real size, e.g. 1:2 (reduced) or 2:1 (enlarged). Written dimensions are always full size.
expand: Scale: the drawing:reality ratio. 1:1 natural, 1:2 reduced, 2:1 enlarged. Preferred series: 1:2, 1:5, 1:10 / 2:1, 5:1, 10:1. The key rule: never measure with a ruler on the drawing — only the written dimensions govern! (prints distort, PDFs aren't to scale).

def: A reference surface/axis (labeled A, B, C) from which geometric features and dimensions are measured.
expand: Datum: the filled triangle with a letter (A, B, C) on a surface/axis — the base from which all GD&T is measured. Choosing the right Datum = the actual assembly surfaces (how the part sits in the assembly). An arbitrary Datum = measurements that don't reflect function.

def: ISO projection method — the view appears on the side opposite the viewing direction. Common in Israel and Europe.
expand: First Angle (ISO, Europe/Israel): the part is 'projected through' — the top view is drawn below, the left view is drawn on the right. The symbol: a truncated cone with the narrow end to the left. Confusing it with third angle = an inverted part! Always check the symbol in the title block.

def: ANSI projection method — the view appears on the same side you're looking from. Common in the US.
expand: Third Angle (ASME, US): the part is 'reflected' — the top view is drawn above, the right view is drawn on the right. More intuitive for most people. The symbol: a cone with the narrow end to the right. American drawings (aerospace!) are almost always this method.

def: A 3D illustrative view at 30° to each axis. Not for measurement.
expand: Isometric: the three axes at 120° to each other, vertical lines stay vertical and the rest at 30°. For illustration only — not for measurement! Common uses: a corner view for orientation, assembly instructions, catalogs. In modern CAD: a 3D view imported directly.

def: An enlargement of a small area on the drawing to clarify fine details, marked with a circle and letter.
expand: Detail View: a circle around a crowded area + a letter (A) → enlarged elsewhere with 'DETAIL A, SCALE 5:1'. Mandatory when small details (a seal groove, a special chamfer, a critical radius) aren't legible at the main scale. The detail's scale is always noted next to it.

def: A thick continuous line marking an edge or surface directly visible. The heaviest line weight on the drawing.
expand: Continuous Thick (0.5-0.7mm): the visible outline edges — the skeleton of the drawing. Hierarchy: the thickest line on the sheet. In CAD: the Object/Visible layer. Everything else (dimensions, extension, center) is half its weight.

def: A dashed line marking an edge/surface hidden behind another part.
expand: Hidden/Dashed (thin dashed): hidden edges — internal holes, steps behind. Modern rule: prefer a section view over a mass of hidden lines! A drawing crowded with dashes is a candidate for a section. The dash pattern: 3mm line, 1mm gap, starting and ending on a line.

def: A thin line of alternating long-short dashes marking an axis of symmetry or hole center.
expand: Center Line (thin long-short chain): axes of symmetry, hole centers, bolt circles (PCD). Mandatory on every round feature — dimensions originate from it! Crosses the outline slightly. Two crossing center lines = the precise center of a hole.

def: A thick chain line with arrows and letters (A-A) marking where the part is "cut."
expand: Cutting Plane (thick chain + arrows + letters): defines where the part is 'cut' and which direction is being viewed. The arrows point in the viewing direction! The resulting section is labeled A-A. Types: full, half (Half Section), offset (Offset) — follows features not on one line.

def: A thin line with arrows at both ends, indicating the measured dimension.
expand: Dimension Line: thin with end arrows, the number above/within it. Rules: 10mm from the outline, 7mm between parallel lines, dimension lines don't cross each other, shortest to longest going outward. Closed filled arrow = the standard.

def: A thin line extending from the edge of the part to allow the dimension line to be placed outside the drawing.
expand: Extension Line: the thin line that carries the feature's edge out to the dimension line. Starts with a small gap (1-2mm) from the outline, and continues 2-3mm past the arrow. Doesn't touch the part! That small gap distinguishes it from the outline itself.

def: A wavy line marking a partial section or a shortened long part.
expand: Break Line: two meanings — the boundary of a partial section, or shortening a long uniform part (a 2-meter shaft drawn as 10cm with a break — the real dimension is still written!). Zigzag for large parts, freehand wavy for small ones.

def: Diagonal lines at 45° marking solid material within a sectioned area.
expand: Hatching (45°, thin lines): the material actually cut in the section. Rules: the same part = same direction and density across all sections; adjacent parts in an assembly = opposite directions; ribs, bolts, shafts, and pins aren't hatched in a longitudinal section! Different patterns = different materials (ISO 128).

def: Successive dimensions, one after another — tolerances accumulate at each link.
expand: Each dimension is measured from the previous one, so tolerances accumulate: three ±0.1 dimensions can stack up to ±0.3 at the end. Suitable only when the distance between adjacent features matters. Rule: avoid chains on critical dimensions — switch to parallel dimensioning from one Datum.

def: All dimensions measured from the same base point — no accumulated tolerance.
expand: All dimensions originate from a single reference point (Datum), so each dimension carries only its own tolerance without accumulation. This is the preferred method for precise parts and maps directly to CNC programming (absolute coordinates, G90).

def: Like parallel dimensioning, with an explicit Datum mark at the zero point.
expand: A formal version of parallel dimensioning where the zero point is marked as a defined Datum on the drawing. Used in full GD&T drawings, and allows a direct link between the dimensioning and the feature control frames (FCF).

def: A dimension without a direct tolerance (enclosed in a box); the tolerance is defined in a separate FCF.
expand: A dimension in a rectangular box (e.g. |50|) defining an exact theoretical location. It has no direct tolerance — the tolerance comes from a feature control frame (usually Position). All measurement is made relative to this theoretical location.

def: The width of a circle measured edge to edge through the center.
expand: Marked with ⌀ before the value (⌀25). On a drawing, the ⌀ symbol indicates the feature is round even if only seen in section. Diameter is a Feature of Size, so MMC/LMC rules and the envelope principle apply to it.

def: The distance from the center of a circle to its edge.
expand: Marked with R before the value (R5). Used for rounded corners and arcs that aren't a full circle. An internal corner R is critical for manufacturing — a milling tool can't produce an R smaller than the tool's radius. SR = spherical radius.

def: A small angled cut at the edge of a part, e.g. C2 = a 2mm chamfer at 45°.
expand: An angled edge break, marked C (e.g. C0.5 = 0.5mm at 45°) or as dimension×angle (2×30°). Important for: removing dangerous sharpness, easing assembly (lead-in), preventing burrs. Almost every machined edge needs a minimal C0.2-C0.5 chamfer.

def: The allowed range of deviation from a nominal dimension.
expand: The difference between the allowed upper and lower limits. A tight tolerance = high precision = high cost (each IT grade step ≈ ×1.5-2 in cost). The golden rule: the widest tolerance that still guarantees function. Most dimensions get a general tolerance per ISO 2768.

def: ISO precision level from IT01 (most precise) to IT18 (coarse). IT7 = typical fits.
expand: ISO 286 defines 20 grades: IT01 (nanometers, metrology) to IT18 (millimeters, castings). Example at ⌀50: IT6=16μm, IT7=25μm, IT9=62μm, IT11=160μm. Standard turning achieves IT9-IT11, grinding IT5-IT6.

def: The relationship between a hole and a shaft — clearance, transition, or interference.
expand: Defined by combining a hole tolerance (uppercase letter) and a shaft tolerance (lowercase letter) — e.g. H7/g6. Three families: clearance (guaranteed gap), transition (depends on actual values), interference (guaranteed overlap). The hole-basis system (H) is the most common.

def: A guaranteed gap between shaft and hole — slides by hand, e.g. H7/f6.
expand: A guaranteed gap in every allowed combination. H7/f6 = free sliding with lubrication (plain bearings), H7/g6 = precise sliding (guides), H7/h6 = close sliding (precise location without load). Assembly is always by hand.

def: A permanent overlap — the shaft is larger than the hole, requiring a press/heat, e.g. H7/p6.
expand: A guaranteed overlap — the shaft is always bigger than the hole. H7/p6 = light press (hand press), H7/s6 = medium press (hydraulic press), H7/u6 = heavy press (heating/cooling). Transmits torque without a key. Disassembly is usually destructive.

def: May result in a small gap or slight overlap, depending on actual values, e.g. H7/k6.
expand: Depends on actual dimensions — may result in a tiny gap or slight overlap. H7/k6 and H7/m6 are the common ones. Ideal for precise location with disassembly possible: gears, pulleys, couplings. Assembled with a plastic mallet.

def: The basic rounded dimension, without tolerance (e.g. ⌀50).
expand: The whole number from which deviations are derived — e.g. for ⌀50H7 the nominal is 50. Two parts in a fit must share the same nominal size. In practice no part is exactly at nominal — always within the tolerance range.

def: A box containing: geometric symbol | tolerance zone | Datum(s) | material modifier.
expand: The FCF is the heart of GD&T: first cell = geometric symbol (position, flatness...), second cell = tolerance zone size (+modifier ⓜ/ⓛ), further cells = Datums in order of precedence. Read right-to-left in Hebrew but always written in the same international order.

def: The condition where a part has the most material (smallest hole / largest shaft). Enables bonus tolerance.
expand: MMC: the smallest allowed hole or the largest allowed shaft. Important because it's the critical condition for assembly — if parts assemble at MMC, they'll assemble in every other condition. The ⓜ symbol in the FCF triggers bonus tolerance.

def: The condition where a part has the least material (largest hole / smallest shaft).
expand: LMC: the largest hole or the smallest shaft. Critical for minimum wall thickness calculations (a hole near an edge) and strength. The ⓛ symbol is relatively rare — mainly in castings and wall-thickness requirements.

def: The tolerance applies regardless of the feature's actual size — the default when there's no M or L.
expand: RFS: the geometric tolerance is fixed and independent of the size actually produced. The default in ASME Y14.5 since 1994 (no ⓢ symbol needed). Stricter than MMC since there's no bonus — used for balance, orientation, and critical location.

def: Additional tolerance gained when a feature deviates from MMC.
expand: When a feature is marked ⓜ and deviates from MMC toward LMC, the difference is added to the geometric tolerance. Example: a hole ⌀10.0-10.2 with Position ⌀0.1ⓜ — if the hole comes out ⌀10.15, the bonus = 0.15 and the actual tolerance = ⌀0.25. Saves unnecessary rejections.

def: A form control — deviation of a line/axis from a straight line. No Datum.
expand: Checks how much a line on a surface or an axis deviates from a perfect straight line. Common application: long axles (preventing bowing), rails. When applied to an axis with ⌀ — controls the bending of the whole axis and can override the envelope principle.

def: A form control — deviation of a surface from a plane. No Datum.
expand: All points on the surface must fall between two parallel planes at the tolerance distance apart. No Datum — measured relative to itself. Critical for sealing surfaces (gaskets), mounting bases, and reference surfaces. Measurement: CMM or a surface plate + indicator.

def: A form control — deviation of a round cross-section from a perfect circle. No Datum.
expand: Each individual cross-section must fall between two concentric circles at the tolerance distance apart. Typical errors: an oval (2-jaw chuck grip), a triangle (lobing from a 3-jaw), chatter. True measurement: a roundness tester (Talyrond), not a micrometer!

def: A form control — combines straightness+circularity+parallelism over the entire cylindrical extent.
expand: The strictest combination: circularity + straightness + uniform diameter along the entire cylinder simultaneously. The most expensive tolerance to manufacture — requires quality grinding. Use only when truly needed (hydraulic pistons, precision shafts).

def: An orientation control — deviation of a surface/axis from parallel to a Datum. Datum mandatory.
expand: The surface/axis must fall between two planes parallel to the Datum. Common on surfaces machined from both sides (plates, blocks). Note: parallelism also controls the flatness of that same surface (flatness can't exceed the parallelism).

def: An orientation control — deviation from 90° relative to a Datum. Datum mandatory.
expand: Deviation from exact 90° relative to a Datum, measured as a distance between two planes (not as an angle!). Critical for bearing shoulders (shaft runout), machine columns, and vertical mounting surfaces.

def: An orientation control — deviation from a nominal angle other than 0°/90°. Datum mandatory.
expand: Controls any angle that isn't 0° or 90° — e.g. a surface at 30°. The angle itself is marked as a basic dimension (in a box), and the tolerance is a zone thickness between two planes. It is not a tolerance on the angle in degrees!

def: The most common symbol — defines the 3D location of a hole/shaft relative to Datums, within a cylindrical zone.
expand: The workhorse of GD&T — about 70% of applications. Defines a cylindrical tolerance zone (⌀) around the exact theoretical location. Advantage over ±: a round zone is 57% larger than an equivalent square, and it supports MMC bonus. Requires basic dimensions + Datums.

def: The center of a cross-section must be within tolerance relative to a Datum axis. Very difficult to measure.
expand: Requires the midpoints of the cross-section to fall within a zone around the Datum axis. Very difficult to measure (midpoints, not surface points!) and was therefore removed in ASME Y14.5-2018. Replaced by Position or Runout, which give the same functional control.

def: A tolerance on the shape of a free-form 2D line, like a wing profile.
expand: A 2D tolerance zone around a defined theoretical profile (usually from CAD). Each cross-section is checked separately. Used for aerodynamic profiles, sealing strips, and templates. With a Datum = also location; without = shape only.

def: Maximum wobble at a single cross-section while rotating about a Datum.
expand: Circular Runout: an indicator (DTI) held against one cross-section during a full rotation about the Datum axis — the total reading (TIR) must be within tolerance. Combines circularity + concentricity in one simple check. The common lathe test.

def: Like runout, but along the entire cylinder — stricter.
expand: Total Runout: the indicator moves along the entire surface during rotation — the whole surface within one tolerance. Adds straightness and taper control on top of Circular Runout. Stricter and more expensive — for precision shafts and rotating sealing surfaces.

def: The most common roughness metric, in micrometers. Ra 1.6 = the default.
expand: Ra: the arithmetic mean of the profile deviations from the center line. Reference values: standard turning 1.6-3.2, grinding 0.2-0.8, lapping 0.025-0.1. Important: two completely different surfaces (scratches vs. waviness) can give the same Ra — so Rz/Rt is added for critical applications.

def: The average of the 5 highest peaks and 5 deepest valleys. Not exactly convertible from Ra.
expand: Rz: the average of the five largest peak-to-valley distances across five sampling lengths. Sensitive to isolated defects that Ra smooths over — a single deep scratch spikes Rz. Critical for sealing (a scratch = a leak path) and fatigue. Typical ratio: Rz ≈ 4-7×Ra depending on the process.

def: The N1-N12 scale (ISO 1302, retired by the new ISO 21920). N6=Ra0.8, N7=Ra1.6.
expand: N1-N12 on the old ISO scale: each grade doubles Ra. Memory anchors: N6=0.8 (good grinding), N7=1.6 (finish machining), N8=3.2 (regular machining), N9=6.3 (coarse). Still common on old drawings and in parts of the industry despite being superseded.

def: The dominant direction of machining marks on a surface (e.g. parallel from grinding).
expand: Lay: the direction the tool left behind. Functional meaning: a dynamic seal needs circumferential Lay (not axial leak paths!), sliding surfaces prefer Lay in the direction of motion, and Ra measurement is always taken perpendicular to Lay. Symbols: = ⊥ × M C R in the finish symbol.

def: The largest diameter of a thread — measured at the crests.
expand: The Major Diameter — the value in the thread name: M10 = major diameter 10mm. In practice an M10 bolt measures 9.8-9.97 (tolerance field g). This is the quick caliper measurement for identifying an unknown thread — together with a pitch gauge measurement.

def: The smallest diameter of a thread — measured at the roots.
expand: The Minor Diameter — the core diameter at the thread root. Determines bolt strength (load-bearing cross-section) and the tap drill diameter for internal threading. Strength calculations use the Stress Area (As), between the minor diameter and the pitch.

def: The theoretical diameter where thread width equals groove width.
expand: The Pitch Diameter (d2) — the diameter where the thread width equals the gap width. This is the critical diameter for the thread fit — measured with the Three-Wire method or a Thread Micrometer. The thread tolerance (6g/6H) is defined mainly on it.

def: The distance between two adjacent thread crests, in mm.
expand: P — the thread-to-thread distance. Defines the thread together with the diameter: M10×1.5. In the inch system it's measured inversely — TPI (threads per inch). Measurement: a Pitch Gauge or comparison to a known bolt. A wrong pitch destroys the thread while turning it in!

def: The default pitch on metric threads, not stated separately. M12=M12×1.75.
expand: The default that isn't written: M10 with no pitch noted = M10×1.5. Advantages: more resistant to damage and repeated assembly, less sensitive to dirt, faster to thread. The right choice for 95% of general applications.

def: A smaller pitch, always stated explicitly, used for vibration/thin walls.
expand: Always stated explicitly: M10×1.25 or M10×1. Advantages: better vibration resistance (small helix angle), fine adjustment, stronger core (larger diameter). Cost: more prone to galling and cross-threading. Use: aerospace, instrument adjustments.

def: The drill diameter before cutting an internal thread = D − P.
expand: The quick formula for metric: D − P (a hole for an M8×1.25 tap = 6.7-6.8mm). Gives about 75% thread height — the ideal compromise: 100% thread adds only ~5% strength but doubles tapping torque and the risk of a broken tap! For hard materials: 60-65% (a slightly larger hole).

def: The length of the perpendicular side of the weld metal triangle, measured from the joint corner.
expand: In an equal-leg Fillet Weld, the leg (z) relates to the throat: a = 0.707×z. The drawing specifies leg or throat — important not to confuse them. An oversized leg = wasted filler metal, thermal distortion, and cost: an a5 weld instead of a4 = +56% metal volume!

def: A weld joining perpendicular surfaces without edge preparation. The most common type.
expand: About 80% of industrial welds. Recommended size: a = 0.7×the thinner of the two thicknesses. No edge prep needed — a big savings. Strength is calculated from the throat area (a×L). Over-welding is the common problem — distortion and cost without useful added strength.

def: A weld requiring edge preparation (V, U, J), for thick joints.
expand: Needed when full penetration (CJP) or partial penetration (PJP) is required at thicknesses above ~6mm. Common preps: V (up to 20mm), X (double-sided, reduces distortion), U/J (large thicknesses, less filler). Angle, Root Gap, and Root Face are defined in the WPS per AWS D1.1.

def: The horizontal line in a weld symbol on which the geometric symbol is placed.
expand: Reference Line — the basis of every weld symbol per AWS A2.4/ISO 2553. Below the line = the arrow side, above = the other side. Attached to it: the weld type symbol, dimensions, a tail with notes (WPS, process), and flags (field weld, all-around).

def: The side the arrow in the reference line points to — a weld below the line = the arrow side.
expand: The arrow points at the joint itself. A symbol below the line = weld on the side the arrow touches; above the line = the other side. In ISO 2553 (Europe) a dashed line marks the other side. Confusing the sides = welding in the wrong place — an expensive mistake.

def: A circle with a number marking a part in an assembly drawing, matching a row in the BOM.
expand: Balloon — the numbered circle on an assembly drawing, pointing to the BOM row. Rules: numbering by assembly order or importance, uniform size, arranged in aligned rows/columns. One item = one balloon (repeats use quantity in the BOM).

def: A line connecting a balloon/note to the specific part in the drawing.
expand: Leader Line — the line from the balloon/note to the item, ending in an arrow (on an outline) or a dot (on a surface). Rules: one straight line without unnecessary bends, doesn't cross other balloons, not parallel to dimension lines, 30-60° angle from horizontal.

def: A bolt, nut, washer, or bearing — not drawn, ordered per a standard (ISO/DIN).
expand: Bolts, nuts, washers, bearings, pins, rings — not drawn! They appear only in the BOM with a full designation (DIN 912 M8×30-8.8 A2). The manufacturer buys, doesn't make it. Exception: if the standard part undergoes further processing — then it's drawn.

def: The dimension/requirement applies to all similar locations on the drawing.
expand: TYP: the requirement applies to all identical occurrences without repeating it — 'R2 TYP' = all similar radii are R2. The danger: ambiguity! ASME recommends explicitly stating quantity instead: '4X R2'. On a new drawing — better to count and specify.

def: A dimension for convenience only — not binding in manufacturing.
expand: A dimension in parentheses (50) = reference only: derived from other dimensions or repeated from another view. Not inspected and has no tolerance! Added for the reader's convenience — a chain sum, an overall dimension. Rejecting a part based on a reference dimension = an error.

def: This dimension doesn't match the drawing's graphic scale.
expand: An underline below a dimension = the dimension is correct but the drawing isn't: something was changed without redrawing (common in the paper era). Rare in modern CAD — but still appears. The rule is always: the number governs, not what looks right to the eye.

def: The general requirement applies unless stated otherwise in that area.
expand: UOS/UNLESS OTHERWISE SPECIFIED: opens the general notes — 'all radii R0.5 UOS', 'tolerance per ISO 2768-mK UOS'. The hierarchy: a local callout overrides a general note. Read the notes before flagging a missing dimension!

def: The highest permitted value.
expand: MAX: an upper limit only, no minimum — 'R0.5 MAX' (tool radius allowed up to half), 'Ra 3.2 MAX'. Zero is fine! Used when only one direction is harmful: a maximum chamfer for a seal, a maximum protrusion. The other side is completely free.

def: The lowest permitted value.
expand: MIN: a lower limit only — 'thread depth 12 MIN' (more is fine), 'C0.3 MIN' to break sharpness. Used when only a deficiency is harmful: thread depth, wall thickness, assembly overlap. An excess doesn't fail the part.

def: The hole/feature goes through the entire thickness of the part.
expand: THRU: the hole passes through all the material — '⌀8 THRU'. No THRU and no depth = dangerous ambiguity! In CNC drilling the difference: a cycle with a defined Z depth vs. a full pass + exit clearance. Always specify THRU or a depth.

def: A conical widening at a hole's mouth to fit a flat-head bolt.
expand: CSK/Countersink: a cone (∨ symbol) for a flush 90° (ISO) or 82° (inch — don't mix them!) bolt head. Spec: top ⌀ × angle. The bolt head must sit flush or slightly below the surface. A combined Drill-CSK tool saves an operation.

def: A cylindrical widening at a hole's mouth to fit a recessed bolt head.
expand: CBORE/Counterbore (⌴ symbol): a stepped bore that hides a socket head bolt. Spec: ⌀ × depth. Standard for M6: 6.6 drill, ⌀11×6.5 counterbore. A flat bottom is mandatory — a flat-bottom drill or an end mill, not a regular drill!

def: A common hardness metric for hardened metals, C scale (for hard materials).
expand: HRC for hardened steels: a diamond indenter + 150kgf load, a direct fast reading. The scales: HRC (hard), HRB (soft — 1/16-inch ball), HRA (carbide). Conversion rules of thumb: HRC 60 ≈ HV 700 ≈ HB 650. On a drawing: '58-62 HRC' after hardening — checked on every batch.

def: A heat treatment that diffuses nitrogen into a surface for high hardness without distortion.
expand: Nitriding: nitrogen diffusion at 500-550°C — below the transformation point = almost zero distortion (unlike carburizing!). Result: a 0.1-0.7mm layer at hardness up to HV 1100 + compressive stress (fatigue benefit!). Gas/Plasma/Salt. Ideal materials: 4140, 4340, Nitralloy steels with Al.

def: An electrolytic oxide coating for aluminum, protecting against corrosion.
expand: Anodizing: the part is the anode in an acid bath — an Al₂O₃ layer builds from the metal itself (half inward, half outward — remember this for tolerances!). Type II standard (5-25μm, colors), Type III hard (25-100μm, HV 400+). The layer is electrically insulating — mask for ground points.

def: A protective coating common in the defense/aerospace industry against corrosion.
expand: Cadmium: aerospace's historic coating — excellent galvanic protection, self-lubricating, uniform friction coefficient for bolts (precise torque), and galvanic compatibility with aluminum. The problem: toxic and carcinogenic — REACH/RoHS restrict it. Substitutes: Zn-Ni, Al-IVD. Still used in military applications per spec.

def: Heating and slow cooling to reduce hardness and internal stress, softening the material for machining.
expand: Annealing: heating above the critical temperature + slow cooling in the furnace — the structure returns soft and balanced. Purposes: softening for machining, erasing work hardening (between forming stages!), reducing stress. Full Anneal for steel: 30-50°C above A3, furnace cool. Result: coarse pearlite, minimal HB.

def: Heating to a high temperature and air cooling, for uniform grain structure in steel.
expand: Normalizing: like annealing but air-cooled — faster, finer grain, slightly higher hardness. Purpose: a uniform, predictable structure after forging/casting/welding (erases thermal history). Standard before hardening in structural steels. Normalized 1045: HB 170-210.

def: Rapid cooling (water/oil) from a hot state to achieve maximum hardness.
expand: Quenching: from 850°C, plunging into a cooling medium — the austenite becomes hard martensite. Speed depends on medium: water (aggressive — crack risk!), polymer, oil (the common one), air (air-hardening steels). The choice depends on Hardenability: 1045 needs water, 4140 needs oil, D2 needs air. Always Temper afterward!

def: Reheating after quenching, to reduce brittleness while retaining hardness.
expand: Tempering: reheating the brittle martensite (150-650°C) — trading hardness for toughness. Rule: higher temperature = softer and tougher. 4140: 200°C→HRC55 (brittle), 450°C→HRC40, 650°C→HRC28 (tough). Caution: 250-350°C = Temper Embrittlement in certain alloys!

def: Moderate heating to reduce internal stresses from machining/welding, without significant hardness change.
expand: Stress Relief: 550-650°C for steel (below the tempering temperature!), holding one hour per 25mm, slow cooling. When mandatory: after heavy welding, between roughing and finishing on precision parts (released stress = distortion!), after straightening. Aluminum: 200-300°C carefully (T6!).

def: Hardening only a thin outer layer, while keeping the core soft and tough.
expand: Case Hardening: a hard shell (HRC 58-64) over a tough core — a combination of wear resistance + impact resistance that no homogeneous material offers. Methods: carburizing (deep, for low-carbon steels), nitriding (precise), induction (local and fast), flame (huge parts).

def: A chemical treatment removing free iron from a stainless steel surface to improve corrosion resistance.
expand: Passivation for stainless: adds nothing — it cleans! Acid (nitric/citric) dissolves iron particles embedded during machining and thickens the natural oxide layer. Without it: mysterious 'rust' on new stainless. ASTM A967 / AMS 2700. Mandatory after every machining operation.

def: A thin, black chemical coating for light corrosion protection and reduced reflection.
expand: Black Oxide: a chemical conversion (magnetite Fe₃O₄) micron thick — doesn't change dimensions at all! Light protection only (oil/wax needed over it), a uniform black look, anti-reflective. Uses: hand tools, bolts, firearm parts, jigs. The cheapest coating.

def: A zinc coating (hot-dip or electroplated) protecting steel from corrosion.
expand: Galvanizing: zinc sacrifices itself galvanically — it corrodes instead of the steel even at a scratch! Hot-dip (50-100μm, coarse, for outdoor structures) vs. electroplated (5-25μm, fine + colored passivation, for bolts and sheet). Zn-Ni (12-15% Ni) = 3x the resistance, the new standard in automotive and aerospace.

def: A polymer powder coating cured in an oven, more durable and uniform than liquid paint.
expand: Powder Coat: electrostatic powder + a 180°C oven = a 60-120μm layer 3x tougher than wet paint, with no drips and no solvents. UV resistance: polyester (outdoor), epoxy (chemical, indoor). Limitations: the part must fit in the oven, sharp edges get less coating (Faraday cage effect), local repair is hard.

def: A location control — defines that a feature's center lies exactly on a symmetry plane/axis relative to a Datum.
expand: Requires the midpoints of a feature (like a slot) to be symmetric about a Datum plane. Like concentricity — hard to measure and removed in ASME 2018. Modern replacement: Position on the median plane.

def: Like profile of a line but in 3D — defines a tolerance on the shape of an entire surface.
expand: The king of modern tolerances — a 3D zone around a theoretical CAD surface. Can control form, orientation, and location in a single tolerance. The basis for MBD (Model-Based Definition) drawings where the CAD is the governing document.

def: The combined extreme boundary (size + location/form) a feature can reach while meeting all requirements.
expand: The extreme combined boundary: for a hole, VC = MMC − geometric tolerance; for a shaft, VC = MMC + tolerance. This is the size a functional Gauge is built to, and the basis for calculating guaranteed assembly between parts.

def: The default (Rule #1): a feature's size also governs its form — it can't exceed an envelope at MMC size.
expand: ASME's Rule #1: a Feature of Size at MMC must have perfect form — size also governs form. A ⌀20h7 shaft measured at 20.0 must be perfectly straight. In ISO it's the opposite (independence) — there you must mark Ⓔ to invoke the envelope.

def: A 3D coordinate system built from 3 Datums (primary/secondary/tertiary) to fully constrain the part for measurement.
expand: DRF: an axis system from three Datums in order of precedence: primary (3 contact points = a plane), secondary (2 points = a line), tertiary (1 point). Mimics how the part sits in the assembly or a Fixture. The order of the Datums changes the measurement result!

def: A specific point/line/area on a rough surface (like a casting) used as a Datum, when a whole surface can't be used.
expand: Datum Target: defined points/lines/areas (A1, A2, A3) on an unmachined surface — a casting, forging, sheet. Allows consistent referencing when the whole surface is too rough. The Fixture is built to touch exactly these points.

def: A tolerance extending in only one direction from the nominal dimension (e.g. +0.2/0).
expand: The entire tolerance goes one direction: 50 +0.2/0, or a Unequally Disposed profile. Useful when deviation is allowed only in a safe direction — e.g. only added material on a sealing surface, or only removal on a fit.

def: A tolerance extending in both directions from the nominal dimension (±0.1).
expand: The tolerance is split evenly around the nominal (±0.1). The default on most drawings and the easiest to manufacture to — the process's statistical center is aimed at the nominal.

def: The difference between the allowed upper limit and the nominal dimension.
expand: ES (hole) / es (shaft) — the distance from the zero line to the upper limit. For ⌀50 +0.03/+0.01: ES=+30μm. In the ISO system deviations are defined in tables by the position letter and the IT grade.

def: The difference between the allowed lower limit and the nominal dimension.
expand: EI (hole) / ei (shaft) — the distance from the zero line to the lower limit. For an H hole: EI=0 always (the nominal is the lower limit). For an h shaft: es=0 (the nominal is the upper limit).

def: The reference line in the ISO system from which upper/lower deviations are measured (= the nominal dimension).
expand: The line representing the nominal dimension in fit diagrams — all deviations are measured from it. The tolerance zone's position relative to the zero line is set by the letter (A-ZC for holes, a-zc for shafts).

def: The most common fit system — the hole is always H (fixed minimum size), and the shaft varies for the desired fit.
expand: Hole Basis: the hole is always H (lower deviation 0) and the fit is set by choosing the shaft. Common because holes are made with fixed tools (drill, Reamer) and it's easier to change a shaft's size while turning.

def: An alternative system — the shaft is fixed (h), and the hole varies. Less common.
expand: Shaft Basis: the shaft is fixed h and the hole varies. Used when the shaft is a catalog item (a chrome-plated h6 shaft, a ground rod) and the housings are made around it. Common in pneumatic systems and standard shafts.

def: The ability to swap a part for an identical one from the same production line without manual fitting — the whole point of the tolerance system.
expand: The principle behind all of tolerancing theory: any part from a batch fits any mating part without manual fitting. Enables mass production, spare parts, and field repair. First achieved in musket manufacturing in France (1785) and matured on Ford's production line.

def: A feature (hole, shaft, slot) for which a single size can be measured — unlike a single flat surface.
expand: FOS: a feature with a size measurable between two opposing points — a hole, shaft, slot, tab. Only an FOS is subject to: MMC/LMC, bonus, the envelope principle. A single surface isn't an FOS and therefore can't take ⓜ.

def: Long-range wavy deviations on a surface, coarser than roughness — caused by machine vibration or distortion.
expand: The mid-frequency deviations — between roughness (dense) and form error (long). Sources: machine vibration (chatter), clamping distortion, spindle bearing wear. Filtered out of Ra by the Cutoff! A surface can be 'smooth' by Ra yet wavy to the touch — check Wt when it matters.

def: A fixed length segment over which Ra is measured, to filter long waves (waviness) out of the calculation.
expand: Sampling Length (lr): the single segment over which a parameter is calculated — equal to the Cutoff λc. The full measurement: 5 such segments (Evaluation Length ln=5×lr), averaged. Default: lr=0.8mm for Ra 0.1-2μm. Deviating from this must be noted on the drawing.

def: A wavelength filter separating roughness from waviness in surface measurement.
expand: λc (Cutoff): the filter that separates roughness from waviness — waves longer than it 'don't count' in Ra. Changing the Cutoff changes the result! 0.25mm for fine finishes, 0.8mm standard, 2.5mm for coarse. Measurements being compared must use the same λc — check the instrument settings.

def: The umbrella term: roughness + waviness + lay + local defects.
expand: Surface Texture: the whole per ISO 21920/ASME B46.1 — roughness (high frequency) + waviness (mid) + Lay (directionality). Above all of it: form error (belongs to GD&T). Each layer is measured and controlled separately since each has a different cause and fix.

def: The default — tightens with a clockwise rotation.
expand: RH — the worldwide default ('righty-tighty'). The thread rises up-to-the-left when viewed from the side. Not stated on drawings. Every thread is right-hand unless noted otherwise.

def: Tightens counter-clockwise, always stated explicitly on the drawing.
expand: LH — always noted: M10×1.5-LH. Uses: places where the working rotation would loosen a right-hand thread — a bicycle's left pedal, flammable gas cylinders (prevents wrong hookup!), turnbuckles (RH+LH combined), rotating shafts.

def: The precision/tolerance level of a thread, e.g. 6g (shaft) or 6H (hole) in the ISO system.
expand: Class: lowercase letter=bolt (g,h), uppercase=nut (H,G). The number=tolerance width: 6=standard, 4=precise, 8=coarse. Common combo 6H/6g. Aerospace: inch 3A/2B. Practical difference: 4h6h for precise fits, 6g for everything else.

def: The distance a nut advances in one full turn. On a single-start thread, Lead=Pitch.
expand: Lead — the axial advance per one turn. On a standard thread Lead=Pitch; on a multi-start thread Lead=Pitch×number of starts. A 2-start lead screw with P=2: advances 4mm per turn — double the speed with the same thread strength.

def: How many parallel thread helixes run along the bolt — a multi-start bolt advances faster per turn.
expand: Multi-Start: how many parallel helixes. Advantage: fast advance (large Lead) with a fine, strong thread. Uses: bottle caps (a quarter turn!), fast lead screws, quick-connect fittings. Identifying it: look at the thread's end and count how many starts you see.

def: An American trapezoidal thread profile (29°), for power transmission and linear motion.
expand: ACME — the American standard for lead screws: a 29° trapezoidal profile, much stronger than a triangular thread for transmitting force. General Purpose and Stub (low). Common: clamp screws, American lathes, gates. The metric equivalent: 30° Trapezoidal.

def: A screw that creates its own internal thread while being driven into a plain hole.
expand: Self-Drilling (TEK): a true drill tip + a cutting thread — drills and threads in one action. Tip numbers #1-#5 by sheet thickness (up to ~12mm steel). Distinct from Self-Tapping which requires a pre-drilled hole. Dominant in light construction and roofing.

def: A support pass on the side opposite the main weld, before or after welding the main groove.
expand: Back/Backing Weld: a pass on the root side. Back Weld = after the main pass (after Back Gouging), Backing Weld = before it as support. Ensures full fusion at the root in CJP. Symbol: a half-circle on the opposite side of the weld symbol.

def: A weld through a round hole in a top plate into a bottom plate, filling the whole hole.
expand: Plug Weld: a hole in the top plate is filled with weld that joins it to the bottom plate. A substitute for rivets or spot welding when there's no access. Parameters: hole diameter (min. t+8mm), taper angle, fill depth. Common in vehicle frames and structural repairs.

def: Like plug welding but through an elongated slot instead of a round hole.
expand: Slot Weld: like a Plug but an elongated slot — a larger joint area for higher shear transfer. Used in long overlaps where a row of plugs isn't enough. Dimensions: width, length, spacing (Pitch) between slots.

def: A long continuous seam, common in resistance (wheel) welding for sheet metal.
expand: Seam Weld: copper wheels press and pass current — a series of overlapping spots forming a sealed seam. Used for fuel tanks, cans, thin tubing. Parameters: current, clamping force, roll speed. Sealed against liquids and gases.

def: The depth to which fusion of the base metal is reached — insufficient penetration weakens the joint.
expand: Penetration: the depth of fusion into the base metal. Incomplete Penetration = a severe defect that concentrates stress at the root — a source of fatigue cracks. Improves with: higher current, lower speed, correct edge prep, proper Root Gap. Checked by RT/UT.

def: The deepest point in the weld, closest to the side opposite the weld.
expand: Root: the most critical area — most failures start there. Typical defects: lack of fusion, Lack of Penetration, cracks. The Root Pass is the most challenging — usually TIG even when the fill is MIG/SMAW. Gas purging on stainless is mandatory.

def: The point where the weld face meets the base metal — a spot sensitive to cracks.
expand: Toe: the meeting point between the weld face and the base metal — a geometric stress concentration and fatigue crack source #1. Improving resistance: a smooth concave weld, TIG Dressing (remelting the toe), or Peening. Undercut at the toe = a defect.

def: The shortest distance from the weld root to its face — determines the actual fillet weld's strength.
expand: Throat: the dimension that determines Fillet strength — the shortest distance from the root to the weld face. Effective throat a = 0.707×z (leg). Strength calc: τ = F/(a×L). A convex weld doesn't add effective throat — just wasted material.

def: A weld performed at the final assembly site, not in the shop — marked with a special flag on the symbol.
expand: Two different symbols: a circle at the corner of the reference line = Weld All Around; a flag = Field Weld performed on site. Field welding = harsher conditions, usually SMAW/FCAW, requires a welder certified for the positions.

def: A formal document recording and approving a change to a drawing/product after release to production.
expand: ECO: the document that puts a change into effect after ECR approval. Contains: what's changing (drawings+new Rev), why, Effectivity (from which serial number/date), and inventory disposition: Use-As-Is / Rework / Scrap. Without a closed ECO, production continues on the old version.

def: A notice distributing an approved change to all relevant parties (production, purchasing, quality).
expand: ECN: the official distribution of an approved change to everyone involved — production, purchasing, quality, suppliers. Ensures everyone works from the same version. In organizations with PLM the notice is automatic + old versions are blocked from download.

def: The actual final state of the product/drawing, including field changes not documented in advance.
expand: As-Built: documentation of what was actually built — including approved deviations, material substitutions, and repairs. Critical for: project handover, future maintenance, and failure investigations. The difference from As-Designed can be significant!

def: A temporary manual mark of a change on a drawing copy, before an official system update.
expand: Redline: a manual mark on a drawing copy in the field/production — a temporary fix until an official update. Valid only with: an authorized signature + date + a following open ECO. A Redline living for months is a ticking bomb of conflicting versions.

def: A group of parts assembled together as an intermediate unit, before assembly into the final assembly.
expand: Sub-Assembly: an intermediate unit with its own part number and drawing — assembled and inspected separately, then entered as one item in the parent BOM. Advantages: parallel assembly, early testing, spare parts at the assembly level. Tree depth = a logistics decision.

def: A note indicating a part is made from another existing part number (cut/machined) rather than direct raw material.
expand: Made From: the part starts from an existing item — 'Made From P/N 12345' (shared stock, a purchased assembly that undergoes machining). The BOM points to the source part number + a drawing of the further processing. Saves a separate raw-material drawing and links traceability.

def: A report/field showing which assemblies a given part appears in — important for change impact analysis.
expand: Where-Used: the reverse query to the BOM — which parent assemblies contain this part? Critical before any change: an ECO on a 'simple' bolt that appears in 40 assemblies = 40 impact checks. PDM/ERP give it at a click; without them — a nightmare.

def: A comprehensive, documented inspection of the first part off a new production run, against every drawing requirement.
expand: FAI: full verification of the first part off the line — every dimension, note, material, and process documented against the drawing. Purpose: catch programming/setup errors before the batch runs. Required again after: a design change, new tooling, a different machine, or a two-year break (AS9102).

def: A machine that maps points in space by contact/optical means, for measuring GD&T and complex dimensions at high accuracy.
expand: CMM: a probe (Renishaw) touching points in space at 1-3μm accuracy — the only tool for true GD&T measurement (Position, Profile, Datum systems). Types: Bridge (the lab standard), Portable Arm (the shop floor), Vision/Laser (contactless). Requires: a stable 20°C, a measurement program, and a skilled operator.

def: A quick inspection tool: one side must enter/pass (Go), the other side must not (No-Go) — with no numeric reading.
expand: Go/NoGo: the 'Go' side must enter (checks MMC), the 'No-Go' side must not (checks LMC). No numeric value — just pass/fail, but 20x faster than measurement and free of operator error. Thread Gauge, Plug Gauge, Ring Gauge — the backbone of serial production control.

def: A document from the manufacturer certifying that the product meets the relevant drawing/standard requirements.
expand: CoC: the manufacturer's declaration that the product meets every order requirement — with full traceability: material Lot/Heat numbers, special-process certificates (coating, heat treat), and dates. Without a valid CoC the shipment isn't accepted in aerospace and defense. Retention: 7-10 years.

def: Periodic checking and adjustment of a measuring tool against a reference standard, to ensure accuracy.
expand: Calibration: comparing the instrument to a standard traceable to a national standard, with a certificate. Frequency: micrometer/caliper yearly, Gauge Blocks 2-3 years, depending on use. A valid calibration sticker = a condition for use. A dropped instrument = immediate recalibration, no matter what the sticker says.

def: A statistical measure showing whether a production process can consistently meet the required tolerance.
expand: The bigger picture: Cp/Cpk (short-term, process variation only) vs. Pp/Ppk (actual performance including all noise). A significantly lower Ppk than Cpk = there are special causes between samples (shifts? material lots?). Typical automotive requirement: Ppk≥1.67 at initial approval, Cpk≥1.33 ongoing.

def: A small circular flattening around a hole, creating a flat seat for a nut/bolt head.
expand: Spotface (⌴ symbol with SF): minimal facing around a hole — just so the bolt head/washer sits square on a rough casting/forging. Depth: minimal for cleanup (0.5-2mm), versus a Counterbore which hides a whole head.

def: Marks the depth of a hole/slot dimension.
expand: ↧ symbol (depth arrow): '⌀10 ↧25' = a 10 drill at 25 depth. In drilling — the depth to the full diameter (not including the 118° drill point!). Threading: the full thread depth is separate from the drilled hole depth (a difference of ~3-4 pitches for the tap).

def: A number of features (holes) distributed at equal distances from each other, without stating each location separately.
expand: EQL SP / Equally Spaced: '6X ⌀8 EQL SP on a PCD 100' = six holes every 60°. Position ensures the angular accuracy. Unequal spacing requires explicit angles + orientation locking (Clocking) to a Datum.

def: Indicates how many times the same requirement repeats, e.g. "4 PLCS".
expand: PLACES/PL or X: '4X ⌀6' = four identical holes, the dimension appears once. Correct counting is critical — the quote is fast and inspection counts! Modern convention: X attached to the number (4X), no space.

def: The inner diameter of a hollow part, like a pipe.
expand: ID: in commercial piping specified by OD×Wall — 'pipe 60.3×3.9' → ID=52.5. A surprise in inch piping: Pipe 2" Sch40 = OD 60.3 (not 50.8!), the '2 inch' is a historical nominal. Always check the Schedule table.

def: The outer diameter of a part, like a pipe or cylinder.
expand: OD: the dimension gripped in the chuck and measured with a caliper. In piping — the constant: every Schedule of a 2" Pipe shares an OD of 60.3, only the wall changes inward. In raw stock selection: stock OD = final dimension + machining allowance.

def: The difference between OD and ID divided by 2, in a hollow part.
expand: Wall = (OD−ID)/2. Determines: pressure rating (Barlow: P=2×S×t/OD), weight, and stiffness. Pipe tolerance: ±10-12.5% — pressure design calculates with the minimum! A 'thin-wall' pipe is a machining chucking challenge (crushing).

def: The quantity isn't fixed in advance and is determined by actual need (e.g. paint coats).
expand: AR/As Required: a non-fixed quantity in the BOM — oils, adhesives, shims for alignment, safety wire. The quantitative guidance moves to the work instruction. In purchasing: AR items are managed as consumable stock, not per assembly order.

def: Every surface of the part is machined/finished, without exception.
expand: FAO/Finish All Over: every face of the part is machined — no surface remains raw stock. Economic meaning: the raw stock needs excess in every direction + full machining time. The finish symbol at the drawing corner with a general Ra defines the level.

def: Steel that has been rolled at room temperature — better dimensional accuracy and surface finish than hot rolling.
expand: Cold Rolled/Drawn: cold drawing = a tight tolerance (h9-h11), a clean surface, and sharp corners — sometimes with no machining at all! The price: residual stresses that release with asymmetric machining (banana bending on a long slot!). 1018 CD, 12L14 — the screw-machine standard.

def: Steel that has been rolled at high temperature — cheaper, coarser tolerance.
expand: Hot Rolled: rolled hot = cheap, black Mill Scale, a wide tolerance, and rounded corners. The choice for structures, welding, and parts machined all around anyway. The scale wears out tools — the first cut goes deep beneath it!

def: See "Center Line" — a common English abbreviation for the same concept.
expand: CL (Center Line, ℄ symbol): a universal abbreviation on drawings and notes — 'distance between ℄ bores', '℄ axis'. Also: machine center, track center. Two crossing center lines define an exact center point.

def: A CAD file in the software's original format (SLDPRT, CATPart) — retains parameters and full editability.
expand: Native: the full format of the source software (SLDPRT, CATPART, PRT) — including the feature tree, parameters, design intent. Mandatory for further development. The problem: version and vendor lock-in. Always keep: native for editing + STEP for archiving and exchange.

def: A universal geometry format (STEP, IGES) for transfer between different CAD programs, without a parameter tree.
expand: Neutral: STEP (the new AP242 — including PMI!), IGES (older, problematic), Parasolid/X_T. 'Dead' geometry — no tree. Uses: transfer to suppliers, CAM, long-term archiving. Check after conversion: missing surfaces, a closed Solid.

def: A modern approach where all manufacturing information (PMI) lives inside the 3D CAD model, instead of a separate 2D drawing.
expand: MBD: the 3D model is the governing document — GD&T, tolerances, and notes (PMI) live on the geometry. No 2D drawing! Advantage: CMM and CAM read directly, zero interpretation. Standards: ASME Y14.41, ISO 16792. Aerospace is leading the transition.

def: All the non-geometric data (dimensions, GD&T, material, notes) embedded in the CAD model in MBD.
expand: PMI: everything that isn't geometry — dimensions, GD&T, finish, notes, material — attached to the 3D model. Two types: graphic (for viewing) and semantic (machine-readable — a CMM builds an automatic measurement program!). The heart of MBD and Industry 4.0.

def: A geometric characteristic — defines how much an axis/line deviates from a straight line. FCF: ⏤. No Datum.
expand: Checks how much a line on a surface or an axis deviates from a perfect straight line. Common application: long axles (preventing bowing), rails. When applied to an axis with ⌀ — controls the bending of the whole axis and can override the envelope principle.

def: A geometric characteristic — deviation of a surface from an ideal plane. FCF: □. No Datum.
expand: All points on the surface must fall between two parallel planes at the tolerance distance apart. No Datum — measured relative to itself. Critical for sealing surfaces (gaskets), mounting bases, and reference surfaces. Measurement: CMM or a surface plate + indicator.

def: A geometric characteristic — deviation of a round cross-section from a perfect circle. FCF: ○. No Datum.
expand: Each individual cross-section must fall between two concentric circles at the tolerance distance apart. Typical errors: an oval (2-jaw chuck grip), a triangle (lobing from a 3-jaw), chatter. True measurement: a roundness tester (Talyrond), not a micrometer!

def: A geometric characteristic — combines circularity+straightness+parallelism over a cylinder. FCF: ⌭. No Datum.
expand: The strictest combination: circularity + straightness + uniform diameter along the entire cylinder simultaneously. The most expensive tolerance to manufacture — requires quality grinding. Use only when truly needed (hydraulic pistons, precision shafts).

def: An orientation control — the surface/axis is parallel to a Datum within a zone. Datum mandatory.
expand: The surface/axis must fall between two planes parallel to the Datum. Common on surfaces machined from both sides (plates, blocks). Note: parallelism also controls the flatness of that same surface (flatness can't exceed the parallelism).

def: An orientation control — perpendicular to a Datum at 90°. Datum mandatory. FCF: ⊥.
expand: Deviation from exact 90° relative to a Datum, measured as a distance between two planes (not as an angle!). Critical for bearing shoulders (shaft runout), machine columns, and vertical mounting surfaces.

def: An orientation control — a defined angle (not 0° or 90°) from a Datum. Datum mandatory.
expand: Controls any angle that isn't 0° or 90° — e.g. a surface at 30°. The angle itself is marked as a basic dimension (in a box), and the tolerance is a zone thickness between two planes. It is not a tolerance on the angle in degrees!

def: A location control — the most important! Defines the location of a point/axis/surface. ⌀ = a cylindrical zone. Datum mandatory.
expand: The workhorse of GD&T — about 70% of applications. Defines a cylindrical tolerance zone (⌀) around the exact theoretical location. Advantage over ±: a round zone is 57% larger than an equivalent square, and it supports MMC bonus. Requires basic dimensions + Datums.

def: The location of an axis/center relative to a Datum. Removed in ASME 2018 → Position used instead.
expand: Requires the midpoints of the cross-section to fall within a zone around the Datum axis. Very difficult to measure (midpoints, not surface points!) and was therefore removed in ASME Y14.5-2018. Replaced by Position or Runout, which give the same functional control.

def: The location of a median plane relative to a Datum. Removed in ASME 2018 → Position used instead.
expand: Removed in ASME Y14.5-2018 along with concentricity. The problem: it required measuring midpoints — slow and ambiguous. New drawings use Position on a median plane, giving the same function with simple measurement.

def: A profile control — deviation of a 2D line from a theoretical profile. With/without a Datum.
expand: A 2D tolerance zone around a defined theoretical profile (usually from CAD). Each cross-section is checked separately. Used for aerodynamic profiles, sealing strips, and templates. With a Datum = also location; without = shape only.

def: A profile control — deviation of a 3D surface from a theoretical profile. More common than line profile.
expand: The king of modern tolerances — a 3D zone around a theoretical CAD surface. Can control form, orientation, and location in a single tolerance. The basis for MBD (Model-Based Definition) drawings where the CAD is the governing document.

def: Circular runout — a DTI on a single cross-section during a full rotation. Datum mandatory (an axis).
expand: Circular Runout: an indicator (DTI) held against one cross-section during a full rotation about the Datum axis — the total reading (TIR) must be within tolerance. Combines circularity + concentricity in one simple check. The common lathe test.

def: A DTI along the entire length of the part during a full rotation. Stricter than Circular Runout.
expand: Total Runout: the indicator moves along the entire surface during rotation — the whole surface within one tolerance. Adds straightness and taper control on top of Circular Runout. Stricter and more expensive — for precision shafts and rotating sealing surfaces.

def: ⓜ = for holes: smallest diameter. For a shaft: largest diameter. Enables bonus tolerance.
expand: The worst case for assembly: the minimum hole meets the maximum shaft. Design for guaranteed assembly is always done at MMC. The ⓜ symbol in the FCF grants bonus tolerance and allows inspection with a functional Go/NoGo Gauge.

def: ⓛ = for holes: largest diameter. For a shaft: smallest diameter.
expand: The condition with the least material. Critical when minimum wall thickness matters: a hole near an edge, a thin ring. The ⓛ symbol grants a bonus as the feature moves away from LMC. Common in castings covered by machining.

def: ⓢ = the ASME default. GD&T applies at any size. No bonus tolerance.
expand: The default in ASME since 1994 — no symbol needed. The geometric tolerance is fixed at any actual size. Required when function is sensitive to the location itself and not just assembly: dynamic balance, aiming, flow.

def: The extreme boundary: hole VC = MMC − GD&T. Shaft VC = MMC + GD&T.
expand: The boundary the mating part must clear: hole VC = ⌀MMC − Position (the largest pin that always fits). A functional Gauge is made exactly to the VC size. Fixture and Tooling calculations are based on it.

def: A theoretical surface/point/axis used as a reference for measuring GD&T. A=primary (3 points), B=secondary (2), C=tertiary (1).
expand: The theoretical Datum is perfect; the Datum Feature is the actual (imperfect) surface it's derived from. The order of precedence (A primary, B secondary, C tertiary) determines the setup: A touches 3 points, B touches 2, C touches 1.

def: The rectangular frame on a drawing: [symbol|value|Datum]. The heart of GD&T.
expand: Read left to right: what's checked (symbol) → how much is allowed (value+modifier) → relative to what (Datums in order). Example: |⊕|⌀0.2ⓜ|A|B|C| = Position within a ⌀0.2 zone with bonus, relative to the A-B-C system.

def: The perfect theoretical location of a feature. Position measures deviation from it.
expand: The exact theoretical point/axis defined by basic dimensions. Actual position deviation = 2×√(Δx²+Δy²) — doubled because the tolerance is the zone's diameter. A formula every CMM inspector must know.

def: Extra tolerance when a feature is off MMC. Bonus = |actual size − MMC|. Triggered by ⓜ.
expand: Works only with ⓜ or ⓛ on a Feature of Size. The logic: a hole larger than MMC leaves more clearance for the pin — that can be used as position deviation. Reduces false rejections and cuts production cost without hurting assembly.

def: ISO 286. IT1-IT18. IT7=common (30μm at ⌀50mm). Higher number = wider tolerance = lower precision.
expand: The tolerance grows with diameter at the same grade: IT7 = 15μm at ⌀10 but 30μm at ⌀80. Grade selection by process: turning IT9-11, grinding IT5-7, lapping IT3-5. Each grade step down ≈ doubling the cost.

def: Always a gap between shaft and hole. H7/f6, H7/g6, H7/h6. Assembles by hand.
expand: A guaranteed gap in every allowed combination. H7/f6 = free sliding with lubrication (plain bearings), H7/g6 = precise sliding (guides), H7/h6 = close sliding (precise location without load). Assembly is always by hand.

def: May be a gap or overlap. H7/js6, H7/k6, H7/m6. Assembled with a light mallet.
expand: Depends on actual dimensions — may result in a tiny gap or slight overlap. H7/k6 and H7/m6 are the common ones. Ideal for precise location with disassembly possible: gears, pulleys, couplings. Assembled with a plastic mallet.

def: Always an overlap — the shaft is larger than the hole. H7/p6, H7/s6. Requires a press/heat.
expand: A guaranteed overlap — the shaft is always bigger than the hole. H7/p6 = light press (hand press), H7/s6 = medium press (hydraulic press), H7/u6 = heavy press (heating/cooling). Transmits torque without a key. Disassembly is usually destructive.

def: A common clearance fit. Clearance +25 to +75μm (⌀50mm). A shaft in a bush.
expand: The common engineering fit for plain bearings and bushes: a guaranteed clearance that allows an oil film. At ⌀50: clearance 25-89μm. The shaft 'floats' on a hydrodynamic film while rotating.

def: A light-press transition. A rubber mallet. Gears, pulleys, chains.
expand: At ⌀50: from a 18μm clearance to a 21μm overlap. Precise location that can be disassembled — a gear on a shaft with a key (the key transmits torque, the fit locates). Assembled with a plastic mallet or a light press.

def: A light press. Pressed/heated. Bearings, fixed bushes.
expand: A guaranteed overlap of 1-42μm at ⌀50. Force transmission by friction alone for light loads; for heavy loads combined with a key. Assembly: a bench press or heating the ring to 80-120°C. Disassembly can damage the surfaces.

def: m=±0.1-0.5mm, c=±0.2-1.0mm. K=geometric. In the title block: ISO 2768-mK.
expand: Applies to every dimension without an explicit tolerance. Part 1 (dimensions): f/m/c/v — m is common. Part 2 (geometry): H/K/L. A typical title-block note: ISO 2768-mK. Saves hundreds of tolerance callouts on a drawing.

def: ISO 8015. Size and geometry are independent. The ISO default. ASME: the Envelope Principle.
expand: ISO 8015: size governs only size, form is checked separately. A shaft at valid size can still be bowed! To get combined control in ISO you must mark Ⓔ (Envelope). Opposite of ASME, where the envelope is the default.

def: ASME Rule #1. A sized feature must stay within an envelope at MMC. Doesn't apply in ISO without ⓔ.
expand: Rule #1 in ASME Y14.5: the MMC boundary is a perfect envelope the part can't exceed. Practical meaning: a full-length Go-Gauge checks both size and form at once. Doesn't apply between different features — only within the feature itself.

def: The most common parameter. Average of absolute deviations. 1μm=39.37μin.
expand: The universal metric, but know its limits: blind to profile shape (sharp peaks vs. rounded = same Ra), to directionality, and to isolated defects. Complements: Rz for defects, Rsk for shape (negative=a load-bearing plateau), Rmr for contact percentage. Parameter choice = per function.

def: Average of 5 high peaks + 5 deep valleys. Rz ≈ 4×Ra (a rough approximation only!).
expand: The modern (ISO) definition: the average of Rz1-Rz5 from five sampling segments, each = max peak + max valley in that segment. Key uses: sealing specs (O-Ring: Rz<4×squeeze), painting (adhesion), and electrical contact.

def: Root mean square. Rq ≈ 1.11×Ra. Sensitive to extreme peaks.
expand: The root mean square — penalizes large deviations more than Ra (due to squaring). The standard in optics and thin coatings (light scattering ∝ Rq²). In electronics: substrate roughness for plating. Approximate conversion: Rq ≈ 1.11×Ra for a random profile.

def: The distance between the highest peak and the deepest valley. Rt ≈ 6-8×Ra.
expand: The highest peak to the deepest valley over the whole evaluation length (not an average!) — the strictest parameter. A single scratch spikes Rt. Uses: critical static sealing surfaces, thin coatings (Rt > coating thickness = breakthrough!).

def: The marking direction: = parallel · ⊥ perpendicular · × crossed · M multi-directional · C circular · R radial.
expand: In the finish symbol: the Lay mark sits to the left of the hook. Meanings: = parallel to the line of sight, ⊥ perpendicular, X crossed (honing!), M multi-directional (lapping/EDM), C concentric (facing), R radial. Seal design: needs C or circumferential — never axial.

def: N1-N12. N7=Ra 1.6μm (default). N1=Ra 0.025μm (mirror). Retired from ISO 21920.
expand: The full conversion table: N1=0.025, N2=0.05, N3=0.1, N4=0.2, N5=0.4, N6=0.8, N7=1.6, N8=3.2, N9=6.3, N10=12.5, N11=25, N12=50 μm Ra. Cost rule: each grade down ≈ +50-100% machining cost. Don't ask for N5 where N8 is enough.

def: Replaced ISO 1302 in 2022. P,R,W parameters instead of N-Grade.
expand: The 2022 revolution: three profiles — P (primary), R (roughness), W (waviness), with unified parameters and a new drawing symbol. The practical change: sharper defined defaults (Setting Class). New aerospace drawings already require it — learn the notation.

def: ✓=machining mandatory · ⊙=no machining. Position: right=Ra · below=method · left=wavelength.
expand: Symbol anatomy: a basic checkmark = some machining; with a top horizontal bar = material removal mandatory; with a circle = removal prohibited (casting/rolling as-is). Values: Ra to the right of the hook, process above the bar, Lay and direction to the left. A symbol at the drawing corner = applies to everything.

def: Vc [m/min] = π×D×n/1000. Relative speed between tool and material. Higher Vc = more tool wear.
expand: Vc is the parameter with the biggest effect on tool life (Taylor's equation). Typical carbide values: steel 150-250, stainless 100-180, aluminum 300-800, titanium 40-60 m/min. Too low Vc = BUE; too high = rapid tool wear.

def: fz [mm/tooth]. The amount of material one tooth removes per revolution. Ranges 0.01-0.5mm.
expand: fz determines the chip thickness per tooth. Vf = fz×z×n. Too low = rubbing that heats and wears; too high = tooth breakage. Typical range: 0.05-0.15mm for finish milling, 0.1-0.3mm for roughing. With Chip Thinning at a small ae you can increase fz.

def: MRR = ae×ap×Vf [mm³/min]. ae=width, ap=depth, Vf=table speed.
expand: MRR is the central productivity metric. In milling: ae×ap×Vf/1000 [cm³/min]. In turning: Vc×fn×ap. Required power: P[kW] = MRR×kc/60000 (kc=specific cutting force). Modern strategies (Trochoidal, HSM) maximize MRR without overloading the tool.

def: Material particles that accumulate on the tool edge. Cause poor finish and wear. Reactive at low temperature.
expand: BUE: machined material sticks to the tool edge under pressure and heat, grows and periodically sheds — ruins the finish and shifts dimensions. Typical for sticky materials (Al, stainless, soft steel) at low Vc. Fix: raise Vc above the BUE zone, a slick coating (DLC for Al), good cooling, a sharp tool.

def: Tool vibration causing a wavy finish and noise. Fix: increase rigidity, decrease ap, change RPM.
expand: Regenerative chatter: waviness from the previous pass amplifies itself. Detection: harsh noise + wave marks. Fixes in order: change RPM (Stability Lobes), shorten overhang, decrease ap, a Variable Helix tool, better clamping. A Tap Test identifies the natural frequency.

def: ap [mm]. Milling depth along the tool axis. Higher ap = more load.
expand: ap: how deep the tool cuts in Z. In modern roughing (HEM/Trochoidal): a large ap (1-3×D) with a small ae — uses the whole flute length and spreads wear. In finishing: a small ap 0.2-0.5mm. Limits: flute length, rigidity, power.

def: ae [mm]. Milling width. ae=D = full slotting. ae=0.1D = finishing.
expand: ae: the radial engagement width. ae=D (Slotting) = maximum loading and poor cooling. ae<0.5D triggers Chip Thinning — the chip is thinner than fz and speed can be raised. Trochoidal: ae=5-10%D only. ae directly affects the engagement angle and heat.

def: Machining on a lathe. The part rotates, the tool feeds. For round/axial parts.
expand: The part rotates (the spindle provides Vc), the tool moves in feed. Operations: OD/ID turning (Boring), facing, grooving, threading, parting. Modern lathes with Live Tooling and a Y-axis also perform milling.

def: Machining on a machining center. The tool rotates, the part feeds. For planar and complex parts.
expand: The tool rotates and the part (or the tool) moves in 3-5 axes. Face Milling for surfaces, End Milling for pockets and walls, Ball Mill for 3D surfaces. Parameters: Vc, fz, ap, ae. Machining centers: VMC (vertical, common), HMC (horizontal, for runs), 5-Axis (complex geometry).

def: Making holes. Vc = π×D×n/1000. Drill size = D−P (metric).
expand: The fastest tool for removing material in holes. Rules: L/D≤4 standard drilling, 4-10 Peck Drilling, above 10 Gun Drill. A Spot Drill before the drill for precise location. A carbide drill with internal coolant = 3-5x the speed of HSS. A 135° point with a Split Point doesn't need a spot.

def: The tool rotates in the same direction as the part's feed. Better finish. Used on CNC.
expand: The tooth enters at full chip thickness and exits at zero — less friction and heat, a better finish, the force presses the part onto the table. Mandatory on CNC. The danger on old machines: Backlash in the screws pulls the part. Conventional only for: old manual machines, a tough casting skin.

def: The tool rotates against the feed direction. For old CNC dust. Less good finish.
expand: The tooth enters at zero and grows to full thickness — rubs before it cuts, heats and work-hardens the surface. Justified use: machines with Backlash, first entry into a hard casting/forging skin (the tooth enters beneath the skin), and sometimes finishing thin walls.

def: Material removal by electrical sparks. For hard/complex materials. Ra 0.8-6.3μm.
expand: Electrical discharges (8,000-12,000°C) vaporize material at a point — no cutting forces! Works on any conductive material at any hardness. Sinker EDM: a graphite/copper electrode shaped like the cavity. Downsides: slow, a White Layer (brittle) that must be removed in fatigue applications.

def: Cutting with a copper/molybdenum wire. Accuracy ±0.005mm. For complex profiles.
expand: A brass wire ⌀0.1-0.3mm cuts a profile through the material while submerged in deionized water. Accuracy ±0.005mm, 4-axis cutting (Taper). Uses: dies, Punch & Die, stress relief in hardened parts, precision slices. The wire is consumed — operating cost is per hour.

def: Material removal with a grinding wheel. Ra 0.1-1.6μm. For high precision and post-heat-treat.
expand: An abrasive wheel (Al₂O₃ for steel, SiC for carbide, CBN for hardened, diamond for ceramics) removes microns. Achieves IT5-6 and Ra 0.1-0.8. Mandatory after hardening. Risks: Grinding Burn (local softening), thermal cracks. Regular Dressing keeps the wheel sharp.

def: Improving dimensional accuracy and finish of internal bores. Ra 0.1-0.8μm. Oil-retaining waves!
expand: Abrasive stones on an expanding head, rotating+reciprocating — create a 30-60° Cross-Hatch that holds oil. Improves roundness, cylindricity, and diameter simultaneously. Uses: engine cylinders, hydraulic pistons, gun barrels. Stock: 0.02-0.05mm.

def: Finishing flat/spherical surfaces. Ra 0.025-0.2μm. Abrasive powder + pressure.
expand: Free abrasive powder (SiC, diamond, B₄C) between the part and a flat lap tool — removes nanometers. Achieves flatness at the light-band level (0.1-0.3μm) and Ra down to 0.01. Uses: mechanical seals, valve faces, gauge blocks, and optical flats. A final finishing process only.

def: CNC programming language. G00=rapid, G01=linear, G02/G03=arc. M03=spindle.
expand: The universal CNC language per ISO 6983. Key ones: G00 rapid, G01 linear, G02/03 arc, G41/42 radius offset, G54-59 zero points, G81-89 drilling cycles. M-codes: M03 spindle, M06 tool change, M08 coolant. Every controller (Fanuc/Siemens/Heidenhain) has its own dialect.

def: Software for automatically generating tool paths from CAD. Mastercam, Siemens NX, Fusion 360.
expand: From a CAD model to tool paths: strategy selection (Adaptive/Trochoidal for roughing, Contour for finishing), parameters, simulation to prevent collisions, and a Post Processor that translates to the specific controller's dialect. Leaders: Mastercam, Fusion 360, SolidCAM (iMachining), NX, hyperMILL.

def: A replaceable carbide blade for an insert holder. ISO CNMG/WNMG/SNMG. 4-8 usable edges.
expand: ISO 1832 code: 1st letter=shape (C=80°, D=55°, W=80° trigon, S=square), 2nd letter=clearance angle, then tolerance, type, size, corner radius. Example: CNMG120408 = 80° rhombic, negative, 12mm, R0.8. A strong shape=W/C for roughing, sharp=V/D for finishing and corners.

def: The maximum stress before fracture. [MPa]. Pairs with: SF = Sy/σ ≥ 1.5.
expand: UTS (Ultimate Tensile Strength) — the peak point on the stress-strain curve. From there Necking begins until fracture. Design uses Rp0.2 (yield), not RM! Values: 1018=440, 4140 Q&T=1000, Ti-6Al-4V=950, Al 7075-T6=572 MPa. RM≈3.45×HB for steels.

def: The stress at which the material enters the plastic region. 0.2% permanent strain. [MPa].
expand: Yield Strength: the stress causing 0.2% permanent plastic strain. Beyond it the part deforms permanently — hence it's the basis for design: SF = Rp0.2/σ_work ≥ 1.5-3. Soft steels show a distinct yield point; aluminum and stainless use the 0.2% Offset method.

def: Relative elongation to fracture [%]. A ductility metric. A>5% = ductile. A<2% = brittle.
expand: A% = (L_final − L₀)/L₀ × 100 on a tensile specimen. A ductility metric: A>15% = a forgiving material that warns before failure; A<5% = brittle. Comparison: annealed 1018=25%, 4140 Q&T=15%, gray iron=0.5%, Al 6061-T6=12%. Critical for bending and forming.

def: Mass per unit volume [g/cm³]. Steel=7.85, Al=2.71, Ti=4.43, CFRP=1.55.
expand: Determines weight and matters greatly in aerospace: replacing steel (7.85) with Al (2.71) = a 65% weight savings; with Ti (4.43) = 44%. Also affects material cost (price per kg × volume × density) and natural frequencies. Mg=1.74 (the lightest structural metal), W=19.3 (counterweights).

def: Heat transfer [W/m·K]. Cu=390, Al=167, steel=50, SS=16, Ti=6.7 — Ti insulates heat!
expand: Determines heat spread: Cu (390) for heat exchangers and electrodes, Al (167) for heat sinks. Stainless (16) is relatively insulating — a problem in machining (heat stays in the tool!) and an advantage for pot handles. Ti (7) is the worst of the metals — critical to its machining.

def: Relative elongation per degree of heat [μm/m·K]. Al=23, steel=12, Ti=8.6, Invar=1.5.
expand: CTE: critical when joining dissimilar materials — Al (23) on steel (12) under varying temperature = stress and bolt failure. Invar (1.2) for measuring tools, Zerodur (~0) for optics. Calculation: ΔL = L₀×α×ΔT. An Al ⌀100 shaft at ΔT=50°: grows 0.115mm!

def: A hardness metric. Hardened steel: HRC 58-65. Q&T steel: HRC 28-42. Tools: HRC 60-65.
expand: Rockwell C: a 120° diamond indenter at 150kgf load — for hard materials (above HRC 20). Fast and cheap, the common shop-floor metric. Benchmarks: cutting tool HRC 58, bearing 60-64, quality knife 58-61, 4140 Q&T 28-32, H13 die 48-52. Below HRC20 switch to HRB.

def: A 10mm ball under 3000kgf. RM≈3.45×HB [MPa] (approximate). For soft-to-medium materials.
expand: Brinell: a 10mm carbide ball at 3000kgf load — a large indent suited to coarse, heterogeneous materials (castings, forgings). The useful relation: RM[MPa] ≈ 3.45×HB for steels — allows estimating strength without a tensile test. Limited to about HB 650.

def: A 136° diamond pyramid. Suits any material including coatings. HV 100 = HB 95 ≈.
expand: Vickers: a 136° diamond pyramid, loads from grams to 100kg — one continuous scale for all materials. The only one suited to: thin coatings (HV0.05), nitrided layers, micro-hardness of individual phases. Conversions: HV≈HB up to 400; HRC 60 ≈ HV 700.

def: An increase in hardness from cold plastic deformation. SS 304 + stainless = strong work hardening!
expand: Cold plastic strain multiplies dislocations that block each other — the material strengthens and hardens. 304 stainless jumps from HB 180 to 400+ under aggressive milling — the next tool pass hits a hardened layer! Prevention: adequate feed (no rubbing), a sharp tool. Exploited: cold rolling strengthens sheet.

def: Failure under cyclic loads. The S-N curve. Endurance Limit = an infinite fatigue boundary.
expand: About 90% of mechanical failures! Fracture below Yield after thousands to millions of cycles. The crack starts at a stress concentration (a corner, hole, surface defect) and progresses silently. The S-N curve (Wöhler) defines life vs. stress. Improvement: larger radii, Shot Peening, polishing, nitriding.

def: A stress below which the material won't fail even after infinite cycles. Steel: Se≈0.5×Sut.
expand: In steels: below ~0.5×RM the part lives forever (beyond 10⁷ cycles). Aluminum and non-ferrous alloys have no such limit — they'll always eventually break! That's why Al aircraft parts are life-limited. Rough value for steel: Se ≈ 0.5×UTS up to a max of 700MPa.

def: Time-dependent strain under constant load at high temperature. Ti/Inconel = high creep resistance.
expand: Above ~0.4×Tm (absolute melting temperature) a material creeps under constant load — slowly elongating until failure. Critical in: turbine blades (Inconel + cooling), steam piping, hot bolts (relaxation). Design per Larson-Miller. Ordinary steel: a problem above 400°C.

def: Energy before fracture. Area under the σ-ε curve. Higher RA + higher UTS = higher toughness.
