expand: The ability to absorb energy before fracture = the area under the stress-strain curve. A combination of strength and ductility — glass is strong but brittle, gum is ductile but weak. Measured with Charpy (J) or Fracture Toughness KIC. Critical for shock, cold, and damage tolerance.

def: UD: E=135GPa, RM=1500MPa, ρ=1.55. Electrically conductive! Corrodes with Al.
expand: Carbon fibers in epoxy: 5x the specific strength of steel. Anisotropic — strong only along fiber direction (hence 0/45/90 layup). Machining: PCD tools, delamination risk when drilling. Corrosion warning: electrically conductive — direct contact with aluminum = a galvanic cell! An insulating layer is mandatory.

def: E=40GPa, RM=1000MPa, ρ=1.90. Cheaper than CFRP. Non-conductive. Boat hulls.
expand: Fiberglass: a third the price of CFRP, transparent to radio waves (radomes, antennas), non-conductive (electrical insulation). E is 3x lower than CFRP — more flexible. Uses: boats, wind blades, chemical tanks, PCB boards (FR-4). Machining wears tools — carbide minimum.

def: Al/SiC: E=100-120GPa, RM=400-500MPa. E 50% higher than Al. PCD for machining only.
expand: MMC: an aluminum matrix + SiC particles/fibers — gets titanium-like E at aluminum weight. Uses: sports brake discs, power electronics (CTE matched to silicon), satellite components. Very hard to machine — PCD only, the SiC eats carbide.

def: RM=100MPa, E=3.6GPa, Tmax=260°C. King of plastics. Aerospace, medical, chemical.
expand: The leading engineering polymer: 260°C continuous, near-total chemical resistance, FDA-approved and implantable. Replaces metal in: seals, bearings, downhole connectors, spinal implants (E similar to bone!). Machining: relatively easy, but expensive — ~$100-200/kg.

def: μ=0.04 — the lowest! Tmax=260°C. Cold Flow under load. Universal resistance.
expand: The lowest friction coefficient in nature (0.04) + total chemical inertness + a range of −200 to +260°C. The big downside: Cold Flow — creeps under load even at room temperature! Hence it's filled with glass/carbon/bronze for bearings. Uses: chemical seals, backup rings, RF insulation.

def: Gas Tungsten Arc Welding. A non-consumable W electrode. High quality. Al, SS, Ti.
expand: GTAW: an arc between a fixed tungsten electrode and the part, manual filler, argon shielding. The highest quality — full control over heat and filler. Mandatory for: sanitary stainless, aluminum (AC), titanium, root passes in piping. Downside: 3-5x slower than MIG, requires high skill.

def: A consumable wire + gas. MIG=argon (Al). MAG=CO₂/mixed (steel). Fast and cheap.
expand: GMAW: a consumable wire fed automatically + shielding gas. MIG=inert gas (argon, for aluminum), MAG=active gas (CO₂/mix, for steel). Fast and productive, easy to learn, suited to robotics. Transfer modes: Short Circuit (thin), Spray (thick), Pulse (good for both).

def: Stick welding (coated electrode). E7018, E6013. Flexible, for the field. Not CNC.
expand: A coated electrode — the coating produces shielding gas and slag. E7018 (basic, low-hydrogen) for structural work, E6013 (rutile) for general use. Advantages: cheap equipment, works in wind and outdoors, any position. E7018 requires oven storage! Slag is removed between passes.

def: A wire with a flux core. Fast, tolerates rust. For construction and piping.
expand: A hollow wire with a flux core: Self-Shielded (no gas — for open outdoor work in wind) or Dual-Shield (with gas — high quality). Deposition rate 2-3x higher than SMAW. The choice for structural construction, shipbuilding, and field piping. Produces slag to remove.

def: An arc beneath granular flux. Deep penetration. Thick plates. The arc isn't visible.
expand: The arc burns beneath a layer of granular flux — no radiation, no spatter. Very deep penetration and deposition up to 20 kg/hour. Automatic only, flat position only. Uses: pressure vessels, spiral pipe, bridge girders. One pass = like 5 SMAW passes.

def: Vacuum welding with an electron beam. HAZ=0.1mm. For sensitive materials and maximum precision.
expand: An electron beam in a vacuum — enormous energy density, a depth:width ratio up to 30:1, a microscopic HAZ. No filler metal, near-zero distortion. Applications: gears (joined after hardening!), jet engine Blisks, missile fuel tanks. Downside: a vacuum chamber = slow and expensive.

def: Laser welding. Small HAZ, fast, high precision. For thin sheet and electronics.
expand: High power density = a narrow weld, fast, minimal HAZ. Keyhole Mode for deep penetration, Conduction for thin sheet. Dominates EV battery manufacturing, electronics, medical. Fiber Laser has replaced CO₂. Challenge: requires precise fit-up — a gap of max 10% of thickness.

def: A document defining welding parameters. AWS D1.1. PQR = Procedure Qualification Record.
expand: The mandatory document for every controlled weld: process, materials, preheat temperature, current/voltage, speed, gas, positions. Backed by a PQR (lab tests proving the parameters work). The welder is qualified via a WPQ for that scope. Required in AWS D1.1, ASME IX, ISO 15614.

def: An area affected by weld heat but not melted. Properties change! Fracture is common here.
expand: The material that was heated but not melted — the microstructure changed without control: hardening (brittle martensite in alloy steels), softening (in the T6 zone of aluminum), or corrosion sensitivity (Sensitization in stainless). Usually the weak link. Reducing it: less heat input, EBW/laser.

def: The maximum temperature between weld passes. 4140: 300°C. Prevents hydrogen cracking.
expand: The maximum temperature of the joint before the next pass. Too high = coarse grain and reduced strength (in stainless: Sensitization); too low in hardenable steels = hydrogen cracks. Typical: carbon steel ≤250°C, stainless ≤150°C, 4140 tightly controlled 200-300°C.

def: Stress Relief 600-650°C/1-2h. After welding alloy steels. Reduces residual stress.
expand: Stress relief at 580-650°C (one hour per 25mm of thickness) — reduces residual stress by about 80% and softens the hard HAZ. Required by ASME depending on thickness and steel type. Critical for H₂S service (NACE). Caution with stainless — the Sensitization range! A local alternative: induction.

def: Corrosion at grain boundaries in SS after exposure to 450-850°C. Prevention: L grade / Ti stabilized.
expand: At 450-850°C chromium bonds with carbon as carbide at the grain boundaries — the boundary is depleted of chromium and gets eaten away. Solutions: L grades (low carbon, 304L/316L), stabilized grades (321 with Ti, 347 with Nb), or Solution Annealing after welding. Test: ASTM A262.

def: Heating steel to the gamma region (800-950°C). A necessary step before quenching.
expand: The first stage in all hardening: heating above A3 (~850°C for 4140) until the entire structure becomes FCC austenite that dissolves carbon. Too low a temperature = partial hardening; too high = coarse grain and brittleness. Hold time: one hour per 25mm of thickness. From there — a rapid quench.

def: A hard crystal structure formed by quenching. High hardness but brittle. Tempering softens it.
expand: Forms when austenite cools too fast for diffusion — carbon is trapped in a distorted BCT lattice. Very hard (up to HRC 65) but glass-brittle — tempering is mandatory! The structure appears needle-like under a microscope. More carbon = higher martensite hardness (up to ~0.8%C).

def: An intermediate structure between pearlite and martensite. Hardness+toughness. Produced by austempering.
expand: Forms during intermediate cooling (300-500°C) or isothermal austempering. The winning combination: good hardness (HRC 45-55) with significantly higher toughness than an equivalent tempered martensite — fewer distortions and less crack risk. Uses: springs, clips, suspension parts.

def: A ferrite+cementite structure. Produced by annealing. Soft, common in normalized steel.
expand: Alternating layers of soft ferrite and hard cementite — like mother-of-pearl (hence the name). Forms during slow cooling (Annealing/Normalizing). The thinner the layers (faster cooling) — the stronger. Fully pearlitic 1080 steel = steel wire, rail track.

def: Austenite that didn't transform during quenching. Lower hardness, higher instability. Cryogenic treatment transforms RA.
expand: Austenite that 'survived' the quench (mainly in high-carbon/alloy steels). The problem: soft, and may transform into fresh martensite in service — dimensional change and cracks! Solution: cryogenic treatment (−80 to −196°C) or multiple tempering. Critical in bearings and gauges.

def: The depth of the coating/hardening layer. Carburize: 0.5-3mm. Nitriding: 0.1-0.5mm.
expand: The hardening depth in surface treatments: Effective Case = down to HV550. Typical: carburizing 0.5-2mm (proportional to √time), nitriding 0.1-0.7mm, induction 1-5mm. Depth by application: a light gear 0.3-0.6, a heavy gear 1-2mm. Checked by micro-hardness cross-section.

def: A hardenability test. Quenches a rod's end and checks hardness along its length. 4340 > 4140 > 1045.
expand: ASTM A255: a ⌀25×100 austenitized rod, its end cooled by a water jet — creating a cooling gradient. HRC is measured along the length: how far from the end hardness was retained = the Hardenability. 1045 drops off after 5mm; 4340 holds HRC50 even at 50mm. The basis for choosing steel by thickness.

def: A material's ability to harden to depth when quenched. Higher Cr, Ni, Mo = higher hardenability.
expand: Not how hard — how deep! 1045 hardens only 3-5mm from the surface (the core stays soft); 4340 hardens a solid ⌀100 all the way to the core. Alloying elements (Cr, Mo, Ni, Mn, B) slow the transformation and allow martensite to form even under slow cooling at the core.

def: Heating/cooling in a molten salt solution. Very uniform. Also enables martempering.
expand: Immersion in molten salts (200-1300°C): heating 5x faster than a furnace (direct conduction), perfect uniformity, zero oxidation/decarburization. Uses: austempering/martempering (a 200-400°C salt as a staged quench medium), tool heating, QPQ. Downside: maintenance and environment.

def: Nitrocarburizing at low temperature (570°C). For ordinary steel ← HV 400-700. Tenifer/Nitrotec.
expand: FNC (Tenifer/Tufftride): nitro-carburizing at 570°C — below the transformation point, almost zero distortion! Creates a hard, wear-resistant white Compound layer 10-25μm + improved fatigue life. On any steel, even soft. An elegant black finish. Common: gears, pistons, firearms (Glock).

def: Salt Bath Nitrocarburizing + polishing + salt bath again. HV 900+. Corrosion resistance + wear resistance.
expand: Quench-Polish-Quench: FNC in salt → polishing → a second dip in an oxidizing salt bath. The layer: nitride + black Fe₃O₄ oxide — corrosion resistance passing 500 hours of salt spray (more than hard chrome!) + low friction. Standard in shock-absorber pistons and gun barrels.

def: Coating thickness after drying [μm]. Measured with an Elcometer. Minimum DFT in specs: 50-75μm.
expand: Dry Film Thickness: the final thickness after drying/curing — what appears in a spec (e.g. 60-80μm epoxy). Measurement: a magnetic Elcometer (on steel) or Eddy Current (on Al), ISO 19840 sets the sampling. Insufficient thickness = insufficient protection; excess = cracking and peeling.

def: WFT = DFT / (% Solids). Measured immediately after spraying with a Nordson comb.
expand: Measured immediately during spraying with a comb gauge — allows instant correction before the paint dries! Calculation: WFT = DFT / percent solids. A paint at 50% solids needing DFT 60μm — spray WFT 120μm. Saves rejections: you can't fix insufficient DFT without an extra coat.

def: A coating adhesion test. ISO 2409 Cross Cut / ISO 4624 Pull-off. 0-5 (0=perfect).
expand: Two methods: Cross-Cut (ISO 2409) — a crosshatch grid and tape pull, rated 0 (perfect) to 5; Pull-Off (ISO 4624/ASTM D4541) — bonding a dolly and a hydraulic pull, result in MPa. Typical requirement: ≥3-5 MPa. Adhesive failure (from the substrate) is worse than cohesive.

def: ASTM B117. Exposure to 5% NaCl. Zinc 200h, EN 1000h, Cadmium 1000h.
expand: ASTM B117: continuous 5% NaCl fog at 35°C. Benchmarks: yellow Zn 96-200h, Zn-Ni 720h, EN 500-1000h, anodize 336h, QPQ 500h+. Important to understand: an accelerated comparative test — doesn't translate directly to service years! Cyclic Tests (ASTM G85) are more realistic.

def: MIL-A-8625 II. 7-25μm. HV 250. Sulfuric acid. Colorable. The most common.
expand: The standard anodize: sulfuric acid, 7-25μm (half etched-in, half built-up), HV~250. The layer is porous — absorbs dye (any color!) and is then sealed. Full electrical insulation. Prep beforehand: masking ground points. Dimensional growth: +50% of thickness per side.

def: MIL-A-8625 III. 25-75μm. HV 400-600. Low temperature. Defense/aerospace.
expand: Hard anodize: the same chemistry at 0°C and high current — a dense layer 25-75μm, HV 400-600 (like hardened steel!). Excellent wear resistance, electrical insulation, natural gray-black. Design mandatory: 50% of the thickness builds outward — holes shrink! Fatigue limit drops ~30%.

def: MIL-DTL-81706. For Al. Electrically conductive! + corrosion resistance + a paint base. Yellow/green.
expand: Chem-Film/Iridite: a thin chemical conversion (0.1-1μm) on aluminum — a characteristic gold color. The magic: electrically conductive (grounding, EMI) + an excellent paint base + corrosion resistance. Meets MIL-DTL-5541 Class 3. Trivalent versions (RoHS) are replacing the carcinogenic Cr6+.

def: PVD. 2-5μm. HV 2300. Tmax 500°C. Gold. A basic cutting-tool coating.
expand: The classic PVD coating: shiny gold, HV 2300, 2-5μm, up to 500°C. Doubles-to-triples tool life and improves chip release. Now considered entry-level — replaced by TiAlN for performance. Still dominates: HSS drills, taps, punches, and decoration (watches, faucets).

def: PVD. HV 3300. Tmax 800°C. Fast dry milling. SS, Ni alloys.
expand: The smart coating: heat forms a self-regenerating Al₂O₃ layer — the hotter it gets, the better it protects (up to 800-900°C). Enables fast dry cutting. AlTiN (Al>50%) is even harder. The choice for milling steels, stainless, titanium. Color: purple-gray to black.

def: PACVD. HV 3000-5000. μ=0.08. Very low friction. Al, medical.
expand: A family of amorphous coatings: hardness 2000-5000HV with friction 0.05-0.15 — a combination no other coating offers. ta-C the hardest, a-C:H the common one. Wins in: aluminum machining (zero BUE!), engine components (lifters), dry bearings, medical. Limit: up to 350°C.

def: WC-Co, CrC. High density, low oxidation. Maximum wear resistance. Shaft restoration.
expand: High Velocity Oxy-Fuel: WC-Co powder accelerated to Mach 2+ — a dense (99%+) coating compacted on impact. 100-500μm at HV 1100-1350 hardness. The official replacement for hard chrome in aerospace (Cr6+ issues): aircraft struts, hydraulic cylinders. Requires grinding to finish.

def: MIL-C-26074. Uniform on complex shapes! HV 500-700 (as-plated) / HV 1000 (heat treated 400°C).
expand: Nickel-phosphorus via a chemical reaction with no current — perfectly uniform thickness even in holes and channels (unlike electroplating!). High-P (10-13%): maximum corrosion resistance, non-magnetic. Mid-P: general purpose. After a 400°C bake: HV 850-950. Standard: MIL-C-26074, AMS 2404. On steel, Al, copper.

def: 60-120μm. VOC=0. Baked at 180-200°C. 6 types: Epoxy/Polyester/PU/TGIC/Fluoropolymer.
expand: Electrostatic dry paint + baking at 180-200°C = a hard 60-120μm layer with no solvents (VOC=0). Excellent mechanical durability, a uniform look. Chemistries: epoxy (indoor, chemical), polyester (outdoor UV), hybrid. Limit: the part must withstand 200°C and be conductive.

def: MIL-DTL-16232. Manganese/zinc. A paint base + reduced wear + reduced glare. Firearms.
expand: A chemical conversion: zinc phosphate crystals (5-15μm, gray) or manganese (5-20μm, black). Zinc = the best paint base (mechanical anchoring); manganese = oil absorption and preventing galling during break-in — standard in gears and firearms. Always with oil/paint — alone it barely protects.

def: AMS 2700. Nitric/citric acid. Removes free Fe from SS after machining. Not a coating — cleaning!
expand: Not a coating — chemical cleaning! Nitric/citric acid removes free iron from a stainless surface (contamination from steel tools during machining) and enriches the natural Cr₂O₃ layer. Without it: rust spots on new 316! Standard AMS 2700 / ASTM A967. Mandatory after every machining of SS.

def: The number of threads per inch. UNC=coarse (low TPI). UNF=fine (high TPI). 1/4"-20 = 20 TPI.
expand: The inch system: 1/4-20 UNC = 1/4 inch diameter, 20 threads per inch. UNC (coarse) for general use, UNF (fine) for vibration and adjustment, UNEF (extra fine). Conversion to pitch: P[mm] = 25.4/TPI. Don't mix with metric — the threads look similar but aren't compatible!

def: d2 = D − 0.6495×P. The diameter where thread width = groove width. The critical metric!
expand: The formula: d2 = D − 0.6495×P. For M10×1.5: d2 = 9.026mm. This is the diameter checked with a Go/NoGo Thread Gauge and determines whether the thread is in tolerance. Tap wear shows up here first.

def: d1 = D − 1.2269×P. The thread root diameter. Tap drill size ≈ D−P.
expand: The formula: d1 = D − 1.2269×P. For M10×1.5: d1 = 8.16mm — hence the approximate drill size D−P. The stress area for strength calcs: As = π/4 × ((d2+d3)/2)² — for M10 = 58mm².

def: The distance between adjacent threads [mm]. M10: P=1.5 (coarse). M10×1.25 (fine).
expand: A worth-memorizing coarse-pitch table: M3×0.5, M4×0.7, M5×0.8, M6×1, M8×1.25, M10×1.5, M12×1.75, M16×2, M20×2.5, M24×3. Common fine pitches: M8×1, M10×1.25, M12×1.5 (car wheel nuts!).

def: 60° tapered. Self-sealing. 1/8"-27 to 4"-8. With Teflon tape/Loctite 545.
expand: A 1:16 taper at a 60° angle — sealing happens in the thread itself (with Teflon/paste). NPTF (Dryseal) seals without sealant. Sizes by nominal pipe diameter: 1/4 NPT ≠ ¼ inch actual! Tightening: 2-3 turns past hand-tight. Not compatible with BSPT!

def: 55° (not 60°! a common mistake). G = straight (BSPP). R = tapered (BSPT). G is common in Israel.
expand: A 55° angle (Whitworth) — doesn't mate with NPT (60°)! G/BSPP = cylindrical, seals with a gasket/O-ring at the shoulder. R/BSPT = tapered, seals in the thread. The standard in Europe, Israel, Asia. G1/4 is common in pneumatics and hydraulics.

def: An SS coil inserted into an enlarged hole. Restores a thread + strengthens aluminum.
expand: A diamond-cross-section stainless wire coil threaded into an oversized bore (a special STI tap). Uses: repairing a stripped thread, and reinforcing a thread in aluminum/magnesium from manufacturing (2x the strength!). Installation: drill → STI tap → thread the coil → break the tang.

def: Spiralock: ≥90° wedge root. Prevents vibration loosening without Loctite. Aerospace.
expand: Spiralock: the internal thread root at a 30° angle — under load the male thread settles on the ramp, creating continuous contact that eliminates the play that lets vibration loosen it. No extra parts, reusable. Used in: aircraft engines, implants, Caterpillar.

def: 29°. ¾"-6 ACME. American lead screws. Common on old lathes.
expand: A 29° profile with a flat crest — thick and strong at the root, tolerant of dirt and wear. General Purpose (2G-4G) for most uses; Centralizing when nut centering matters; Stub for limited height. Efficiency: 30-50% (self-locking in most cases — an advantage in elevators!).

def: 30°. Tr 20×4. Metric lead screws. Lathes, compressors.
expand: The metric equivalent of ACME: a 30° profile, marked Tr20×4 (diameter×pitch). Lead screws of European lathes, clamps, gates, and jacks. Materials: a hardened-thread C45 screw, a bronze nut (cheap replacement when worn). Efficiency ~40% — self-locking.

def: C [kN] — the basic dynamic load from the catalog. L10 = (C/P)^p × 10⁶.
expand: C from the catalog: the load at which 90% of bearings will survive a million revolutions. Formula: L10 = (C/P)^p million revolutions (p=3 for balls, 10/3 for rollers). Meaning: doubling the load = one-eighth the life for balls! So safety margins on load pay off greatly.

def: C0 [kN] — static load. For stationary bearings and slow rotation.
expand: C0: the load creating a permanent indentation of 0.0001×rolling element diameter — the limit for a stationary or slow-rotating bearing (below 10 RPM). Check: P0/C0 ≤ 0.5 for quiet running. Important for shock loads at a stop and slow slewing bearings.

def: 90% of bearings will live at least L10 hours. L10 = (C/P)^p × 10⁶ / (60×n).
expand: The life at 90% probability: L10h = (C/P)^p × 10⁶/(60×n) hours. Target values: general industry 20-30K hours, pumps 40-50K, industrial gearbox 100K. Note: L10 assumes proper lubrication — in practice 80% of bearing failures are lubrication, not fatigue!

def: P = X×Fr + Y×Fa. X,Y from the catalog. When Fa/Fr ≤ e: P=Fr.
expand: P: translating a combined load (radial+axial) into an equivalent radial load. P = X×Fr + Y×Fa where X,Y depend on the ratio Fa/Fr against a threshold e from the catalog. Below e the axial is negligible (P=Fr); above it — the axial dominates and shortens life significantly.

def: Internal clearance larger than CN (standard). Recommended for high temperature and interference-fit mounting.
expand: Internal play larger than standard (CN). When to use C3: an interference fit on the shaft (the press eats up clearance!), high operating temperature (the inner ring expands), electric motors (the standard!). C4 for extreme conditions. A new bearing feeling slightly 'loose' = correct, that's the designed clearance.

def: Higher precision, lower noise, higher rigidity. DB/DF/DT arrangement in angular contact. Excess preload = heat!
expand: An intentional internal load that eliminates play: doubled rigidity, rotational accuracy, prevents ball skidding at high acceleration. Mandatory in: mill spindles (DB back-to-back), differential pinions (set by Nm of drag!), ball screws. Too much preload = heat and rapid failure.

def: 6xxx. The most common! Radial+axial. Up to 16,000 RPM. 6205=⌀25mm bore.
expand: The 6xxx: 80% of bearings in the world. Cheap, fast, quiet, carries radial + moderate axial (up to ~25% of C0), available everywhere. Versions: ZZ (metal shields), 2RS (rubber seal + lifetime grease). Motors, pulleys, skates — everything.

def: 7xxx. Used in pairs! Spindle bearing. 15°/25°/40°. High radial+axial.
expand: The 7xxx: an angled contact line (15°=speed, 25°=universal, 40°=heavy axial) — carries strong axial load in only one direction! Hence always in pairs: DB (back-to-back, stable against moment loads), DF (face-to-face, tolerant of misalignment), DT (tandem, heavy one-directional axial). Spindles in P4+Preload.

def: 3xxxx. Heavy loads. Requires preload! Automotive axles, milling spindles.
expand: The 3xxxx: tapered rollers — carries heavy radial and axial simultaneously. Adjustable: play/preload is set at assembly (an adjusting nut or a shim). Always in opposing pairs. Dominates: car wheels, differentials, heavy gearbox shafts. Timken = the generic name.

def: The default. −20 to +120°C. Mineral. Fills 30-50% of the cavity volume.
expand: The consistency scale from 000 (liquid) to 6 (block). NLGI 2 = the universal default (like peanut butter). NLGI 3 for vertical/fast, NLGI 1-0 for gearboxes and centralized lube systems. Golden rule: never mix different thickeners (lithium+polyurea = soup!).

def: m = dp/z. The basic unit for metric gears. ISO 54: 1,1.25,1.5,2,2.5,3,4,5,6,8,10.
expand: The basic unit of a metric tooth: m = D/z [mm]. Every tooth dimension is derived from it: addendum height = m, dedendum = 1.25m, thickness ≈ 1.57m. Two gears mesh only at the same module! Preferred series: 1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10. Inch: DP=25.4/m.

def: dp = m×z. The basic diameter. Center distance: a = m×(z1+z2)/2.
expand: Pitch Diameter: the theoretical circle at which two gears 'roll' without slipping — where a tooth meets its mate. dp = m×z. The exact center distance: a = m(z1+z2)/2. Not measured directly — derived from an Over-Pins or Span measurement.

def: ha = m. Tooth height above the pitch diameter. da = dp + 2×m.
expand: The height above the pitch circle: ha = 1×m (standard). Outside diameter for turning the blank: da = m(z+2) — the first formula calculated in gear manufacturing! With positive profile shift the head grows: da = m(z+2+2x).

def: hf = 1.25×m. Tooth height below the pitch diameter. df = dp − 2.5×m. This is where breakage occurs!
expand: The depth below the pitch line: hf = 1.25×m — the extra 0.25 creates clearance for the mating tooth's head + room for a root radius. Root diameter: df = m(z−2.5). The root radius is critical for fatigue — that's where the maximum stress occurs (Lewis).

def: 20° = standard. 14.5° = old. 25° = heavy loads. db = dp×cos(α).
expand: α: the angle at which force transfers between the teeth. 20° = the worldwide standard (balancing strength/smoothness). 14.5° is rare (old systems, quiet). 25° for heavy loads (a wider tooth base, fewer minimum teeth). Must match between meshing gears!

def: The gap between teeth. 0.05-0.1×m. Too little=squeal. Too much=vibration. Measured with a DTI.
expand: The side clearance between meshed teeth: essential for lubrication and thermal expansion! Standard value: 0.04-0.06×m. Zero backlash = thermal seizure and failure; excess = a knock on direction reversal (lash). Adjustment: an enlarged center distance or a thinned tooth. Precision servo: dual anti-backlash.

def: Cuts into the tooth root when z<17 (at 20°). Weakens the tooth. Fix: profile shift.
expand: Below 17 teeth (at 20°) the cutting tool cuts into the tooth root — creating a 'waist' that weakens exactly where stress is highest. Standard fix: positive profile shift (x=+0.3-0.5) that moves the tool away. Small pinions are always shifted positively.

def: σ = Ft×Kv/(b×m×Y). Y=form factor (0.245-0.422). Kv=dynamic factor.
expand: Models the tooth as a beam in bending: σ = Ft/(b×m×Y). The factor Y depends on tooth count (more teeth = a thicker base = a larger Y = lower stress). Modern: AGMA/ISO 6336 add dynamic, load-distribution, and surface factors — but Lewis is still the quick estimate.

def: The average number of tooth pairs in contact. ε≥1.2 (spur). ε≥1.5 (helical). ε<1 = a problem!
expand: How many tooth pairs carry load on average: ε=1.6 means part of the time one pair, part of the time two. Safe minimum: 1.2 (spur). A helical gear adds an Overlap Ratio — total 2-4: always several teeth working = quiet and smooth. A higher ε = less noise and less stress per tooth.

def: Shifting the tool relative to the gear. x>0 = outward. x<0 = inward. Prevents undercutting.
expand: x: shifting the cutting tool from the nominal position (positive=outward). Uses: preventing undercut in a small pinion, matching a non-standard center distance, balancing strength between pinion and gear (x1>0, x2<0). Changes tooth thickness and diameters — calculated per ISO 21771.

def: Q6-Q13. Q6=general, Q10=precision, Q13=ultra. DIN 1-12 (reversed).
expand: The American precision scale (higher = more precise): Q6-7 general gears, Q8-9 automotive, Q10-11 machine tools, Q12-13 aerospace/metrology. Europe: DIN 3962 is reversed (1=most precise!) — don't confuse the conversion. Precision determines: noise, load sharing, and allowable speed.

def: Self-locking! Ratio up to 1:70. Efficiency 30-90%. High heat! EP oil mandatory.
expand: A huge ratio in a single stage (up to 1:70) + self-locking (at small lead angles — the load can't turn the worm!). The cost: full sliding = 30-90% efficiency and heat. Classic materials: a hardened, ground steel worm + a bronze gear (sacrificial). Lubrication: heavy GL-4/5 oil.

def: Percent squeeze = (d2−h)/d2×100. Static 15-25%, dynamic 10-20%.
expand: The squeeze is what seals: (d₂−h)/d₂×100. Static 15-25%, dynamic 10-20%, rotary 5-12% (friction heat!). Too little = immediate leakage; too much = rapid compression set, friction, and tearing during assembly. The first calculation in every groove design.

def: O-ring volume as a percent of groove volume. 65-80%. Above 80% = extrusion under heat.
expand: How much of the groove the rubber occupies: ring volume/groove volume = 65-85%. Free space is mandatory! The rubber isn't compressible — it moves: thermal expansion (rubber expands 10x more than steel!), fluid swell, and pressure. A 100% fill = the groove bursts itself or tears the ring.

def: The American standard for O-ring sizes. -006 to -475. d1=inner diameter, d2=cord.
expand: The American catalog: 5 series by cord thickness — 0xx (1.78mm), 1xx (2.62), 2xx (3.53), 3xx (5.33), 4xx (6.99). The number = an identifier, not a size! -214 = ID 24.99×3.53. Always specify: AS568-214 + material + hardness (N70 = NBR Shore 70). Metric: ISO 3601.

def: PTFE. Mandatory above 70 bar! Prevents O-ring extrusion into the groove corner.
expand: A rigid PTFE ring on the low-pressure side — blocks the extrusion gap the rubber would otherwise squeeze into. The rule: above 70 bar (or a large gap) = mandatory. Bidirectional pressure = two rings. Types: Solid (best), Split/Spiral (easy assembly). Multiplies seal life.

def: −40 to +120°C. Excellent for mineral oil and fuel. The most common. Not for water+steam.
expand: The workhorse: 70% of seals worldwide. Excellent: mineral oils, fuels, grease, water. Fails: ozone and sun (cracking!), ketones, DOT brake fluid, temps above 120°C. The default choice for hydraulics and pneumatics. Shore 70 = standard, 90 for high pressure.

def: −20 to +200°C. Defense, chemical. Acid resistant. 5x the price of NBR.
expand: The premium: 200°C continuous, excellent fuel/oil/acid resistance, no issue with ozone and UV. Fails: steam, hot water, ketones, brake fluid. Versions: A (general), B/F (more fluorine=more chemical resistance), GLT (cold down to −40°C). 5-8x the price of NBR — you pay for the temperature.

def: −50 to +150°C. Water, steam, brakes. Not for mineral oil! Automotive.
expand: The water specialist: steam up to 150°C, coolant, DOT 3/4 brake fluid (!), perfect ozone resistance, dilute acids and bases. The absolute forbidden: mineral oil and fuel — swells and disintegrates within days! The classic mistake: an EPDM seal accidentally installed in an oil system.

def: k = G×d⁴/(8×D³×n) [N/mm]. δ=F/k. Higher d = higher k (to the 4th power!).
expand: k = G×d⁴/(8×D³×n): the constant linking force to deflection (F=kδ). Sensitivities: wire diameter to the 4th power (d×2 = k×16!), coil diameter to the 3rd power inversely, number of coils in inverse proportion. Series connection: 1/k=Σ1/ki; parallel: k=Σki.

def: Kw = (4C-1)/(4C-4) + 0.615/C. Corrects for curvature+direct shear in a spring.
expand: The stress on the inside of the coil is higher than nominal due to curvature + direct shear. Kw = (4C−1)/(4C−4) + 0.615/C. For C=6: Kw=1.25 — the stress is 25% higher than the simple calculation! Mandatory in spring fatigue calculations. A small C = a larger correction.

def: C = D/d. Ideal 4-12. C<4 hard to manufacture. C>12 unstable (buckling).
expand: C = D/d (mean coil diameter / wire diameter). The healthy range: 4-12. C<4: high inner stresses, hard to coil, tool breakage. C>12: a 'soft' spring that tangles, buckling, poor tolerances. Manufacturing optimum: 6-9.

def: Spring length under no load. Ls=Solid Length (fully compressed) = n×d+d (closed ends).
expand: L0 — the length in the free state, the first dimension on a spring drawing. Along with: wire diameter, outer/inner diameter, number of active coils, and winding direction. Typical tolerance: ±2%. A spring shorter than L0 = it took a set (overloaded in the past).

def: Ls = (n+2)×d (closed ends). The spring can't be shorter than this.
expand: Ls — the length fully compressed, coil against coil: (n+2)×d for closed and ground ends. A critical design rule: the maximum operating load must stop short of Solid with a safety margin (15% of deflection) — reaching Solid = infinite stress and immediate set.

def: Sideways buckling when L/D>4. Solution: an internal/external guide. Also splitting into two support columns.
expand: A slender compression spring (L0/D > 4 at parallel ends) bows sideways like a column — instead of compressing. Solutions: an internal guide (a rod) or external (a cup) with clearance and lubrication, splitting into two shorter springs, or well-ground ends.

def: High-rate impact of small balls. Compressive stress in a surface layer. Improves fatigue resistance 20-40%.
expand: Bombarding the surface with steel/glass shot — each impact creates a plastic dimple that the layer beneath resists = residual compressive stress (up to −600MPa). Fatigue cracks don't open under compression! Fatigue life ×3-10. Mandatory: springs, gears, con rods. Control: an Almen Strip.

def: Rapid corrosion when dissimilar materials touch + an electrolyte. Difference>250mV = danger.
expand: Two metals + an electrolyte = a battery that eats the anodic one. The distance on the galvanic series determines severity: Al against stainless = the Al disappears! The always-fatal combo: a bad area ratio (a small anode + a large cathode). Protection: insulation (a gasket, sealant), coating, or a sacrificial anode (Zn).

def: Deep localized holes. Stainless in a chloride environment. PREN predicts resistance. Dangerous!
expand: Stainless's enemy in chlorides: a microscopic flaw in the passive layer becomes a concentrated anodic cell — a deep pit that progresses silently until it punctures! Resistance estimate: PREN = Cr+3.3Mo+16N. Seawater needs PREN>35 (316L is borderline!). Prevention: 2205 Duplex, Super Austenitic, cleanliness.

def: Fracture under stress+corrosion. Al 7075 = sensitive. SS in KOH. Ti = very resistant.
expand: The deadly trio: tensile stress + a specific environment + a sensitive material = a sudden brittle crack far below yield! Known combos: stainless+hot chloride (above 60°C), brass+ammonia, 7075-T6+seawater, steel+H₂S. Protection: T73 instead of T6, compressive stress (peening), material selection.

def: Corrosion in closed crevices (bolts, contact). Stainless is sensitive. Prevention: sealant.
expand: In a narrow crevice (under a bolt head, a gasket, a bearing seat) oxygen depletes — creating a locally acidic-pH cell that accelerates attack. Stainless is especially sensitive (the passive layer needs oxygen!). Prevention: full sealing (sealant), continuous welding instead of spot, drainage, super duplex.

def: Corrosion+erosion combined. Pumping equipment, heat exchangers. Ni-Al bronze = resistant.
expand: Fast flow + particles tear away the protective layer — corrosion at a mechanical rate! Identified by a horseshoe/wave pattern in the flow direction. Victims: pipe elbows, impellers, heat exchangers. Solutions: speed limiting (Cu-Ni: 3.5 m/s), large radii, Ni-Al Bronze, HVOF.

def: PREN = %Cr + 3.3×%Mo + 16×%N. >35=seawater. >40=super duplex.
expand: Pitting Resistance Equivalent Number = %Cr + 3.3×%Mo + 16×%N. The scale: 304=19, 316L=24, 2205 Duplex=35, Super Duplex 2507=42, 254SMO=43. Rule of thumb: seawater needs 40+. Allows comparing alloys on paper before testing.

def: Zinc leaching from brass in water/steam environments. Prevention: Naval Brass (C464) + Sn.
expand: Standard brass (above 15% Zn) in hot/stagnant water: the zinc dissolves selectively, leaving a weak, reddish porous copper sponge — the faucet breaks by hand! Identification: red spots on yellow. Prevention: DZR brass (CW602N with As), Naval Brass, or Admiralty. Mandatory in European water fixtures.

def: Sealing between mating surfaces. Prevents galvanic corrosion. PR-1422/PR-1776. Mandatory in aerospace.
expand: In aerospace: every Al-Al or Al-steel contact is sealed with a polysulfide sealant (PR-1440/AC-236) during wet assembly — blocks moisture entry into the gap and breaks the galvanic path. Fasteners are also dipped. The standard that keeps aircraft free of contact corrosion for 50 years.

def: Ti64, SS 316L, AlSi10Mg, Inconel. ±0.1mm. Ra 6-15μm. Aerospace, defense.
expand: Direct Metal Laser Sintering: a laser melts metal powder layer by layer (20-60μm). Qualified materials: Ti-6Al-4V, 316L, AlSi10Mg, Inconel 718, 17-4PH. Mandatory afterward: support removal, stress relief, and usually HIP + interface machining. As-built Ra 6-15μm.

def: Like DMLS — full melting. Higher density. Higher residual stress. Stress relief mandatory.
expand: Technically identical to DMLS (a historical marketing distinction) — full melting of the powder. The main challenge: residual stress from rapid cooling — the part can distort when separated from the plate! Hence: stress relief before cutoff, smart supports, and process simulation (Netfabb, Amphyon).

def: ABS, PLA, PEEK, Ultem. ±0.5mm. Ra 12-50μm. Cheap, fast, anisotropic.
expand: The simplest and cheapest: molten filament laid down in layers. The critical point: anisotropy — inter-layer (Z) strength is only 30-70% of in-plane strength! Design the print direction along the load direction. Engineering grades: PEEK, Ultem 9085 (aerospace-certified), PC, Nylon+CF.

def: Nylon PA12, PA11, TPU. ±0.3mm. No supports! Functional parts.
expand: A laser sinters nylon powder — the unmelted powder self-supports = no supports, full geometric freedom, and dense nesting for batch production! PA12 the standard, PA11 tougher, TPU flexible. A grainy surface — vapor smoothing for finish. Economical for runs of 100-10K.

def: UV resin. ±0.1mm. Ra 1.6-6.3μm. High precision. Brittle. Jigs, medical.
expand: A UV laser cures liquid resin — the best precision and surface finish in the field (25-100μm layers, Ra 1-3μm). Uses: visual prototypes, castable patterns, dental, a master for silicone. The weakness: relatively brittle resins sensitive to UV over time.

def: Vacuum. Ti64, CoCr. No residual stress. Medical implants.
expand: Electron Beam Melting (Arcam): an electron beam in vacuum, a hot powder bed (700°C) — almost no residual stress, no need for stress relief! Faster than DMLS, coarser (Ra 25-35μm). The niche: titanium implants (trabecular!), TiAl blades. Vacuum = zero oxidation.

def: 900-1200°C + 100-200MPa. Closes porosity in metal AM. Improves mechanical properties.
expand: Hot Isostatic Pressing: 900-1200°C + argon at 100-200MPa from every direction — fully closes internal porosity. Mandatory for AM in aerospace/medical (fatigue!) and critical castings. Result: 100% density, dramatically reduced fatigue scatter. Cost: a facility queue + hundreds of dollars.

def: Up to 45° without supports. 30° is safe. Above 45° = supports mandatory (DMLS/FDM).
expand: The 45° rule: beyond 45 degrees from vertical — supports are mandatory (the material 'sags'). Smart design: replace an overhang with a self-supporting slope, a chamfer instead of a bottom radius, diamond/teardrop holes instead of round horizontal ones. Fewer supports = less post-processing = cheaper.

def: A lattice structure in AM. 40-60% weight reduction with higher strength/volume. Unique to AM!
expand: Internal lattices (Gyroid, Octet, BCC): optimal strength/weight — a 40-60% weight cut while retaining sufficient stiffness. Applications: implants (E matched to bone — prevents stress shielding!), energy absorption, heat exchangers. Software: nTopology, Materialise 3-matic.

def: Removing supports after printing. DMLS: tools/cutting. FDM: manual/dissolvable.
expand: The hidden cost of metal AM: the supports are welded to the part! Removal: Wire EDM (from the plate), manual breaking, milling. Minimizing design: smart build orientation, self-supporting angles, perforated supports. In polymers: SLS has no supports at all, FDM uses dissolvable (PVA), SLA breaks off easily.

def: Pressure transmits equally in every direction in a fluid. F=P×A. Mechanical advantage = A2/A1.
expand: The basis of hydraulics: pressure in an enclosed fluid transmits equally in every direction — F=P×A. The hydraulic lever: a small piston (10cm²) at 200bar pressure pushes a large piston (100cm²) with 10x the force! The cost: an inverse distance ratio. That's how a 2-ton jack works with one hand.

def: Q [L/min] = A[m²] × v[m/s] × 60,000. Power kW = P[bar] × Q[L/min] / 600.
expand: Q determines speed, P determines force: v = Q/A. Power: P[kW] = Q[L/min]×p[bar]/600. A 40L/min pump at 210bar = 14kW. Line design: suction 1.2m/s, pressure 4-6m/s, return 2-3m/s — too fast = heat and losses, too slow = expensive piping.

def: Limits maximum pressure. Mandatory in every system! Protects against bursting. NO = normally closed.
expand: The protection you can't do without: opens at a set pressure and flows to the tank. Cracking pressure (start of opening) vs. full flow (10-20% higher). Direct acting is fast for small ones; pilot operated is precise for large ones. Important: a relief valve running continuously = all the energy turns to heat!

def: Flow in one direction only. Prevents backflow. Ball/Poppet/Swing type.
expand: A ball/poppet on a spring: forward flow opens, backward locks. Typical cracking: 0.3-3bar. Pilot-Operated Check (POC): opens backward on a pressure command — absolute load locking (a boom won't drift down!). A pair of POCs = securing a cylinder in both directions.

def: A 4/2 or 4/3 directional valve. Controls the cylinder's direction. Normally open/closed.
expand: The notation: 4/3 = 4 ports (P,T,A,B), 3 positions. The center position sets the behavior: closed (everything locked), open (everything to tank — released), float (A,B to tank), tandem (P to tank — pump idles, load locked!). Actuation: solenoid, lever, pilot. Sizes: CETOP 3/5.

def: VG 32/46=hydraulics. VG 100-680=gears. Viscosity mm²/s @40°C.
expand: VG = viscosity in cSt at exactly 40°C. Hydraulics: VG32 (cold/fast), VG46 (the standard in Israel), VG68 (hot/slow). Gears: VG150-460. The choice: optimal viscosity at the pump is 16-36cSt at operating temperature. A high viscosity index = stable across temperatures.

def: A gear/hydraulic oil additive. Protects at extreme pressure. Worm gears = EP mandatory!
expand: Extreme Pressure (sulfur-phosphorus): under contact heat and pressure it forms a sacrificial chemical film on the metal — prevents microscopic welding (scuffing) in hypoid gears and shock loads. GL-5 = full dose. Caution: attacks bronze! Worm gears = GL-4 only or a dedicated oil.

def: σ = M×c/I [MPa]. M=moment, c=distance from neutral axis, I=moment of inertia.
expand: σ=M×c/I: the fibers farthest away suffer the most — that's why an I-beam puts material far from the axis! Cases worth remembering: a round beam σ=32M/πd³. Doubling beam height = a quarter the stress (I∝h³). Failure always starts at the outermost edge.

def: τ = T×r/J (torsion) [MPa]. J=polar moment of inertia. J_solid=πD⁴/32.
expand: Torsion: τ=16T/πd³ for a round bar — doubling the diameter = one-eighth the stress! A hollow tube is efficient in torsion (the core material barely works). Direct shear: τ=F/A in bolts and pins — a bolt in double shear carries double.

def: σv = √(σ²+3τ²). SF = Sy/σv. A yield criterion for ductile materials.
expand: Converting a combined stress state into one number to compare against Sy: σv=√(σ²+3τ²) for bending+torsion. The criterion for ductile materials (steel, aluminum). In FEA: the famous color map. Brittle materials (castings) — use a maximum principal stress criterion instead.

def: I_rect = b×h³/12. I_circle = π×D⁴/64. I_hollow = π(D⁴-d⁴)/64.
expand: I: resistance to bending — depends on the 3rd/4th power of geometry: a rectangle bh³/12, a circle πD⁴/64. The design lesson: material far from the neutral axis is worth gold — a tube, an I-beam, a honeycomb. Doubling the height = 8x the stiffness!

def: σ_max = Kt × σ_nom. A hole = Kt≈3. A keyway = Kt≈2.5-3. Higher r → lower Kt.
expand: Every geometric change concentrates stress: a hole Kt≈3, a sharp shoulder 2-3, a keyway ~2.5. Under static ductile loading the material 'forgives' (local yielding); under fatigue — the crack starts exactly there! Protection: generous radii, gradual transitions, polishing critical areas. Peterson = the reference book.

def: SF = Sy/σ_max. Static: 1.5-2.5. Fatigue: 2-4. Critical defense: 4-10.
expand: SF=strength/stress: how much reserve there is. Selection by uncertainty: 1.25-1.5 (known loads, tested aerospace), 2-2.5 (general), 3-4 (shock, a person beneath). Fatigue and bearings: SF on life, not on stress. More SF = more weight and cost.

def: M_max = P×L/4 (center). δ_max = P×L³/(48×E×I). Two supports.
expand: Two supports, a center point load: M=PL/4, deflection δ=PL³/48EI. A distributed load: M=wL²/8, δ=5wL⁴/384EI. Note the sensitivity: doubling the span = 8x the deflection! These formulas solve 80% of everyday problems.

def: M_max = P×L (root). δ_max = P×L³/(3×E×I). Fixed at one side.
expand: Fixed at one end: M=PL at the root (that's where it breaks!), δ=PL³/3EI — 16x the deflection of a beam supported at both ends over the same span! Every arm, shelf, and protruding pin is a cantilever. Reinforce: increase the cross-section at the root, not the tip.

def: A free body diagram. All forces + moments on an isolated body. The first step in analysis.
expand: The step you can't skip: isolate a body, draw all the forces and moments (including reactions!), and solve ΣF=0, ΣM=0. Most calculation errors = a missing FBD or a reversed direction. Also in FEA: wrong boundary conditions = a pretty, wrong result.

def: Principal stresses = planes with no shear. σ1,2 = σ/2 ± √((σ/2)²+τ²).
expand: The planes where shear vanishes — that's where the true maximum tension σ1 lives. Mohr's circle converts between the systems. Uses: crack direction (perpendicular to σ1!), composite fiber direction, and a brittle-fracture criterion. In FEA: Max Principal for brittle materials.

def: RPN = S×O×D. Maximum 1000. Action threshold: >100 (general) / >50 (defense).
expand: RPN = Severity × Occurrence × Detection (1-10 each, max 1000). Action rule: RPN>100 requires attention, but: S=9-10 is always addressed — even at low RPN! (a life-threatening risk isn't offset by good detection). The new AIAG-VDA replaced it with Action Priority (H/M/L).

def: 1=no effect. 5=moderate. 9=life-threatening without warning. 10=catastrophic.
expand: The score for effect on the customer/safety: 1=unnoticed, 5-6=degraded performance, 8=loss of function, 9-10=safety/regulatory (10=no advance warning!). Severity can't be reduced by controls — only a design change lowers Severity. So a high S is a design red flag.

def: 1=impossible. 5=moderate. 10=almost certain. The probability of the failure occurring.
expand: The probability of the failure occurring: 1=nearly impossible (Cpk>1.67), 4-6=occasional (a reasonably controlled process), 10=nearly certain. Lowering O: process improvement, poka-yoke, a design change. Estimated from: historical data, Cpk, and experience with similar processes.

def: 1=certain detection. 5=moderate. 10=impossible to detect. Higher D → higher RPN.
expand: The ability to catch the failure before the customer: 1=certain detection (a physical poka-yoke), 4=statistical inspection, 7=visual inspection, 10=no control. Note the reversed direction — good detection = a low score! Improving D is cheaper than improving O, but preventing is better than detecting.

def: Top-down. AND/OR gates. P(AND)=P₁×P₂. IEC 61025. Complements FMEA.
expand: A top-down analysis: starting from the catastrophic event (the top event) and breaking it down through logic gates into root causes. AND = all factors needed (probabilities multiply — redundancy!), OR = one is enough (probabilities add). Complements FMEA, which works bottom-up. Standard: IEC 61025.

def: MIL-STD-1629A (defense). IEC 60812 (civilian). AIAG/VDA 2019 (automotive).
expand: The systematic method: for every component/step — what can fail, what's the effect, what's the cause, and how is it detected. Types: DFMEA (design), PFMEA (process). The process: a cross-functional team, RPN, corrective actions, follow-up. A living document — updated with every change and field failure!

def: Cpk = min(CPU,CPL). ≥1.33=good. ≥1.67=Six Sigma. <1.0=defects expected!
expand: The key metric: Cpk = min[(USL−μ), (μ−LSL)]/3σ — the worse side governs! Meaning: 1.0 = 2,700 PPM defective, 1.33 = 63 PPM (the accepted threshold), 1.67 = 0.6 PPM (safety-critical). A high Cp with a low Cpk = a stable process that just needs centering — the cheap fix.

def: 3.4 defects per million. Cpk=1.67. DMAIC: Define-Measure-Analyze-Improve-Control.
expand: The goal: a spread small enough that even with a ±1.5σ center shift, it stays at 3.4 DPMO. The methodology: DMAIC for improving an existing process, DFSS for new design. Belts: Green (part-time), Black (leads projects), Master (mentors). Tools: SPC, DOE, MSA, regression analysis.

def: Control charts. UCL/LCL = μ±3σ. Nelson rules for detecting anomalies. Western Electric.
expand: The principle: distinguish natural variation (Common Cause — don't touch it!) from a special deviation (Special Cause — stop and address it). The tool: X̄-R charts with ±3σ limits. Adjusting a stable process on every measurement = tampering that increases spread! Nelson Rules identify patterns.

def: MSA. %R&R <10%=excellent. 10-30%=acceptable. >30%=a problem! ndc≥5.
expand: Is the measurement system itself reliable? Repeatability = the same inspector, the same part (equipment variation); Reproducibility = between inspectors (method variation). Test: 10 parts×3 inspectors×3 trials. Result: %GRR<10% excellent, 10-30% borderline, >30% = the measurement is noisier than the process!

def: AS9102. 100% of dimensions, material CoC, process certificates. Engineer signature.
expand: Per AS9102: three forms — Form 1 (part identification), Form 2 (materials and special processes with certificates), Form 3 (every numbered characteristic on the drawing + the actual result). A Partial FAI after a localized change. Aerospace's way of confirming the process is capable — before the run.

def: Must include: name+part number · Rev · Lot/Heat · material standard · signature.
expand: A minimal Certificate of Conformance: manufacturer details, part number+revision, order number, quantity, a statement of conformance, an authorized signature. Plus traceability: raw material Heat/Lot, coating/heat-treat certificates (with the standard: AMS/MIL). Supplier auditing starts here.

def: A document approving a change to a drawing/BOM. Process: ECR → analysis → Board approval → implementation.
expand: The change chain: ECR (request+justification) → a CCB committee → ECO (the binding order) → ECN (distribution). The ECO defines Effectivity: from a given S/N, a date, or Immediate + disposition of existing inventory. A documented cut-in = configuration traceability.

def: The first step in a change process. Cause + effects + cost + time. Before an ECO.
expand: The gateway to the process: who's requesting, what's the problem (a field failure? a cost reduction? a supplier?), the proposed solution, and an impact estimate — cost, inventory, customers, related documents (Where-Used!). The CCB approves/rejects. A good ECR = half the work of the ECO.

def: A,B,C... (not I,O,Q,S,X,Z!). Rev - = before any change. P = preliminary.
expand: The rules: letters A→B→C skipping I,O,Q,S,X,Z (confusion with digits). Before the first release: Rev '-' or draft digits. A typo fix = a new Rev anyway! The physical part is sometimes marked with a Rev — critical drawing-to-part matching.

def: A list of every assembly/drawing using the part. Essential for change impact analysis.
expand: Before every ECO — the first query: where else does this part live? A thread change on a shared bolt could break 15 other assemblies. PLM gives the answer in a second; manual file management = an invitation for trouble.

def: An approved state definition of a product. FBL/DBL/PBL. Configuration management.
expand: A configuration anchor point: FBL (functional — requirements), ABL (allocated), PBL (product — the full manufacturing documentation). From the moment it's fixed — every change only through an ECO. A configuration audit compares: what's documented against what's actually built.

def: Software for managing drawings, BOM, processes. Windchill, Teamcenter, Agile.
expand: The system holding everything: CAD files with versions, BOM, electronic ECO workflows, signatures. The players: Windchill, Teamcenter, 3DEXPERIENCE, SolidWorks PDM (the small one). The key advantage: a single source of truth — no 'the version on Joe's desk'.

def: USML — American regulation. Requires marking on defense drawings. ECCN.
expand: The American regulation for USML items: a drawing of a missile component = an 'export' even by email to a foreign person! Requirements: document marking, access restriction (US Persons or a license), approved servers. Violation = million-dollar fines and imprisonment. Israel has an equivalent.

def: Dual-use and civilian. ECCN. Commerce Control List. Free/restricted/prohibited.
expand: The regulation for dual-use items: every item gets an ECCN from the CCL — from which the license requirement is derived by destination and use. EAR99 = the least restricted. Traps: 5-axis CNC machines, sensors, encryption — all controlled!

def: A defense standard for engineering drawings. Title block, Rev, forbidden letters, symbols.
expand: The historic standard for American defense drawings — replaced by ASME Y14.100 but still alive in old contracts. Defines: title block structure, Rev control, parts lists, and drawing types (Detail, Assembly, Installation). Old military documents follow it.

def: Part Number · Rev · Material · Scale · Projection · ISO 2768-mK · Approved.
expand: The drawing's DNA: P/N + Rev (the unique identifier!), material+spec, finish, general tolerance, scale, projection angle, signatures, and a CAGE Code in defense work. The first field checked: does the Rev match the order.

def: A stainless coil insert installed into an STI bore — strengthens threads in Al and protects against galvanic corrosion.
expand: Helicoil/Wire Insert: an 18-8 stainless coil in a diamond cross-section. The hidden advantage: distributes load evenly across all the threads (in a standard thread the first thread carries 30%!). In aluminum — a design mandate from manufacturing, not just a repair. A Screw-Lock version with a serrated coil for locking.

def: A special tap for drilling Helicoil holes — larger than standard. Never use a regular tap!
expand: An STI (Screw Thread Insert) tap: creates an oversized thread exactly the size the coil will fill — the final result: a precise standard thread. Every standard size has a dedicated STI tap + its own drill diameter (in the manufacturer's table). Don't try it with a larger regular tap!

def: A solid stainless insert with locking keys pressed into the host material — higher pull-out strength than a Helicoil.
expand: Keensert/Keysert: a solid bushing with external and internal threads + locking keys. Advantages over Helicoil: fast installation (no tang to break), higher pull-out strength, replaceable. The choice for heavy loads and quick field repairs.

def: Four keys in a Keensert insert pressed inward after installation, preventing rotation or pull-out.
expand: The Keys of a Keensert: 2-4 built-in pins that, after threading, are hammered and driven inward — cutting through the parent thread and locking the bushing against rotation forever. Removal: drilling out the keys. This is what allows breaking bolts loose with force without the bushing spinning.

def: An insert installed from one side only — expands behind the panel and creates a thread in thin material without access to the other side.
expand: Blind Rivet Nut: installed from one side only — crushes behind the sheet like a rivet and creates a thread. The only solution for closed profiles and panels without rear access. Materials: steel, stainless, aluminum. Shapes: round (spins under load!), hex (locked).

def: A trade name for a rivet nut — an expanding nut for joining thin sheet.
expand: A trade name that became generic for a rivet nut. Installation: a manual/pneumatic tool pulls the thread and the body collapses, forming a rear flange. Critical: an exact drill diameter and a calibrated tool — over-crushing ruins the thread, under-crushing spins. For sheet 0.5-6mm.

def: A press-in fastener for thin sheet metal — mechanical pressure makes the material flow around the insert and lock.
expand: PEM: the insert is pressed into a bore in the sheet — a special collar makes the sheet material flow into the locking groove. Requires: sheet softer than the insert (zinc-plated steel in an Al/soft-steel sheet), a minimum thickness, and pressing (not hammering!). Standard in electrical cabinets and electronics.

def: A threaded insert for polymer materials — types: ultrasonic, heat-set, press-in, expansion.
expand: A whole family for threads in plastic: Ultrasonic (vibration melts it in), Heat-Set (soldered in), Press-In (cold pressed for thermosets), Molded-In (inside the mold). All with a knurled/serrated exterior for grip. Bolts directly in plastic = single-use; an insert = forever.

def: A plastic insert installed with heat (a soldering iron/oven) — the plastic melts around it and locks. Common in 3D printing.
expand: The insert is placed on the bore and a soldering iron (or a dedicated tool) heats it — the plastic locally melts and flows into the grooves, solidifies, and locks. Most common in 3D printing (PLA/PETG/ABS)! Temp: ~200-250°C depending on the polymer. Alignment matters — crooked = a crooked thread.

def: A thermoplastic insert installed with 20-40kHz vibration — local heat melts the plastic around the insert.
expand: 20-40kHz vibration creates friction that melts the plastic around the insert within a second — fast and consistent for mass production. The flowing plastic fills grooves in opposing directions = resistance to both pull-out and rotation. Thermoplastics only.

def: An aerospace-qualified insert per NAS1130 — an aluminum/titanium locking ring pressed in and locked permanently.
expand: The aerospace-qualified insert (NAS1394/MS51830): a threaded bushing + a serrated locking ring pressed to penetrate the parent material. Resists extreme temperature and vibration, full traceability. In aircraft structure — only qualified inserts, not commercial Helicoils!

def: The axial force required to pull an insert from the host material — a key parameter for insert selection.
expand: Pull-Out: the axial force that tears out the insert. Rules of thumb: proportional to engagement depth and the shear strength of the host material. Always design so the bolt fails before the insert (a failure hierarchy). Verification test: a tensile machine with a dedicated fixture per NASM1312.

def: A Helicoil version with no tang to break — requires a special installation tool. Common in aerospace and hard-to-reach spaces.
expand: A Helicoil with no tang: installed with a dedicated tool that rotates from a small notch — no breaking step and no risk of a forgotten tang in the system (FOD!). Mandatory in aerospace and medical. Also allows height adjustment and removal without damage. A higher tool cost — worthwhile in runs.

def: An internal thread with a wide 30° ramp — self-locking under vibration without Nyloc/Loctite.
expand: Ingenious geometry: a 30° ramp at the internal thread root. Under load — the bolt thread edges are pressed onto the ramp: continuous line contact across all threads instead of a point on the first one, no radial play — nothing left to move under vibration. Passes the Junker Test with no loosening. No consumable component.

def: The American GD&T standard — the current 2018 edition removed Symmetry and Concentricity in favor of Position.
expand: The American bible of GD&T. The 2018 edition: removed concentricity and symmetry, added MBD tools. Defaults: automatic RFS, the Envelope (Rule #1). Most American aerospace and defense drawings follow it — know which edition applies!

def: The European GD&T standard — the Independence Principle as default, different from ASME Rule #1.
expand: European GD&T: the Independence Principle (ISO 8015) as the default — size doesn't govern form (the opposite of ASME!). The dangerous differences: Ⓔ is required for the envelope, a slightly different Datum interpretation. A drawing mixing standards = ask for written clarification.

def: The fit and tolerance system standard, IT grades — defines 18 precision grades and hole/shaft letters.
expand: The fit system: a letter (tolerance zone position) + a digit (IT — width). Holes in uppercase, shafts in lowercase. The common pairings: H7/g6 clearance, H7/k6 transition, H7/p6 press. The deviation table sits on every designer's desk.

def: A general drawing tolerance — Part 1: dimensions f/m/c/v, Part 2: general GD&T H/K/L.
expand: The drawing's safety net: a tolerance for every 'exposed' dimension. Part 1 dimensions (f/m/c/v — fine to very coarse), Part 2 geometry (H/K/L). 'ISO 2768-mK' in the title block = ±0.1-0.3 typical + K geometry. Without it — every dimension is open to argument.

def: The American Welding Society's structural steel welding code — the most common in construction and industry.
expand: The structural steel welding code: welder qualification (WPQ by position and thickness), process approval (WPS/PQR), NDT acceptance criteria, and Prequalified Joints (joints exempt from PQR). Bridges, structures, heavy frames — all follow it.

def: Fusion weld quality levels: B high, C medium, D low — defines allowable imperfections.
expand: The dictionary of weld defects: every defect (undercut, porosity, lack of fusion) gets a limit by grade — B (strict, dynamic/fatigue), C (standard), D (lenient). On a drawing: 'ISO 5817-B'. The NDT inspector works directly against it.

def: The American anodizing standard: Type I chromic, Type II sulfuric, Type III hard anodize.
expand: The military anodize spec: Type I (chromic — environmentally banned), Type II (standard sulfuric), Type III (hard). Class 1 (natural) / Class 2 (dyed). A full example: 'Anodize per MIL-A-8625 Type III Class 1, 50μm'. The language of aerospace.

def: The aerospace quality management standard — based on ISO 9001 with additional requirements for defense and critical components.
expand: ISO 9001 + aerospace's requirements: risk management, FAI (AS9102), full traceability, counterfeit prevention, and qualified special processes (Nadcap). Without a certificate — no entry into Boeing/Airbus/IAI's supply chain. Rev D is current.

def: The automotive QMS standard — includes APQP, PPAP, FMEA, MSA, SPC as mandatory parts.
expand: Automotive's QMS: mandatory Core Tools — APQP, PPAP, FMEA (AIAG-VDA), MSA, SPC. Emphases: zero defects, CSR (customer-specific requirements per OEM), and process audits. A Tier-1/2 supplier must be certified.

def: The passivation standard for stainless steel — defines 7 methods by steel type and use environment.
expand: The aerospace passivation spec: nitric methods (Type 1-8 by concentration and temperature) and citric. Selection by stainless grade — martensitic grades are sensitive to over-etching! Includes verification tests: Copper Sulfate, salt. On a drawing: 'Passivate per AMS 2700'.

def: The heat treatment standard for steels — defines temperatures, times, and cooling conditions for different steel types.
expand: A family of aerospace heat treatment specs: /1 carbon and low-alloy, /2 corrosion-resistant, /3 martensitic... Includes: temperatures, baths, atmosphere control, target hardness, and testing. The card accompanying every batch at a qualified HT facility.

def: The aerospace Helicoil Wire Thread Insert standard — replaces MIL-I-8846.
expand: The aerospace Helicoil spec (formerly MS21209): coil dimensions for every thread, material (SS 18-8 / bronze), locking/free-running, and installation requirements. On a drawing: 'Install insert per NASM 21209-C0820' — the code defines everything.

def: The aerospace Key-Lock Insert (Keensert) standard.
expand: The spec for Key-Locked inserts (Keensert style): dimensions, materials (steel/coated SS), locking torques, and minimum pull-out forces. The choice when needed: fast field replacement, high loads, or a large-diameter thread.

def: The bolt strength class standard: 4.6/5.8/8.8/10.9/12.9 — defines Rm and Rp0.2 for each class.
expand: Bolt strength classes: the code X.Y — tenths: X×100=UTS[MPa], Y: Sy=X×Y×10. Decoding 8.8: UTS=800, Sy=640. The scale: 4.6 (soft), 8.8 (the structural standard), 10.9 (hardened), 12.9 (maximum — beware of hydrogen!). Stamped on the head.

def: The stainless bolt standard: A2-70/A2-80/A4-70/A4-80 — A2=304, A4=316.
expand: Stainless bolts: A2 (304, general) / A4 (316, marine-chemical) + a strength number: 70 = UTS 700MPa (the standard), 80 = cold-worked. A4-80 = the best for harsh environments. Note: about 15% weaker than 8.8 — don't swap one-for-one under load!

def: The European structural steel standard: S235/S275/S355/S420/S460 — defines chemical and mechanical composition.
expand: European structural steels: S235/S275/S355 — the number = minimum Sy [MPa]. Suffixes: JR/J0/J2 = Charpy test temperature (20/0/−20°C) — critical for structures in cold! S355J2 = the workhorse of welded construction.

def: The quality management system standard — the current 2015 edition is based on Risk-Based Thinking.
expand: The base for all quality systems: a process approach, risk management (2015 edition), continual improvement, and management involvement. It doesn't define product quality — it defines a method! The certificate = a minimal entry ticket to most tenders.

def: A NATO quality standard for defense suppliers — parallels ISO 9001 with additional defense requirements.
expand: NATO's quality requirements for defense contracts: sits on ISO 9001 + additions — Government Quality Assurance (a government representative inspects at your facility!), configuration management, and enhanced traceability. In Israel: the Ministry of Defense requires it on foreign contracts.

def: The German standard for Wire Thread Inserts (Helicoil) — parallels NASM 21209 in Europe.
expand: The German/European standard for Wire Thread Inserts: dimensions, post-installation tolerances, and materials. The civilian equivalent to NASM 21209. Important for purchasing: Helicoil is a brand — the standard allows equivalence between manufacturers (Böllhoff, KATO, Recoil).

def: The aerospace Rosan Inserts standard — connections with a locking ring for structural parts.
expand: The spec for heavy aerospace threaded inserts (Rosan style): a bushing + a serrated locking ring. For loads and vibration beyond Helicoil. On aircraft structure drawings — the full number defines size, material, and finish.

def: The CMM accuracy testing standard — defines the test method and accuracy metrics for every CMM.
expand: How you know the CMM is accurate: acceptance testing and periodic verification — measuring gauge blocks and a sphere across the full work volume. The result: MPE (maximum permissible error) = E0=(1.5+L/333)μm etc. The calibration certificate cites it.

def: The aerospace shot peening standard — defines intensity (Almen Intensity), coverage, and process control.
expand: The aerospace shot peening spec: intensity (Almen A/N/C), coverage (98-200%), shot type (cast steel/cut wire/ceramic), and process control. Qualified peening = locked parameters + an Almen strip every shift. Engine and landing gear parts — mandatory.

def: The heat treatment furnace calibration (pyrometry) standard — defines calibration classes A/B/C/D for furnaces.
expand: Pyrometry — measurement control in heat treatment furnaces: thermocouple calibration, SAT (system accuracy test), TUS (temperature uniformity survey — Class 1-6). Nadcap HT lives and breathes this spec. An unsurveyed furnace = an invalid heat treatment.

def: A metric comparing a process's natural spread width to the tolerance width. Cp excludes centering, Cpk includes it.
expand: The bigger picture: Cp/Cpk (short-term, process variation only) vs. Pp/Ppk (actual performance including all noise). A significantly lower Ppk than Cpk = there are special causes between samples (shifts? material lots?). Typical automotive requirement: Ppk≥1.67 at initial approval, Cpk≥1.33 ongoing.

def: Process capability regardless of centering: Cp=(USL-LSL)/6s. 1.33+ acceptable, 1.67+ Six Sigma.
expand: The potential: (USL−LSL)/6σ — how many times the spread fits within the tolerance, ignoring centering. Cp=2.0 with Cpk=0.8 = an excellent process sitting in the wrong place — simple centering fixes it. A low Cp = a fundamental problem: a noisy process or an unrealistic tolerance.

def: Process capability including centering: Cpk=min[(USL-x)/3s,(x-LSL)/3s]. 1.33+ required under IATF.
expand: The calculation: the side closer to the limit governs. Example: μ=10.02, σ=0.01, tolerance 10±0.05 → Cpk=(10.05−10.02)/0.03=1.0 only, despite Cp=1.67. Conversions worth remembering: Cpk 1.0=2700ppm, 1.33=63ppm, 1.5=6.8ppm, 1.67=0.6ppm.

def: Defects per million opportunities — a Six Sigma metric. Cpk=1.33 gives DPMO of about 63, Cpk=1.67 gives about 0.57.
expand: Defects Per Million Opportunities — normalizes by the number of failure opportunities per unit (a complex product ≠ a simple one). The sigma scale: 3σ=66,807 | 4σ=6,210 | 5σ=233 | 6σ=3.4 DPMO. A fair comparison across different lines and products — hence industry adopted it.

def: A process improvement methodology — Six Sigma = a DPMO under 3.4, i.e. 99.99966% correctness. Includes DMAIC as the improvement cycle.
expand: Beyond statistics — a culture: decisions from data, mapped processes, continuous improvement in ROI-focused projects. A typical Black Belt project: 3-6 months, a measurable saving. The powerful tools: DOE (design of experiments), regression, MSA. Motorola 1986 → GE in the '90s → all of industry.

def: The Six Sigma cycle: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control. A data-driven problem-solving method.
expand: The map: Define (a project charter, voice of the customer) → Measure (MSA! then a baseline) → Analyze (statistically proven root causes) → Improve (DOE, a pilot) → Control (SPC, a control plan, documentation). The common mistake: jumping to Improve without Analyze — a solution without a diagnosis.

def: Measurement system analysis (MSA): equipment variation (EV) + appraiser variation (AV). %GRR of tolerance, max 10% excellent, above 30% unacceptable.
expand: Breaking down measurement variation: EV (Equipment Variation — the tool) + AV (Appraiser Variation — the inspectors). If AV>EV: a method/training problem, not equipment! A complementary metric: ndc≥5 (how many categories the system actually distinguishes). Before any Cpk analysis — GRR first, otherwise you're measuring noise.

def: The ratio of tolerance to measurement uncertainty: TUR=T/(2U). 4:1 or better per ANSI Z540.3.
expand: Test Uncertainty Ratio: how many times more accurate the measurement is than the tolerance being checked. The rule: 4:1 minimum (uncertainty ≤ a quarter of the tolerance), 10:1 ideal. A low TUR = a wide gray zone around the limits: accepting bad parts and rejecting good ones. Fix: a more accurate instrument or guard banding.

def: The maximum acceptable defect level in a sample — ISO 2859. Level II is common, AQL=1.0% is common for mechanical parts.
expand: Acceptable Quality Limit for acceptance sampling per ISO 2859: a table of lot size → sample size → acceptance number. AQL 1.0 = up to 1% defective is considered acceptable. Critical=0.065-0.25, Major=1.0, Minor=2.5-4.0. Important: AQL≠zero defects — aerospace customers require 100% inspection or Cpk instead.

def: Analysis of the measurement system — includes bias, linearity, stability, GRR. AIAG MSA 4th Edition.
expand: The full Measurement System Analysis: Bias (deviation from truth — calibration), Linearity (bias across the range), Stability (over time), GRR (repeatability+reproducibility). Per the AIAG MSA Manual. Before SPC and before Cpk — first prove the measurement itself is capable!

def: Statistical control of a process with X-bar/R, I-MR control charts — detecting and reacting to special variation.
expand: The application: pick a critical characteristic → an X̄-R chart (subgroups of 3-5) → limits from the first 25 subgroups → monitor. An out-of-limit point or a pattern (7 rising, 7 on the same side) = stop and investigate. The limits are the voice of the process (±3σ) — not the tolerance! A process can be in control and out of spec.

def: Control chart limits — 3 sigma from the mean. Different from the tolerance limits USL/LSL!
expand: The control limits: μ±3σ of the process — derived from the data, not the drawing! The critical distinction: UCL/LCL (the voice of the process) vs. USL/LSL (the voice of the customer). A point outside UCL but within USL = the process changed even though the part is good — investigate before there are defects.

def: Preliminary process capability before establishing control — uses overall sigma. Ppk lower than Cpk indicates instability.
expand: The actual performance: the same formula as Cpk but with overall σ across all the data (not the within-subgroup average). Always Ppk≤Cpk; a large gap = variation between groups (shift changes, material lots, adjustments). PPAP requires Ppk≥1.67 at initial approval — because there's no stability history yet.

def: First-piece inspection per AS9102 — measuring and documenting every drawing dimension before production runs.
expand: The logic: measuring the first part verifies the whole preparation chain — programming, fixturing, tooling, understanding the drawing. AS9102 Rev C is current. Efficiency: real-time FAI support (an inspector at the machine) saves rework loops. Digital FAI: software like Net-Inspect, DISCUS.

def: The production-part approval process in automotive (IATF) — 18 elements including PFMEA, control plan, MSA, Cpk.
expand: Production Part Approval Process — automotive's approval package (IATF 16949): 18 elements including PSW, dimensional FAI, MSA, initial SPC (Ppk≥1.67), FMEA, control plan. Submission levels 1-5 (3 is common). The message: prove the process is capable — not just that the part came out good.

def: A control plan describing monitoring and control measures at every production stage — part of APQP/PPAP.
expand: The living document of production: for every stage — the checked characteristic, spec, measurement method, sample size/frequency, control method (SPC/Go-NoGo/visual), and reaction to a deviation. Stages: Prototype→Pre-Launch→Production. Derived directly from the PFMEA: high risk = tight control.

def: An advanced product quality planning methodology in automotive — 5 stages from concept to mass production.
expand: Advanced Product Quality Planning — automotive's five-stage development framework: planning → product design (DFMEA) → process design (PFMEA, control plan) → validation (PPAP, Run@Rate) → production and feedback. The principle: quality planned in advance, not inspected after the fact.

def: High-speed tool steel M2/M42 — up to 600 degrees. Cheaper than carbide, suited to drills, mills, taps.
expand: M2/M35/M42 steels — resistant up to 550-600°C, cheap, very sharp and tough (doesn't break easily). Still relevant: drills, taps, broaches, tools with special shapes, and old machines with vibration. M42 (8% cobalt) for harder materials.

def: WC-Co tools — 3x harder than HSS, up to 1000 degrees. Used for inserts, broaches, and solid drills.
expand: WC-Co: tungsten carbide grains in a cobalt matrix. Hardness 1500-2000HV, resists up to 800-1000°C — enables 3-5x the Vc of HSS. More cobalt = tougher; less = harder. ISO grades: P (steel), M (stainless), K (cast iron), N (non-ferrous), S (superalloy).

def: A cutting tool for hard steels above 45HRC — second hardest after diamond. For hard turning.
expand: Cubic Boron Nitride — the second hardest after diamond, but chemically stable against iron (diamond dissolves in hot steel!). The use: hard turning of 45-65HRC steels instead of grinding, hard castings. Vc: 100-200 m/min in hardened material. Expensive — inserts with a brazed CBN tip.

def: A polycrystalline diamond tool for non-ferrous materials: Al, Cu, CFRP, plastic. Forbidden on steel because carbon reacts.
expand: Polycrystalline diamond — the absolute hardest, but breaks down in iron above 700°C (carbon diffusion). So only for non-ferrous: aluminum-silicon (engine blocks), copper, CFRP, graphite, glass. Tool life 50-100x carbide in aluminum. Vc in aluminum: 1000-3000 m/min.

def: A gold PVD coating on HSS/carbide tools — reduces friction, extends life 2-4x.
expand: The classic (gold) coating — PVD 2-4μm thick, hardness 2300HV, reduces friction and extends tool life 2-3x. Now considered basic — largely replaced by TiAlN/AlCrN for high performance. Still common in: taps, HSS drills, and punches.

def: A PVD coating for fast dry cutting — forms a protective Al2O3 layer under heat. Preferred for steels and Ti.
expand: The modern standard for carbide: cutting heat forms a self-regenerating Al₂O₃ layer that insulates the tool — the hotter it gets, the better it protects! Ideal for fast dry cutting of steels and stainless. AlTiN (more Al) for even higher heat. A dark purple-gray.

def: An amorphous carbon coating — very low friction. Excellent for Al/Cu and magnesium. Hardness 2000-5000HV.
expand: Diamond-Like Carbon: a friction coefficient of 0.05-0.15 (the lowest) — chips slide without sticking. The choice for aluminum and copper (fully prevents BUE), plastics, and engine components (lifters, pins). Not for hot steel — breaks down above 350°C.

def: The material removal rate: MRR=Vc*fn*ap (cubic mm per minute). A machining efficiency metric.
expand: The productivity metric: how many cm³ of material comes off per minute. Comparing strategies is always through MRR vs. tool life. iMachining/Adaptive raise MRR 2-3x with constant tool loading. Required power: P=MRR×kc/60000 — check the spindle can handle it.

def: An insert with a wiper radius — allows double feed at the same Ra. Improves productivity in turning.
expand: An edge geometry with a short straight segment after the radius — 'irons out' the feed peaks. Result: the same Ra at double feed, or half the Ra at the same feed. In finish turning = double the productivity for free. Limitation: requires rigidity (the straight segment increases contact), not for thin parts.

def: Insert classification per ISO 1832: S=square, C=triangle, T=triangle, R=round. SNMG120408 = a 12mm square, R0.8.
expand: Decoding: 1st letter shape (S=90° square, C=80° rhombic, D=55° rhombic, V=35°, W=trigon, T=triangle), 2nd letter clearance angle (N=0°), 3rd letter tolerance, 4th letter type/chip breaker. Digits: size, thickness, radius. CNMG120408 is the most common turning insert in the world.

def: Machining without coolant fluid — requires TiAlN-coated tools. Advantages: environment and cost. Disadvantage: high heat.
expand: No cutting fluid — saves about 15% of operating cost (fluid, filtration, disposal). Requires: a TiAlN/AlCrN coating that works hot, chip clearance with compressed air, and a machine that dissipates heat. Ideal for cast iron (the graphite self-lubricates) and milling steel. Problematic: aluminum (BUE), deep drilling.

def: Lubrication at a minimal rate, about 50 ml/hour — a compromise between dry and wet. Reduces coolant use by 95%.
expand: Minimum Quantity Lubrication: an oil mist at 20-100 ml/hour (vs. liters in flood) directly to the cutting zone. Advantages: dry chips ready for recycling, no fluid handling, halfway to 'green'. Works great in aluminum and drilling. Through-Tool MQL = the best.

def: Self-excited vibration in machining — causes wave marks and shortens tool life. Fixed by changing Vc/fn, trimming, a stability lobe diagram.
expand: Regenerative vibration that feeds itself: the wave from the previous revolution changes the current chip thickness.
