The smart fix: change RPM to a stable zone (a stability lobe) — sometimes faster is actually better! Tools: a harmonizer/tap test, variable-pitch cutters, an anti-vibration bar (Silent Tools).

def: Taylor's equation VcTn=C — n about 0.25 for HSS, n about 0.5 for carbide. Doubling Vc shortens tool life by a factor of 2^(1/n).
expand: Taylor's equation: Vc×T^n=C. Meaning: raising Vc by 20% shortens tool life by about 50% (carbide). So the economic optimization: if the tool is cheap and the machine is expensive — run fast and swap often. Criterion: VB=0.3mm flank wear for roughing, 0.1-0.15 for finishing.

def: Machining at very high speeds — Al above 1000 m/min. The heat goes into the chip, not the part. Requires a fast spindle.
expand: High Speed Machining: above a certain speed the heat goes into the chip instead of the tool (Salomon). In aluminum: 1000-3000 m/min with a 20-40K RPM spindle. Principles: small ap/ae, regular fz, huge speed — small forces that enable thin walls and precision. Mandatory: CAM with look-ahead.

def: Machining with electrical discharges — perforates any conductor regardless of hardness. Wire EDM for cutting, sinker EDM for cavities.
expand: Electro-erosive machining: sparks at 8,000-12,000°C vaporize material — hardness is irrelevant! Sinker for cavity shapes (a graphite electrode), Wire for pierced profiles. A critical downside: a brittle White Layer on the surface — must be removed in fatigue applications (polishing/etching).

def: A 6xxx bearing — carries radial and light axial loads. The most common. L10 life is calculated per C/P to the 3rd power.
expand: The mother bearing: an inner ring+outer ring+balls+cage. E.g. 6205: code 62=medium series, 05×5=⌀25 bore. Correct fitting: the rotating ring gets an interference fit (k5/m5), the stationary one a clearance fit. Installation: force only on the pressed ring — never through the balls!

def: A 7xxx bearing — carries significant Fa at a 15/25/40 degree angle. Mounted in pairs face-to-face X or back-to-back O.
expand: The angle determines everything: 15° (C) for maximum speed, 25° (AC) for a combination, 40° (B) for heavy axial. Universal Matching (suffix UA/UO) = bearings matched for pairing in any arrangement. A typical milling spindle: a 7014 P4 DB pair with light preload, lifetime grease.

def: An Nxxx bearing — high radial stiffness, doesn't carry Fa. Types N/NU. Higher C than balls at the same size.
expand: Line contact = huge radial capacity and maximum stiffness. NU (axially free — the free end of a shaft!), NJ (locates one direction), NUP (locked). High speed like balls. Uses: heavy gearboxes, rolling mill rolls, the free end of long shafts that expand thermally.

def: A 32xxx bearing — carries high Fa+Fr, requires preload. Common in automotive axles and heavy gearboxes.
expand: All the lines meet at one apex on the axis — pure rolling with no slip. Separable: the inner ring+rollers (the Cone) separates from the outer (the Cup) — convenient for assembly. Direction: always an opposing pair, and the preload is set manually (a defined drag torque or a measured endplay).

def: A 22/23xxx bearing — compensates for shaft misalignment. Carries heavy loads, a spherical outer raceway.
expand: Self-Aligning: the outer raceway is spherical — the inner is free to angle up to 2-3°. Forgives misalignment between supports (long shafts, welded frames). Spherical Roller (22xxx/23xxx) = the same principle with rollers for heavy loads — the leading bearing in heavy industry.

def: C — the constant load a bearing can carry for L10=10^6 revolutions. From the catalog. Units kN.
expand: C in the catalog — the basis for every life calculation. Comparing bearings: 6205 C=14kN vs. NU205 C=28.6kN — the roller bearing is double at the same size! But: the rating assumes perfect lubrication, precise alignment, and no contamination — in the field, derate 30-50% or use the corrected aISO.

def: C0 - the maximum load under static conditions. P0/C0 maximum 0.5 typical. Critical for shock loads.
expand: C0 — the limit before harmful plastic indentation. Uses: slow-rotating bearings (a slewing ring, a crane), momentary shock loads, and a stationary bearing under vibration (false brinelling!). Rule: P0 ≤ 0.5×C0 for smooth running, up to full C0 only for rare, exceptional loads.

def: P = X*Fr + Y*Fa - weights radial and axial load using X,Y factors from the catalog.
expand: P — converting (Fr, Fa) into a single radial load for the life formula. The mechanism: when the ratio Fa/Fr exceeds e, the axial component starts 'costing more' (a large Y). In a standard ball bearing, a large axial load kills life quickly — that's when you switch to angular contact or tapered.

def: Initial tightening of a bearing to remove internal play — improves accuracy and prevents skidding. Critical in spindle bearings.
expand: Three methods: a spring (a wave spring — fixed and simple, small spindles), a defined gap (a measured shim), or controlled torque (a nut + a drag gauge). The field metric: operating temperature — a bearing with excess preload heats above 70°C and enters a failure spiral.

def: Internal play: C2 reduced, CN standard, C3 wide, C4 very wide. C3 common for high temperatures.
expand: The internal play before mounting. The logic chain: an interference fit on the shaft eats ~80% of the fit as clearance; heat adds more; what remains is the true operating clearance — the target: slightly above zero. Hence an electric motor (a hot shaft) = C3 standard.

def: ABEC 1/3/5/7/9 precision grades — parallels ISO P0/P6/P5/P4/P2. ABEC5 is enough for a CNC spindle.
expand: Precision grades: ABEC 1/3/5/7/9 = ISO P0/P6/P5/P4/P2. The precision relates to dimensions and runout — not speed! A skateboard 'ABEC 11' is marketing. When to pay for P4/P5: spindles, metrology equipment, precision robotics. Most machines: P0 is excellent.

def: The American federal aviation regulations — defines design, manufacturing, and authority requirements.
expand: Federal Aviation Regulations: Part 21 (production and certification), Part 25 (airworthiness of passenger aircraft), Part 145 (repair stations). The manufacturer operates under a Production Certificate with an FAA-approved quality system. In Israel: the CAAI is the equivalent.

def: An FAA-designated engineer for approving technical documents — required for approved aerospace projects.
expand: Designated Engineering Representative: a private engineer delegated by the FAA authority to approve technical data (8110-3) — repairs, changes, substitutions. Saves months versus going through the authority directly. In STC and repair projects — the central figure.

def: A material review board for nonconforming parts — decides: use-as-is, rework, scrap, or return.
expand: Material Review Board: the forum for nonconforming parts — engineering+quality (+the customer in defense) decide: Use-As-Is (with documented justification!), Rework, Repair (via an approved process), or Scrap. An MRB crib = the cage holding parts awaiting a decision. UAI authority = only for the qualified.

def: A critical characteristic where deviation endangers safety/performance — marked on the drawing, requires SPC and 100% inspection.
expand: KC: characteristics whose variation is critical to safety/fit — marked on the drawing (a diamond/flag) and requiring: SPC or 100% inspection, proven Cpk, and enhanced documentation. AS9103 defines the management of it. Fewer KCs is good: only what's truly critical.

def: An aerospace bolt with a locking collar — fast installation, defined torque, common in aircraft skins.
expand: Aerospace's structural fastener: a precision pin + a collar that tightens until the hex breaks off at exactly the right preload — built-in torque, no torque wrench needed! One-sided access is enough for installation. HL-18/20... by diameter. Millions of units in every aircraft.

def: A blind rivet for aerospace — one-sided access, strength close to a solid rivet, FAA-approved.
expand: The structural blind rivet: installed from one side only (blind) with a mechanical stem lock — shear strength close to a solid rivet! For areas without rear access: control surfaces, closed panels. Installed with a dedicated gun, visual inspection per the manual.

def: A chromate conversion coating (Alodine 1200) for aluminum — corrosion protection and electrical conductivity.
expand: A trade name that became the generic term: a chromate conversion coating for aluminum (MIL-DTL-5541). Class 1A = maximum protection, Class 3 = electrical conductivity (grounding!). A characteristic gold-brown. Trivalent (Cr3+) replaces the carcinogenic version. The base beneath every aerospace primer.

def: Blasting steel/glass shot to create compressive stress in the surface layer — extends fatigue life. Almen test for control.
expand: Controlled shot blasting = a compressive stress layer (up to −60% of the material's strength) at a depth of 0.1-0.5mm — fatigue cracks don't open! Fatigue life ×3-10. Applications: springs, gears, propeller nuts, after hard chrome (which reduces fatigue life). Control: Almen + coverage.

def: A standard steel strip used to test shot peening intensity — measuring the strip's curvature = Almen intensity.
expand: The intensity gauge of peening: a standard steel strip (A=regular, N=fine, C=heavy) that bows from the stresses. The arc height at Almen deviation = the intensity. A saturation curve proves process stability. Every shift — a new strip is documented.

def: Counterfeit parts — a critical problem in aerospace. AS6081 defines prevention and inspection procedures for suppliers.
expand: The epidemic of counterfeit components: a gray market, 'recycled' components from scrap, re-marking. The defense (AS5553/AS6174): purchase only from authorized sources, full traceability to the manufacturer, acceptance testing (XRF for coating, cross-sections). In aerospace: a suspect part is destroyed, not returned!

def: The ability to trace a part through the supply chain — Heat number, Lot, certificate of origin. Mandatory in aerospace.
expand: The golden chain: from a finished part → a production lot → process certificates → raw material Heat → the original mill. In aerospace it's bidirectional: also forward — which aircraft did it go into? (a recall!). Implementation: Heat/Lot numbers on every certificate, part marking, and records kept 7-30 years.

def: Contact pressure between two geometries: p0 = F/(pi*a*b) for balls. Critical for gears, bearings, and cams.
expand: Point/line contact = a tiny area = enormous pressures: a ball bearing under normal load reaches 2-3 GPa beneath the surface! That's where contact fatigue (spalling) starts. Design: an allowable pressure per material and hardness — hardened bearing steel at 62HRC handles 4GPa. The basis for gear, bearing, and cam calculations.

def: Gear tooth strength: sigma = Ft*Kv/(m*b*Y). Y = the Lewis factor depending on tooth count. The basis of gear design.
expand: The classic model (1893!): the tooth as a bending beam with a factor Y from a table by tooth count. Still the basis for a quick estimate: σ=Ft/(b×m×Y) against material strength / SF. Modern standards (AGMA 2001, ISO 6336) wrap it with K factors for dynamics, load sharing, and surface.

def: A compression spring correction factor: Kw=(4C-1)/(4C-4)+0.615/C. C=D/d. Corrects for shear stress in the coil.
expand: In a compression spring, the inside of the coil suffers more: curvature + direct shear. Kw=(4C−1)/(4C−4)+0.615/C. The rule: C=4 → Kw=1.40 (+40% stress!), C=8 → Kw=1.18, C=12 → Kw=1.12. Sometimes neglected for a static calc; for fatigue — never.

def: C=D/d (mean diameter to wire diameter). C below 4 is hard to manufacture, C above 12 tends to buckle. Optimal 6-9.
expand: C = D/d (mean coil diameter / wire diameter). The healthy range: 4-12. C<4: high inner stresses, hard to coil, tool breakage. C>12: a 'soft' spring that tangles, buckling, poor tolerances. Manufacturing optimum: 6-9.

def: The hours of bearing life at which 90% will survive: L10h=(10^6/60n)*(C/P)^p. p=3 balls, p=3.33 rollers.
expand: From revolutions to hours: L10h = (10⁶/(60×n)) × (C/P)^p. Example: a 6208 bearing (C=32.5kN) under a 4kN load at 1500RPM: (32.5/4)³×10⁶/90000 ≈ 6,000 hours. Doubling the load = ÷8 life! So bumping up one bearing size is almost always worthwhile.

def: A conical spring washer — the h0/t ratio determines linearity: h0/t<0.4 nearly linear, h0/t=1.41 a zero point.
expand: A disc spring: enormous force in a tiny deflection. The magic is in the h₀/t ratio — above 1.4 you get a constant-force zone, even snap-through. Stacking: in series (same direction = force doubled), in parallel (opposed = deflection doubled). Uses: bearing preload, live bolts, clutches.

def: Calculating electrochemical coating thickness: m = I*t*M/(n*F). F = 96485 coulombs. Thickness = volume/area.
expand: Faraday's law for electroplating: the mass deposited ∝ current×time. Thickness = I×t×M/(n×F×ρ×A). Practically: nickel ~12μm per hour at 1A/dm². The coverage isn't uniform — corners and edges get more (current density!), recesses get less. Hence electroless is better for complex geometry.

def: Error-proofing an assembly by design — an asymmetric pin, a key, a non-symmetric shape. Forces correct assembly only.
expand: A design that makes an error impossible: an asymmetric pin (only one orientation fits), connectors with different shapes (can't be swapped), a sensor that blocks continuation without the part. 100x better than end-of-line inspection — the error simply can't happen. Also applied in CNC fixtures: an inverted part won't fit.

def: A bolt tightened beyond the elastic limit — a single-use replacement. Common in cylinder heads and structural fasteners.
expand: TTY: the bolt is tightened deliberately beyond its yield point (a torque+angle method: 40Nm then 90°+90°). The advantage: uniform, maximum clamping force, indifferent to friction. The cost: the bolt stretches plastically — single use! Modern cylinder heads: always new bolts.

def: An initial clamping force in a bolt — 70-90% of Fy*As. Prevents loosening and keeps the joint tight.
expand: The force that holds the joint: 70-90% of the bolt's capacity. The principle: as long as preload exceeds the external load — the bolt barely feels cyclic loads (the gasket/parts carry them)! Insufficient preload = the bolt absorbs all the fatigue cycles = fracture.

def: Thread failure in shear — prevented by a minimum thread engagement depth of 1D in steel, 2D in aluminum.
expand: Thread Stripping: shear failure of the threads instead of a bolt breaking. The rule: engagement depth ≥ 1×d in steel, 1.5×d in aluminum, 2×d and up in plastic — so the bolt breaks before the threads tear (a predictable, visible failure). A stripped thread in an expensive block = a Helicoil repair.

def: 0.8mm stainless wiring connecting bolts and preventing rotational loosening — common in aerospace and engines.
expand: Aerospace safety wiring: 0.5-0.8mm stainless wire threaded through drilled bolt heads in pairs — always in a direction that pulls toward tightening! Twisting: 6-8 twists per inch with a dedicated tool. Even if a bolt slightly loosens — the wire stops it. NASM33540 defines everything.

def: A nut with a nylon ring — prevents loosening through friction. Single use recommended, up to 120 degrees only.
expand: A nut with a nylon collar that the bolt cuts a thread into — continuous friction preventing self-rotation. Prevailing torque: felt throughout the turn, not just at the end. Limits: up to ~120°C, and 2-3 uses max (the nylon relaxes). An all-metal (Stover) version for heat.

def: An anaerobic adhesive for locking threads: 222 low strength, 243 medium, 263 high, 270 maximum. Clean the part first.
expand: An anaerobic adhesive — cures only in metal contact with no air (inside the thread). Colors: 222 purple (weak, M2-M6), 243 blue (medium, removable with tools — the standard!), 271/277 red (strong, disassembly only with 250°C heat), 290 green (wicks into an assembled thread). A clean surface = half the job.

def: CNC code - G0 rapid, G1 linear feed, G2/G3 arc. M3 spindle forward, M30 program end.
expand: The skeleton: G00/G01/G02/G03 moves, G17-19 planes, G40-42 radius offset, G43 length offset, G54-59 work coordinate systems, G80-89 canned cycles, G90/91 absolute/incremental. The G83 drilling cycle (peck) is the most common in daily work.

def: Tool offsets on a CNC machine: H length, D radius. Allows using different tools without changing the program.
expand: Two offsets per tool: H (length, G43) measured with a presetter or by touch-off; D (radius, G41/G42) allows programming the final contour with the machine compensating. Tool wear? Adjust in tenths in the offset without touching the program. An error in H = a collision!

def: Radial deviation of a rotating tool from the axis center — affects Ra and tool life. Maximum 0.005-0.01mm.
expand: A tool not rotating on center: one tooth works hard and the others less — poor Ra, short tool life (one tooth wears), and an oversized diameter. Targets: <10μm general, <5μm finish, <3μm HSM. Improvements: a hydraulic/shrink-fit holder, cleaning the taper, checking with an indicator.

def: The state of the surface layer after machining: Ra, residual stress, structural distortion, micro-cracks. Critical for fatigue.
expand: Beyond Ra: what's happening beneath the surface? Residual stress (compression=good for fatigue, tension=bad), a white layer (EDM/aggressive grinding), work hardening, micro-cracks. In aerospace and medical checked with: XRD for stress, metallography for layers. Shot peening adds intentional compression.

def: A rolling circular cutting path — very small ae, large ap. Excellent for hard materials and deep slots.
expand: The tool rolls arcs: a small ae (5-10%D) with a huge ap (2-3×D) — a constant, small engagement angle, low heat, and the whole flute length works. Result: 2-3x the MRR in slots and hard materials (Ti, Inconel, 17-4). Every modern CAM: Adaptive/Dynamic/iMachining.

def: Corrosion between two different metals in the presence of an electrolyte — the EMF potential gap determines severity. Al+steel=a problem.
expand: The principle: the active metal (anode) sacrifices itself to the noble metal (cathode). The distance metric: seawater potential — Mg the most anodic, graphite/gold the most cathodic. The design rule: bolts should always be more noble than the plate (an SS bolt in an Al plate = fine; the reverse = disaster).

def: Accelerated corrosion in narrow crevices — low O2 concentration creates an anode. Common in bolted joints.
expand: Crevice: in narrow crevices the oxygen concentration plummets — the area becomes anodic against the exposed surface. Attacks gaskets, threads, and overlaps. Stainless is at high risk. Prevention: pocket-free design (full welding), sealing, and drainage. Resistance test: ASTM G48 Method B.

def: Localized pitting corrosion — common in 304 stainless in the presence of chloride. Prevented by 316 SS (Mo) or a coating.
expand: Pitting: a localized flaw in the passive layer → a hole that deepens at a dizzying rate (an extreme area ratio). Cl⁻ is the main trigger. The danger: negligible metal loss but a punctured tank/pipe! Monitoring: can't be seen by eye — UT/RT. Material selection by PREN.

def: A salt environment resistance test at 5% NaCl — 100 hours baseline, 500 hours good, 1000 hours excellent for outdoor parts.
expand: ASTM B117: continuous 5% NaCl fog at 35°C. Benchmarks: yellow Zn 96-200h, Zn-Ni 720h, EN 500-1000h, anodize 336h, QPQ 500h+. Important to understand: an accelerated comparative test — doesn't translate directly to service years! Cyclic Tests (ASTM G85) are more realistic.

def: Cracking from tensile stress in a corrosive environment — 7075-T6 sensitive in NaCl, 304 SS in chloride.
expand: Stress Corrosion Cracking: fully brittle, branching cracks — no plastic warning! The stress can be purely residual from welding/machining. Historical examples: bridge collapses, pipeline bursts. Diagnosis: metallography shows a branched inter/transgranular crack.

def: Grain boundary corrosion — common in unstabilized 304 stainless. Prevented by using 304L/316L.
expand: Intergranular Corrosion: attack along chromium-depleted grain boundaries after sensitization (450-850°C — welding!). The structure crumbles like sugar. Test: ASTM A262 Practice E. Prevention: 304L/316L (C<0.03%), stabilized 321/347, or solution annealing.

def: An engineering order documenting a specific drawing change — defines a date, an author, and required approvals.
expand: Engineering Order: a localized engineering instruction — a temporary change, a deviation authorization for a defined batch, or a one-time work order. Unlike a permanent ECO — an EO has an expiration: a quantity or a date. Tracked so it doesn't become a 'creeping permanent'.

def: A product data management system — SolidWorks PDM, Windchill, Teamcenter. Manages versions and BOM.
expand: Product Data Management: the vault of CAD files — check-in/out (no overwrites!), automatic versioning, assembly-part links, and permissions. SolidWorks PDM is the common one in Israel. The difference from PLM: PDM=files; PLM=the whole lifecycle and processes.

def: Product lifecycle management from the first version to retirement — includes PDM, ERP, changes, and documents.
expand: The big picture: from an idea to decommissioning — requirements, CAD, BOM, ECO, manufacturing, service. A digital thread: the continuous information thread between every stage. Implementation is hard (processes!) but the result: one source of truth for the whole organization.

def: A complete product definition in 3D CAD including GD&T — eliminates 2D drawings. ASME Y14.41 / ISO 16792.
expand: Model-Based Definition: the model = the drawing. All the PMI is on the 3D, with no 2D at all. The chain: design → CAM reads directly → CMM builds an automatic inspection program → zero translations and interpretations. STEP AP242 = the format. The next generation is already here.

def: A digital copy of a physical product with real-time sensor data — enables monitoring and predictive maintenance.
expand: The digital twin: a live model of the physical product, fed by real-time sensors. Uses: predictive maintenance (the engine 'feels' a wearing bearing), performance optimization, risk-free scenario simulation. GE, Siemens lead; the infrastructure: IoT+cloud+FEA.

def: The arithmetic mean of the deviation from the center line. The most common parameter.
expand: Ra is calculated over an evaluation length divided into 5 equal segments. Represents the average of peaks and valleys from the mean line. Ra=0.8 for clearance fits, Ra=0.2 for dynamic seals. Limitation: Ra isn't sensitive to isolated scratches — two different surfaces can give the same Ra.

def: The average of the 5 highest peaks and 5 deepest valleys. More sensitive than Ra to defects.
expand: Rz = the average of (Rz1+Rz2+Rz3+Rz4+Rz5), each Rzi = a peak-to-valley within a sampling window. More important than Ra for sealing: a single scratch = a high Rz, Ra stays low. Rz/Ra = 4 for grinding, 7 for turning. Rule: Rz = 4-7 x Ra.

def: The maximum height among all sampling windows. The worst case.
expand: Rmax = Max(Rzi) across all windows. If Rmax >> Rz — there's an isolated defect (a scratch, a bubble). Needed for the worst case: high-pressure seals, fatigue, critical seals.

def: ISO 1302 classification. N1=Ra 0.025 (fine) to N12=Ra 50 (as-cast).
expand: N1-N3: polishing/lapping (optics, bearings). N4-N6: grinding (fits, gears). N7: Ra 1.6 = a good default for most. N8: Ra 3.2 = general ISO 2768. N9-N12: coarse. Each N grade step = x1.5-2 in cost!

def: The direction of the machining marks on the surface. Significant for sealing and wear.
expand: Marks: = parallel, ⊥ perpendicular, x crossed (honing), M multi-directional, C circular. For sealing: Lay perpendicular to the leak direction = better. Honing: a 30-60° Cross-Hatch = retains oil. Ra measurement must be taken perpendicular to Lay!

def: A separating wavelength between roughness and waviness. Default: 0.8mm.
expand: lambda-c separates roughness (short waves) from waviness (long waves). The default 0.8mm suits Ra 0.1-2.0. Changing lambda-c changes Ra! It must be noted on the drawing if different. 5 windows x lambda-c = the evaluation length.

def: A mid-frequency form error. Between roughness and form error. Caused by vibration.
expand: Waviness is caused by: chatter, thermal distortion, repeating machine errors. Measured in Wa, Wz. Waviness = a process problem, not a tool problem. Fix: change RPM, improve clamping, check spindle bearings.

def: Thermal damage in grinding: microstructure change, reduced hardness, residual tensile stress.
expand: Caused by: high Vc + insufficient coolant + infrequent dressing. Detection: color change (heat/blue), Temper Etch per AMS 2649. Consequences: fatigue life drops x3-10, sudden failure. Prevention: adequate coolant, low infeed, frequent dressing, a CBN wheel. In aerospace: 100% Temper Etch!

def: Abrasive machining with axial + rotational motion. Ra 0.05-0.4. Cross-hatch.
expand: Honing is used for engine cylinders, hydraulic cylinders. Creates a cross-hatch at a 45-60 degree angle = oil retention + piston braking force. Plateau honing = 2 stages: roughing then finishing = a negative Rsk = excellent load-bearing.

def: Rubbing with an abrasive slurry. Ra 0.01-0.1. The most precise for surface finishing.
expand: Lapping for valves, gauge blocks, optics. Abrasive grains (Al2O3, SiC, diamond) in a fluid. Removes only 0.001-0.01mm. Multi-direction = uniform Ra, Lay=M. Not suited to hard parts without a diamond tool.

def: Finishing with an oscillating stone. Ra 0.01-0.05. For bearing rollers.
expand: An oscillating stone at 80-1000Hz + coolant. Removes 0.001-0.005mm. Creates a negative Rsk (a plateau) = excellent load-bearing. 3M Superfinishing Tape is common for rollers. After superfinishing: bearing life x2-5!

def: Pressing a hard roller/ball on the surface. Ra 0.05-0.2 without material removal.
expand: Burnishing = improving Ra with no chips! Plastic pressing of the peaks. Also creates residual compressive stress = higher fatigue life. Fast: 1-3 minutes per part. Suited to shafts, hydraulic cylinders.

def: Electrochemical removal of a metal layer. Ra 0.1-0.4. Mainly for stainless.
expand: Electropolish = the opposite of coating. The part = the anode, removes 5-20 microns from the peaks (smooths it!). Advantages: low Ra, excellent passivation, no burrs, a bright appearance. Uses: medical, food, pharma (GMP). Usually 304/316 stainless only. Acid: H2SO4+H3PO4.

def: Designing a part to be easy and cheap to manufacture. 80% of cost is set at the design stage!
expand: DFM includes: choosing the right material, minimal tolerance, minimal Ra, standard dimensions, minimum setups, tool access. Golden rule: a change on the drawing = ₪100, in production = ₪10,000, in the field = ₪100,000! Removing one feature = a significant cost reduction.

def: Designing parts to be easy to assemble. Fewer parts, a simple assembly direction.
expand: 3 DFA questions: does the part move relative to its neighbors? Is it a different material? Is disassembly required? If not — merge it into one part! A snap-fit = 1.5 seconds. A bolt = 6 seconds. A 50% part-count reduction = a 30% assembly cost reduction.

def: A design that prevents incorrect assembly. A pin, a slot, a color, a different size.
expand: Poka-Yoke (Japanese: preventing an inadvertent error). Examples: 2 locating pins (round + diamond) = one orientation only. Asymmetric USB-A = one direction. An asymmetric part = eliminated scrap. Far better than end-of-line QC.

def: The ratio: raw stock weight purchased / finished part weight. BTF=1.0 = ideal, no waste.
expand: BTF 1.1 = a shaft from bar (little waste). BTF 1.6 = complex pockets. BTF 4 = hogging out from a plate. BTF 20 = a monolithic aerospace part (95% goes to chips!). Ti-6Al-4V at BTF=10 = very expensive. Near net shape (casting) = BTF 1.5-3 = enormous savings.

def: A manufacturing process yielding a shape close to final. Minimal additional machining.
expand: NNS processes: investment casting (±0.1mm), die casting, MIM, powder metallurgy, precision forging. BTF=1.1-1.5 instead of 5-20! Advantage: material and machining savings. Disadvantage: high tooling cost = ROI only at volume.

def: A preparation operation before machining: fixturing, tool setup, zero setting. Every setup = a cost.
expand: Setup includes: positioning the part, setting the work offset G54, tool length offset, running the first part, corrections. Typical time: 30-120 minutes. Cost = time x rate / quantity. At 100 parts = small. At 1 part = 50-80% of the price! DFM: reduce setups = done-in-one.

def: A small notch at a pocket corner, allowing a round tool to reach a sharp corner.
expand: A milling tool = round = always a corner radius. If a sharp corner is needed: a dog bone (a small circle at the corner) or a T-bone (a straight slot). Without it: EDM only = 10x the cost! Rule: a larger corner R = a lower cost.

def: A feature not directly accessible to a tool. Requires a special tool or an additional setup.
expand: Undercut examples: a groove beneath a shoulder, a side hole, a thread relief. Solutions: a T-slot tool, back boring, multi-axis. DFM rule: avoid undercuts! If unavoidable: DIN 509 Type E/F/G/H. Cost: x2-5 vs. a simple feature.

def: A small angle on the walls of a cast part, allowing release from the mold.
expand: Required in: die casting (0.5-3 degrees), sand casting (1-5), plastic injection (1-5), forging (3-7). Without draft: the part sticks in the mold = breakage = scrap. Side action/cam = draft=0 possible but a much higher tooling cost.

def: An extra layer of material on stock/a casting for finish machining. 0.1-5mm depending on process.
expand: Stock: grinding = 0.1-0.3mm per side. Finish milling = 0.3-1mm. Roughing = 1-3mm. Sand casting = 2-5mm. Forging = 3-8mm. Too much = a long machining time. Too little = doesn't clean up to finish. Plan uniform stock = less chatter.

def: A test with fluid at 1.25-1.5x working pressure. The safest. ASME B31.3.
expand: Principle: an incompressible fluid = a failure, not an explosion! ASME B31.3: 1.5xP_design. ASME VIII: 1.3xMAWP. Required: a vent at the high point, a calibrated pressure gauge ±1%, a 10-30 minute hold time. Pass criteria: no pressure drop, no leak, no permanent distortion.

def: A test with gas (air/N2). 1.1x working pressure. Very high danger!
expand: Compressed gas = enormous stored energy. A failure = destructive! Hence only 1.1x P (lower than hydro). Required: safety engineer approval, a barricade, gradual ramp-up 25-50-75-100%, N2 preferred over air. Detection: soap water / a snoop. When: when water is prohibited (O2 lines, catalysts).

def: The maximum working pressure allowed for a pressure vessel. The basis for calculating test pressure.
expand: MAWP is calculated from: wall thickness, material, design temperature. Test pressure = MAWP x 1.3 (ASME VIII) or 1.5 (ASME B31.3). Marked on the nameplate. A lower MAWP = greater thickness = higher cost and weight.

def: A leak test with sensitivity down to 10^-12 mbar L/s. The most sensitive.
expand: He = a small molecule = penetrates any leak. A mass spectrometer detects He ions. Methods: sniffer (He inside, a sniffer outside), vacuum (He outside, MS inside = higher sensitivity), bombing (pressurize with He then measure outgassing He). Uses: space, nuclear, medical, HVAC.

def: An automatic test: pressurize, wait, measure the drop. Go/no-go.
expand: Principle: pressurize with air, wait 30-120 seconds, measure the pressure change. A large change = a leak. Problem: a 1-degree temperature change = a significant pressure change! Solution: differential pressure = a reference volume. Manufacturers: ATEQ, InterTech. Common on automotive production lines.

def: Integrity tests without damaging the part: PT, MT, UT, RT, PAUT, ET.
expand: PT (dye penetrant): open surface cracks. MT (magnetic particle): ferromagnetic only. UT (ultrasonic): internal cracks + thickness. RT (X-ray): full internal composition. PAUT (phased array): replacing RT. ET (eddy current): coatings, tubing. Calibration mandatory before every test!

def: NDT: dye penetrates open cracks, cleaning, developer, cracks appear.
expand: Stages: 1) thorough cleaning, 2) applying penetrant (dwell 10-30 minutes), 3) removing excess, 4) developer (pulls dye out of cracks). Visible = red, UV = glowing green (more sensitive). Limitation: open surface-breaking cracks only! Standards: ASME V Art.6, ASTM E165.

def: Sound waves at 1-25MHz to detect internal defects and measure wall thickness.
expand: Straight beam (0 degrees): thickness + lamination. Angle beam (45/60/70 degrees): weld cracks. TOFD: precise defect sizing. PAUT: a sensor array = full scanning. A couplant is mandatory (gel/water). Calibration: an IIW block. Advantage over RT: no radiation, faster.

def: Measuring fracture energy under impact. A V-notch specimen. Units: joules. Per ASTM E23.
expand: A 256J pendulum strikes a 10x10x55mm specimen with a V-notch. Energy absorbed = toughness. DBTT: carbon steel in the cold = sudden fracture! ASME VIII: Charpy is required for MDMT. Requirements: 27J (general), 20J (minimum). Adding Ni lowers the DBTT.

def: A destructive test: raising pressure to failure. Determines burst pressure. Water only!
expand: Medium: water only for safety! Safety factor: burst/MAWP >= 4 (ASME). Barlow: P_burst = 2 x UTS x t / OD. Uses: design validation, R&D, material failure. A pressure gauge + a data logger. Water = no explosion if the vessel fails.

def: Engineering below 120K (minus 153 degrees). Liquefied gases, special materials.
expand: Cryogenic = below 120K by definition. Temperatures: LNG=-162, LOX=-183, LN2=-196, LH2=-253, LHe=-269 degrees Celsius. Challenges: thermal contraction, BCC brittle fracture, boil-off gas, insulation. Uses: LNG, space, nuclear, MRI.

def: Nitrogen at minus 196 degrees (77K). The most common cryogenic liquid.
expand: LN2: available, cheap, non-flammable, non-toxic (unless it displaces oxygen!). Uses: cryogenic treatment, biological preservation, shrink fitting, superconducting magnets. Dangers: asphyxiation (O2 depletion in a closed space!), cold burns. PPE: cryogenic gloves + a face shield!

en: Crystal Structure Cryogenic Behavior FCC BCC
def: FCC = flexible in cold. BCC = brittle in cold. A golden rule for selecting cryogenic material.
expand: FCC (Al, Cu, Ni, austenitic SS): high toughness at any temperature! No ductile-brittle transition. BCC (carbon steel, ferritic SS): a DBTT exists = brittle in cold! Rule: cryogenics = FCC only! SS 304, 316, Al 5083, Inconel 718 = excellent choices.

def: The temperature below which BCC steel transitions to sudden fracture. Dangerous!
expand: C-Mn steel: DBTT around 0 to minus 40 degrees. Adding Ni lowers the DBTT. 9% Ni steel: DBTT < minus 196 degrees = suitable for LNG! Adding C and Mn raises the DBTT (worse). DBTT doesn't exist in FCC. Measured with the Charpy impact test.

def: Cooling tools to minus 196 degrees. Converts retained austenite. Increases tool life.
expand: DCT: slow cooling to minus 196 degrees (24-36 hours) then slow warming. Retained austenite (RA) = austenite not transformed during hardening = soft and unstable. DCT converts RA to martensite = hardness + wear resistance. Results: tool life x2-5! Also reduces residual stress. Materials: D2, M2, H13, 52100.

def: Gas evaporating from a cryogenic tank due to heat absorption. Must be managed to avoid excess pressure.
expand: BOG is caused by: ambient heat, pumps, filling. Rate: an LNG tank about 0.05-0.1% per day. Management: re-liquefaction, a fuel gas system, venting. Never seal a cryogenic vessel hermetically = BOG pressure = explosion! A PRV (pressure relief valve) is mandatory on every cryogenic vessel.

def: Aluminum layers + spacers in vacuum. The best thermal insulation for cryogenics.
expand: MLI = 20-80 layers of aluminized Mylar with a spacer (Dacron) between them, in vacuum. Thermal coefficient: k < 0.0001 W/mK (1000x the insulation of polystyrene!). Requires vacuum < 10^-2 mbar. Uses: LH2, LHe tanks, space. At atmospheric pressure: MLI barely insulates!

def: A valve with an extended neck to keep the packing away from the cryogenic fluid.
expand: The extended neck creates a temperature gradient: cryogenic fluid at the bottom, packing at ambient temperature at the top. Prevents: packing freeze-up, malfunction. Types: globe, ball, gate, check. Mandatory for LN2/LHe/LOX. Also: a bellows seal = zero leakage.

def: OEE = availability x performance x quality. World class >= 85%.
expand: Availability = uptime / scheduled time. Performance = actual rate / theoretical. Quality = good parts / total. OEE=85% = world class. OEE<65% = a problem. A 1% OEE improvement = 1% higher output with no investment. SMED = single minute exchange of die = reducing setup time.

def: A one-time cost: CAM programming, fixtures, special tools, FAI. Not in the per-part price.
expand: NRE = everything paid once: CAM programming (₪500-5000), a dedicated fixture (₪1000-20000), special tools, the first FAI. Shown separately in a quote! Break-even = NRE / (price - variable cost) = the minimum quantity for viability.

def: Every doubling of quantity lowers cost by a fixed percentage. An 80% LC = a 20% drop per doubling.
expand: Wright's formula: C_n = C1 x n^b. LC=80%: b = log(0.8)/log(2) = -0.322. Example: C1=₪1000, C1000 = 1000 x 1000^(-0.322) = about ₪177! Uses: large-run costing, aerospace. The decline is realistic — not infinite.

def: Indirect costs: rent, electricity, coolant, insurance, management. Usually 25-45%.
expand: Overhead: rent/depreciation, machine depreciation, electricity (CNC = 15-40kW x ₪0.5 per kWh), coolant + oils, cutting tools (5-15% of the hourly rate), insurance, management + sales. Calculation: OH rate = indirect costs / production hours. A small shop: 25-30%. Aerospace: 40-50%.

def: A per-unit price reduction as quantity rises. Results from spreading NRE + the learning curve.
expand: A typical structure: 1-9 units = ₪500, 10-49 = ₪350, 50-99 = ₪250, 100-499 = ₪180, 500+ = ₪130. Results from: lower NRE/part, lower setup/part, learning, less scrap. A quote always comes with price breaks! A customer can save a lot by ordering a larger quantity.

def: The time from order to receipt. Includes: material + machining + finishing + inspection + shipping.
expand: Components: material (off-the-shelf=1-3 days, special=2-8 weeks!), CAM programming (1-3 days), machining (3-14 days), coating (3-10 days), FAI (2-5 days), shipping (1-2 days). Typical total: 2-4 weeks simple, 6-12 weeks complex. Urgency: x1.3-2.0 price!

def: A full inspection of the first part to confirm compliance with all drawing requirements. AS9102.
expand: FAI per AS9102 Rev.B: 3 parts: design documentation, product accountability, characteristic accountability. Checks: every dimension, material (mill cert), coating, marking, NDT. Cost: ₪200-500. Required: a new part, a design change, a new machine, a production break. PPAP = the automotive version.

def: Prevention cost + appraisal + internal failure + external failure. Goal: minimum COQ.
expand: Rule: ₪1 prevention = ₪10 appraisal = ₪100 internal failure = ₪1000 external failure! Prevention: training, design, SPC. Appraisal: inspections, audits. Internal failure: scrap, rework. External failure: warranty, recalls, reputation damage.

def: The percentage of rejected parts out of total production. Target: < 2%. Direct impact on cost.
expand: Scrap Rate = rejected parts / total. A 5% scrap rate = the real cost is 5% higher + wasted material and time. Real cost/part = cost / (1 - scrap rate). 10% scrap = x1.11 cost. Fix: SPC, poka-yoke, process control. Lower scrap = straight to profit.

def: The relative speed of motion between the tool and the part. m/min. Vc = pi x D x n / 1000.
expand: Vc = pi x D(mm) x n(RPM) / 1000. Raising Vc = more heat = shorter tool life (Taylor). Lowering Vc = BUE = poor Ra. Recommended Vc: Al=400-800, steel=80-200, SS=80-180, Ti=30-60, Inconel=20-40 m/min. Limits: maximum RPM, vibration, coolant.

def: The tool's advance distance per revolution. mm/rev. A major factor in Ra during turning.
expand: fn = Vf(mm/min) / n(RPM). Ra formula: Ra = fn^2 / (8 x Rnose) x 1000. A wiper insert: the same Ra at double fn = higher productivity! Roughing fn: 0.2-0.5mm. Finishing fn: 0.05-0.15mm. A worn nose: poor Ra even at low fn.

def: The feed per milling tooth. mm/tooth. Vf = fz x z x n.
expand: fz = Vf / (z x n). Raising fz = higher Ra + higher MRR. Lowering fz = lower Ra. Too low fz = rubbing (friction without cutting) = heat! Chip thinning: ae < D/2 = a thinner chip = fz can be raised. Roughing fz for Al: 0.05-0.15mm. Finishing: 0.01-0.05mm.

def: The tool's penetration depth in the Z axis. mm. Affects cutting force and vibration.
expand: ap in turning = the layer thickness. In milling = the depth in Z. Raising ap = higher force, higher MRR, vibration. Roughing ap: 2-5mm (steel), 3-8mm (Al). Finishing ap: 0.2-0.5mm. Trochoidal: a small ae + a large ap = high MRR without excessive heat!

def: The contact width between the tool and material. mm. Stepover in ball milling.
expand: ae = the milling width. ae/D: 50-100% = slotting (a full slot). 30-50% = a shoulder. 5-10% = trochoidal. Lowering ae = a lower Ra (ball mill). Scallop height = ae^2 / (8 x R). Raising ae = higher force + heat. Chip thinning when ae < D/2.

def: The volume of material removed per unit time. cm3/min. Directly tied to machining time and cost.
expand: MRR (turning) = Vc x fn x ap (cm3/min). MRR (milling) = ae x ap x Vf / 1000. Raising MRR = shorter time = lower cost. Spindle power: P = MRR x kc / 60,000,000 kW. Trochoidal: MRR x2-3 higher with no rise in power!

def: Vc x T^n = C. Raising Vc = a sharp drop in tool life. n = the tool material factor.
expand: Formula: T = (C/Vc)^(1/n). n for carbide = 0.2-0.4. Rule: Vc x2 = T x (0.5)^(1/n). n=0.25: Vc x2 = life x0.177 = very short! Raising Vc by 20% = a 50% drop in life! Raising fn affects it less than Vc. VB: 0.3mm roughing, 0.1-0.2mm finishing.

def: Material buildup on the tool edge at low cutting speed. Causes poor Ra and inaccuracy.
expand: BUE forms at low Vc + high pressure + insufficient coolant. Material sticks to the tool = grows = poor Ra + higher force. Shed BUE = a scratch on the surface. Prevention: raising Vc, adequate coolant, a TiN/DLC coating (low friction). Al especially tends toward BUE.

def: Self-excited vibration in machining. Marks on the surface, noise, poor Ra, short tool life.
expand: Mechanism: a wave on the surface = a varying force = vibration = a larger wave. A stability lobe diagram: RPM vs. ap = stable/unstable zones. Fix: change RPM to a stable zone, decrease ap, a variable-helix end mill, an anti-vibration bar. FRF = frequency response function = a tap test.

def: A rolling circular path. Small ae + large ap = high MRR + low heat.
expand: Trochoidal: ae=5-10% D, ap=1-3xD. Advantages: MRR x2-3 higher, low heat (the tool doesn't stay in continuous contact), tool life x2-5, suited to SS, Ti, Inconel. CAM: Mastercam Dynamic, Fusion 360 Adaptive. Downside: longer programming time.

def: Turning hard parts, HRC45-65, with CBN/ceramic. An alternative to grinding.
expand: CBN: Vc=80-200 m/min, ceramic: 150-400. ap=0.05-0.3mm, fn=0.05-0.15mm. Advantages vs. grinding: shorter time, shape flexibility, lower machine cost. Disadvantages: higher Ra (0.4-0.8 vs. 0.1-0.4), less precise roundness. Suited to: small quantities, complex shapes.

def: Climb (down): the tool enters at full thickness, the chip decreases. Better Ra. Always on CNC.
expand: Climb: the tool enters at full chip thickness and drops to zero. Good Ra, good tool life, no BUE. Conventional: the thickness rises from zero to full. Poor Ra, higher heat. When to use conventional: old machines with backlash, the first pass on a casting skin. Modern CNC: always climb!

def: Material stiffness: the ratio of stress to strain in the elastic range. GPa.
expand: E is fixed for each material family — doesn't change with heat treatment! Steel=207, stainless=193, Al=69, Ti=114, Mg=45 GPa. Meaning: an Al part deflects 3x more than steel under the same load. Hardening 4140 doesn't change its stiffness — only its strength. To change stiffness: change geometry or material.

def: The ratio of lateral contraction to longitudinal elongation under tension. ~0.3 for metals.
expand: When a rod is stretched — it narrows: ν = lateral strain/longitudinal strain. Metals ≈ 0.27-0.34, rubber ≈ 0.5 (preserves volume!), cork ≈ 0 (hence good for stoppers). Important in FEA, wall-thickness pressure calcs, and interference fits (the shaft shortens slightly under pressing).

def: A steel with lead — the best machinability. For screw-machine parts at volume.
expand: The lead (0.15-0.35%) breaks chips and lubricates the tool — 160% the machinability of 1212! High Vc, excellent Ra, long tool life. The cost: must never be welded (toxic fumes!), low strength, prohibited for food contact/strict RoHS. A lead-free substitute: 1215, 1144.

def: The basic American structural steel: Sy=250MPa. Plates, profiles, welding.
expand: ASTM A36: the cheapest and most available in structural shapes. Excellent welding with no preheat (low CE). The European equivalent: S235JR. Not for precise dimensions (hot rolled, scale) and not for hardening. For higher loads: A572-50 or S355.

def: The common machining brass: 3% lead = 100% machinability (the reference!).
expand: C360 is the machinability benchmark — every material is measured against it. A very short chip, a bright Ra, high speeds. Uses: fittings, plumbing hardware, instrument parts. Warnings: dezincification in hot water (switch to DZR), forbidden with ammonia (SCC).

def: Commercially pure titanium: perfect corrosion resistance, moderate strength, weldable.
expand: Grade 2 = the most common pure titanium: Sy=275MPa (like A36!) but a density of 4.5 and fantastic chemical resistance (chlorine, seawater, oxidizing acids). Relatively easy TIG welding. Uses: heat exchangers, chemical, implants. For strength: Grade 5 (Ti-6Al-4V) is 3x stronger.

def: 36% nickel: near-zero CTE (1.2 ppm/°C). For metrology tools and precision molds.
expand: Invar = Invariable: thermal expansion 10x lower than steel! Uses: aerospace composite tooling (autoclave!), metrology tools, laser frames, watches. Machining: gummy and hard (like soft stainless), work-hardens. Expensive — used only when CTE is critical.

def: An 80% nickel alloy with enormous magnetic permeability — 'absorbs' magnetic fields.
expand: Mu-Metal routes magnetic fields through itself instead of through the protected area. Uses: shielding sensitive components, MRI, precision electronics. Critical: after every machining/bending operation, a hydrogen anneal at 1100°C is mandatory — otherwise the magnetic properties are destroyed! Gentle machining only.

def: A zinc-aluminum die-casting alloy: cheap, precise, excellent finish. Zamak 3/5.
expand: Zamak melts at only 385°C — tooling lasts 10x longer than aluminum! Casting accuracy ±0.075mm, a surface ready for coating. Uses: handles, locks, carburetors, toys (die-cast miniatures). Weaknesses: creep above 80°C, cold brittleness, intergranular corrosion in humidity (old Zamak).

def: Gray cast iron: flake graphite. Excellent vibration damping, cheap, brittle.
expand: The flake graphite = a vibration sponge (10x steel!) + self-lubrication when machined + complex castability. Hence: machine bases, gearbox housings, brake discs, cylinders. The weakness: low tension (250MPa) and brittleness — never under shock! Machining: an easy brittle chip, usually no coolant.

def: Nodular (magnesium) graphite: the strength and ductility of steel with casting advantages.
expand: Adding Mg turns the graphite into spheres — 18% elongation (vs. ~0 in gray)! GJS-400-18: Sy=250, UTS=400. Uses: crankshafts, steering knuckles, pressurized valve bodies. Welding possible with care (a Ni rod). ADI (austempered) reaches 1000MPa+.

def: Co-Cr-W: retains hardness at red heat. Valve faces, hot tools, hardfacing.
expand: Common Stellite 6: HRC 40 retained even at 600°C + wear and corrosion resistance. Main application: hardfacing (welding a layer onto valve faces, seats, blades). Machining: very hard — CBN/grinding. Also: chemical pumps, high-temperature bearings.

def: Spindle revolutions per minute. Derived from Vc: n = Vc×1000/(π×D).
expand: The most everyday calculation: milling a ⌀10 carbide tool in steel (Vc=180) → n=5730 RPM. The rule: a small diameter = a high RPM! A ⌀1 drill needs 30,000+ RPM for optimal Vc — on an 8K machine it runs too slow and the tool wears out. The machine's limit governs in practice.

def: The tool's advance speed. mm/min. Vf = fz × z × n.
expand: The F in a CNC program: a ⌀10, 4-flute mill, fz=0.05, n=5730 → F=1146 mm/min. The common mistake: copying F between different tools — but Vf depends on z and n! Always recalculate from fz. Feed slowdown at corners (built into CAM) prevents overload.

def: The effective chip thickness in milling — the basis for chip thinning.
expand: At a small ae, the tooth cuts only a thin arc — hm is smaller than fz! Approximate formula: hm=fz×√(ae/D). The practical conclusion: at ae=10%D you can raise fz by 1.6x and get the same chip load. Without compensating: rubbing, heat, and short tool life. Every modern CAM calculates it automatically.

def: Deep drilling in stages: drill-retract-return. Breaks chips and cools.
expand: Above L/D=4 the chip jams and the drill breaks. G83: descends Q depth, fully retracts (chip clearing), returns. G73 (chip break): only a tiny retraction — faster, for a brittle chip. Carbide with internal coolant: often no peck needed up to L/D=8! Typical Q: 1-3×D.

def: Tapping with full spindle-axis synchronization: no floating holder. G84.
expand: The controller locks the n↔F ratio exactly per the pitch — the tap threads and withdraws with a spindle reversal. Advantages: fast, precise, allows deep threading. Requirements: a machine with rigid tap, a good holder. A tension-compression holder = the old safety net for machines without perfect synchronization.

def: Milling a thread with a helical motion — one tool for every diameter at the same pitch!
expand: The tool spins fast and follows a helical (screw) path (helical interpolation). Advantages: one tool = M8 to M30 (same pitch), no tap jamming in an expensive hole!, threading close to the bottom, diameter control (correction in the offset). Mandatory in hard materials and large holes.

def: Coordinated circular/helical motion of the axes. The basis for milling circles.
expand: G02 (clockwise) / G03 (counter-clockwise) + I,J or R. Helical = a circle + Z simultaneously: ramp entries, thread milling, enlarging holes (instead of boring!). Circular milling of a hole: diameter flexibility, low forces, chip clearance — sometimes preferable to a large drill.

def: A gradual angled entry into material — instead of a vertical plunge that ruins a tool.
expand: A standard end mill doesn't drill! Entries: linear ramp (2-5° in steel, up to 10° in Al), helical (a spiral — best for pockets), pre-drill (a starter hole). A straight plunge is allowed only for a center-cutting tool at shallow depth. Modern CAM sets it automatically by tool.

def: The material the roughing pass leaves for finishing: 0.2-0.5mm walls, 0.1-0.3 the floor.
expand: A uniform allowance = a quality finish: the tool works at constant load. The rule: walls 0.3-0.5mm (radial), floors 0.15-0.25 (axial). Too much = an overloaded finishing pass; too little = the roughing pass 'touches' the final surface with vibration marks. Semi-finish on precision parts: an intermediate 0.1 layer.

def: A telescoping length-measuring bar measures circular deviation — diagnoses machine errors in 10 minutes.
expand: The machine performs a G02/G03 circle and the ballbar (Renishaw QC20) continuously measures the radius. The graph reveals: backlash (jumps at reversals), squareness error (a 45° oval), servo mismatch, lag. Standard: ISO 230-4. Periodic testing = smart maintenance before parts get rejected.

def: The energy per weld length: HI = V×I×60/(v×1000) [kJ/mm]. Governs the HAZ.
expand: High HI = a wide HAZ, coarse grain, distortion; too low in hardenable steels = fast cooling and cracks! Ranges: stainless ≤1.5 (sensitization!), structural steel 1-3, duplex a narrow window 0.5-2.5 kJ/mm. The WPS defines a range — and the welder is measured against it.

def: The ferrite percentage in an austenitic weld: FN 3-10 prevents solidification cracking.
expand: A 308L weld with a little ferrite (FN 5-8) resists hot cracking; FN=0 = a risk! FN>10 = a problem in cryogenics and corrosion. Prediction: the Schaeffler/DeLong diagram by composition. Measurement: a magnetic ferritoscope. Critical in chemical equipment, nuclear, and LNG.

def: Flowing argon on the root side — prevents oxidation (sugaring) in stainless and titanium.
expand: Stainless welded without purge: a black, oxidized root ('sugaring') = corrosion + sanitary rejection. The technique: dams + argon down to O2<0.1% (an oxygen meter!). Titanium requires an additional trailing shield. Sanitary/semi-sanitary piping: purging is law, not a suggestion.

def: Magnetic fields deflecting the arc — mainly DC, at corners and ends.
expand: The arc 'escapes' the joint: uneven penetration, porosity, spatter. Causes: DC + an asymmetric ferromagnetic mass, the ground cable's field. Fixes: move the ground (or two on both sides), switch to AC, reduce current, backstep technique, demagnetize residual magnetism (after MT!).

def: Side-to-side torch oscillation — a wide bead in one pass. Limited by the WPS!
expand: Weaving fills fast but: HI spikes (width×), the HAZ grows, an undercut risk at the edges. The common rule: weave width ≤ 3×electrode diameter. Vertical-up position: essential. Sensitive/duplex steels: stringer only (no weave) per the WPS. A brief pause at the edges prevents undercut.

def: The exposed wire length from the torch. Affects current and penetration — keep it constant!
expand: In MIG: extending stick-out raises resistance → the current drops → less penetration! Range: 10-15mm (short arc), 15-20 (spray), FCAW up to 25-40. A welder moving toward and away from the joint = an uneven weld. This is why a robot is more consistent than a person — a perfectly constant CTWD.

def: A groove cut into the weld edge that wasn't filled. Concentrates stress — a fatigue defect!
expand: Caused by: high current, high speed, a wrong angle, jittery weaving. The danger: a sharp notch exactly at the toe = doubles fatigue risk. ISO 5817 limits: B ≤0.5mm, C ≤1mm continuous. Fix: light grinding (if within thickness limits) or a thin fill pass.

def: Hammering the weld: releases stress and turns tension into compression. With caution!
expand: Two worlds: slag peening with a hammer = cleaning only; controlled peening (mechanical/UIT) = a genuine fatigue improvement by turning toe stresses to compression. Modern HFMI/UIT: qualified ultrasonic hammering — improves the fatigue class by 30-50%! Prohibited on the root and cover pass without code approval.

def: Multiple surfaces controlled by one continuous tolerance zone — as if one plane.
expand: Example: two separated mounting surfaces that need to sit together on a plate — flatness with CZ forces them into the same plane ±. Without CZ: each is flat individually but at different levels! ISO: CZ within the FCF. The ASME equivalent: a 'X SURFACES' note or a shared profile.

def: ISO: multiple features treated as a single geometric feature. UF before the callout.
expand: UF unites segments into one entity — e.g. 3 arcs of the same interrupted cylinder measured as one whole cylinder. Useful for symmetric, interrupted parts. The difference from CZ: UF creates one feature (also for size!), CZ only unifies a form tolerance zone.

def: ISO's name for a basic dimension (in a box): a perfect location with no self-tolerance.
expand: TED in ISO = Basic Dimension in ASME: the boxed dimensions defining the theoretical framework. Tolerance comes only from an FCF that references them. Angles too can be TED (30° in a box). A CMM measures deviation from TED — not TED itself.

def: ASME: every FCF sharing the same DRF is checked together — as one whole.
expand: The ASME default: multiple Position/Profile callouts to the same Datums (at the same RFS) = one combined pattern! Each can't be 'adjusted' separately on a CMM. To cancel it: a SEP REQT (separate requirement) note. In ISO it's the opposite — everything is separate unless SIM is noted. A critical difference in measurement programming!

def: Measurement while the part is clamped to a fixture — simulates assembly. Opposite of free state Ⓕ.
expand: Sheet and flexible parts distort when free but 'straighten out' during assembly. The drawing can require measuring in a restrained condition (a note: RESTRAINED per fixture F-123, torque X). Ⓕ (free state) = the opposite: must be checked unclamped. Without a note: the ASME default = free state.

def: ASME: separate segments of the same size are treated as one feature. Symbol ⌯CF.
expand: A shaft with a slot in the middle = two segments; CF unites them into one cylinder for size and Rule #1 purposes — one envelope for both! Without CF each segment is measured separately and could be non-coaxial. The ISO equivalent to UF. Common in stepped shafts and sliding fits.

def: The rule: the rotating ring = press fit, the stationary one = clearance fit. k5/m5 shaft, H7/J7 housing.
expand: A ring rotating relative to the load must be press-fit — otherwise it 'creeps' and wears its seat! A standard rotating shaft: k5-m6. A stationary housing: H7 (or J7 for precision). A rotating load on a housing (a wheel): the opposite! The wrong fit = bearing failure cause #1 after lubrication.

def: The ring slowly rotates in its seat — wears the shaft/housing. A result of a loose fit.
expand: Signs: a polished/blackened seat, smeared material, noise. The damage: the shaft wears below size — an expensive fix (plating/reclamation). Prevention: the correct fit for the load direction. Emergency fixes: Loctite 641/648 (bearing mount), but that's a patch — not a substitute for the correct fit.

def: Grease ages before the bearing! Life is temperature-dependent: every +15°C = half the life.
expand: Rule of thumb: lithium grease at 70°C ≈ 10-20K hours; at 100°C a quarter of that! 2RS 'Sealed for Life' = for the grease's life, not forever. Relubrication: quantity = 0.005×D×B grams, intervals per the manufacturer's table. Too much grease = heat (churning)! High-speed bearings: fill only 30%.

def: DN = shaft diameter × RPM. A speed limit metric: grease ~500K, oil ~1M.
expand: nDm is more precise: RPM × mean diameter. Limits: grease 400-600K, oil bath ~700K, oil-air/jet 1-2M, hybrid spindles (ceramic balls) up to 3M! Above the limit: grease heat, cage slip. The fix at high RPM: a smaller bearing or advanced lubrication.

def: Steel rings + Si3N4 balls: 60% lighter, stiffer, electrically insulating. For spindles.
expand: Ceramic balls: 40% the density, high E, zero micro-welding = less centrifugal heat and +30-50% speed. A huge bonus: electrical insulation — saves motors from EDM bearing damage (VFD currents!). 3-5x the price. Spindles, EVs, turbos — the new standard.

def: Indentations from rolling-element spacing under vibration without rotation — transport and idle machines!
expand: A stationary bearing + vibration (transport, a neighboring machine) = the rolling elements 'dance' in place and push the lubricant aside — shiny indentations at the rolling spacing (true brinelling = dark, impact indentations). Prevention in transport: locking the shaft, preload. Stand-by machines: turn manually every week!

def: A pressure reservoir: a compressed nitrogen bladder. Emergency, shock absorption, flow supplementation.
expand: Bladder/piston/diaphragm — N2 is compressed and stores energy. Uses: emergency backup (brakes!), pump pulsation absorption, hydraulic shock, peak flow supplementation. Pre-charge: 80-90% of minimum working pressure — checked semi-annually! Safety: depressurize before any service. PED standard for large volumes.

def: Vacuum bubbles at the pump inlet that collapse under pressure — erode metal. A gravel-like noise!
expand: Caused by: a blocked suction (a filter!), thick/cold oil, a long/thin suction line, a low level. The collapse on the pressure side pits metal and destroys a pump within weeks. Detection: a gravel-like noise, vibration, foam in the tank. Fix: NPSH — widen suction, warm the oil, lower the pump.

def: The pump supplies only the pressure+flow required — enormous energy savings.
expand: The LS line reports the highest load pressure to the pump; the pump (variable) produces the load + a constant Δp (~20bar) only. Versus a fixed system that dumps excess through relief = heat! Savings: 30-50% energy. The standard in mobile equipment: excavators, forklifts, combines.

def: Continuous opening per an electrical signal — controls speed and position. The heart of modern hydraulics.
expand: Instead of open/closed: the spool moves proportionally to mA/V. Proportional (±5% hysteresis) for most applications; servo (internal feedback, keep it clean!) for simulators and aircraft. With position feedback (an LVDT on the cylinder) = precise closed loop. Oil cleanliness: ISO 4406 16/14/11 and below!

def: A particle count code: 18/16/13 = particles at 4/6/14 microns. A lower code = cleaner.
expand: Each digit = a doubling range: dropping from 18 to 17 = half the particles! Requirements: general hydraulics 20/18/15, proportional 18/16/13, servo 16/14/11. 80% of hydraulic failures = contamination! A 3μm filtration investment = double component life. Sampling: from a dedicated point, not the tank.

def: Built-in deceleration before end of stroke — a plunger chokes the outlet. Prevents shock.
expand: At the end of stroke a plunger enters a pocket and forces oil through an adjustable orifice — smooth deceleration instead of a 'bang'. Without it: hydraulic shock, mount breakage, noise. An adjustable cushion (a screw) on both sides = standard on fast cylinders. An external alternative: proportional valve deceleration.

def: Fast local electromagnetic heating + quench — a hard layer only where needed.
expand: An induction coil heats the surface to 900°C in seconds (skin effect!) and immediately quenches. Depth by frequency: 10kHz=3-5mm, 100kHz=1-2mm. Advantages: local (only the pulley, not the whole shaft), fast, in-line, the core stays tough. Materials: 1045, 4140 (C>0.35%). Minimal distortion.

def: Heating with a gas flame + quench — for huge parts that don't fit in a furnace.
expand: An oxy-acetylene torch heats locally with a trailing quench spray. Less controlled than induction but: no size limit! Uses: rail track, giant gears, machine ways in place. Depth 2-6mm. Requires a skilled operator — overheating = melting/cracking.

def: Quenching into a salt bath at 250-400°C and holding — bainite: tough without tempering.
expand: Instead of martensite+tempering: an isothermal hold creates bainite directly. Advantages: minimal distortion (no thermal shock), excellent toughness at HRC 45-52, no quench cracks. Uses: clips, springs, nails, ADI (austempered ductile iron = a steel substitute!).

def: Quenching into a hot bath above Ms, temperature equalization, then slow cooling — less distortion.
expand: The problem with a standard quench: the surface cools before the core = stress and distortion. Marquench: a hold at 180-250°C (above Ms), the core equalizes, then everything transforms to martensite together in air. The result: the same hardness, half the distortion! Mandatory for thin, precise parts. Still needs tempering.

def: Carbon loss from the surface during heating — a soft layer that ruins fatigue life!
expand: Heating in air: surface carbon oxidizes and escapes — 0.1-0.5mm of soft ferrite on hardened steel! Result: low surface hardness, poor fatigue (springs are especially sensitive!). Prevention: a controlled atmosphere/vacuum, or leaving stock for removal. Test: micro-hardness in cross-section.

def: An automotive requirement for HT suppliers: pyrometry, process tables, an annual self-assessment.
expand: AIAG CQI-9 = automotive's 'Nadcap': process tables for every process (temperatures, times, tests), pyrometry requirements (SAT/TUS like AMS 2750), and a documented annual assessment. An automotive HT supplier without CQI-9 = not in the supply chain. Version 4 is current.

def: A pure Al coating in vacuum — the aerospace substitute for cadmium. MIL-DTL-83488.
expand: IVD-Al: galvanic protection like cadmium without the toxicity! Resists 500°C+, conductive, suited to HSLA steels (no hydrogen embrittlement since there's no bath!). After coating: glass bead peening for density + chromate. Uses: structural bolts, landing gear, fuselage. Downside: line-of-sight.

def: 12-15% Ni: 3-5x the resistance of standard zinc. The new standard in automotive and aerospace.
expand: Zn-Ni gives 720-1000 hours of salt spray (vs. 96-200 for zinc)! Resists 200°C, less hydrogen embrittlement than cadmium, friendly to aluminum contact. Became a requirement in automotive (chassis bolts) and aerospace as a Cd substitute. Finish: clear/black with a Cr3+ passivation.

def: A conversion layer on zinc/aluminum: yellow/clear. Resistance + a paint base.
expand: The chromate 'heals itself' — scratched and chemically regenerates! On zinc: yellow (thick) / blue-clear (thin) / black. The old Cr6+ is banned (RoHS) — modern Cr3+ is close in performance. On aluminum = Alodine/Chem-Film. Always the step after galvanizing and before painting.

def: Hydrogen from plating penetrates hardened steel — a sudden, delayed fracture! Baking mandatory.
expand: Steels above HRC 32 (especially 39+): atomic hydrogen from the bath accumulates at defects and creates a delayed fracture (days later!). Prevention: baking at 190-220°C within 4 hours of plating, for 8-24 hours depending on strength. 12.9 bolts plated without baking = a ticking bomb. ASTM F519 tests for it.

def: Super-anodize with plasma: a thick, hard ceramic layer on Al/Mg/Ti. Keronite/MAO.
expand: High voltage creates micro-plasma discharges that build a ceramic (corundum!) up to 200μm at HV 1000-2000 — double hard anodize! Exceptional wear/corrosion resistance, even on castings and magnesium (which standard anodize struggles with). More expensive; names: Keronite, MAO, micro-arc.

def: A polymer deposited from vapor in vacuum: a uniform layer that penetrates every crevice. Electronics and medical.
expand: Parylene condenses as a gas — coats with a perfectly uniform thickness (microns) even inside holes and crevices spraying can't reach! Pinhole-free, biocompatible (implants!), excellent insulation. Types: N (penetration), C (common), F (temperature). Expensive and hard to repair — but no substitute in critical tasks.

def: Forming a thread by cold pressing between rollers — no chips. Strong and fast.
expand: The thread forms by plastic flow: the material fibers follow the profile (not cut!) + compressive stress at the root = 2-3x the fatigue life of a cut thread! Commercial bolts: 100% rolled. The starting diameter = the pitch diameter. Aerospace: 'rolled after HT' for maximum strength.

def: UN fit classes: 2A/2B standard, 3A/3B precise (aerospace). A=bolt B=nut.
expand: 1A/1B loose (fast, dirty), 2A/2B the commercial standard, 3A/3B tight — aerospace and precision bolts. The difference: the tolerance field on the pitch diameter. 3A without plating! (the plating eats the clearance) — or note 'after plating'. Metric equivalent: 6g/6H vs. 4h6h.

def: A thread check: Go must thread freely the full length, NoGo up to 2 turns.
expand: Go checks the thread isn't too tight (the internal pitch diameter isn't too large); NoGo (a red ring) checks it isn't loose — allowed to start only up to 2 turns! Calibrated periodically. A truncated NoGo = checks pitch diameter only. This is the only quick way to check threads in production.

def: 75% thread height = the standard. 100% adds 5% strength but doubles tap breakage!
expand: The formula: %=(D-Drill)/(1.299P)×76.98 approximately. The paradox: going from 75% to 100% adds only ~5% pull-out strength but the tapping torque triples! Hard materials (Ti, SS): 60-65% is acceptable. Soft ones (Al): 75-80% is fine. The rule: D-P gives ~77% — excellent almost always.

def: A fluteless tap that forms a thread by pressing — no chips, no clogging!
expand: A form tap compresses the material into a thread shape: no chip stuck in a blind hole!, a strong thread (continuous fibers), the tap almost never breaks (it's solid). Requirements: a ductile material (Al, copper, soft steel, thin SS), a larger drill (a separate table!), good lubrication. RPM double that of a cutting tap.

he: Helical Coil vs Solid — השוואת קשיחים
en: Wire Insert vs Solid Bushing Choice
def: A coil (Helicoil): light, distributes load. Solid (Keensert): strong, fast, replaceable.
expand: Coil: a smaller drill, negligible weight, elastic load distribution — the classic aerospace choice. Solid: installs without a special pull-out tool, high pull-out force (a coarse external thread), locking keys. Choice: a fast field repair=solid; a production run in aluminum=coil; extreme load=solid.

def: A spring with hooks that works in tension. Built-in initial tension in the coiling.
expand: Unlike compression: the coils sit tight with initial tension — the spring resists even the initial opening. The weak point: the hooks! 70% of failures are at the hook root (stress concentration) — an English/German/side hook depending on application. For heavy loads: a compression spring in a reversed mechanism is better.

def: A spring that works by arm rotation. Clothespins, mousetraps, door hinges.
expand: The torsion loads the wire in bending (not torsion — the name is misleading!). The iron rule: always load in the winding direction (closes the coils) — the reverse dramatically shortens life! The calculation: moment per unit angle. Support on an internal rod is mandatory (it contracts under load — allow 10% clearance).

def: A pressurized N2 cylinder: nearly constant force through the stroke. Trunk lids, hatches.
expand: Unlike a mechanical spring (linear force) — a gas strut gives nearly flat force (a small k) + built-in damping. Selection: force = weight×arm/piston-arm (moments!). Forbidden: opening it, heat above 80°C, painting. Mounted rod-down (seal lubrication). A leak = replacement.

def: Rectangular wire = more material by volume: double the force of a round spring in the same space.
expand: A worldwide color code by load: blue=light, red=medium, gold=heavy, green=extra heavy (manufacturers vary — check the catalog!). Designed for die life: millions of cycles at 25-30% deflection. Never compress beyond 50%! Replace in sets — one fatigued spring distorts the whole tool.

def: Permanent loss of length/force from overload or heat. Presetting prevents it in advance.
expand: A spring compressed past its yield point 'forgets' its length — a set. Causes: an excessive design stress, temperature (music wire above 120°C!), an inadvertent solid condition. The manufacturing fix: presetting/scragging — a deliberate compression to solid in production that fixes it in advance. A hot spring: 17-7PH, Inconel.

def: The cost of a machine hour: depreciation+interest+space+energy+maintenance+tools / annual hours.
expand: The calculation: a ₪800K machine, 8-year depreciation=₪100K, interest ₪30K, space ₪20K, electricity ₪25K, maintenance ₪40K, tools ₪60K = ₪275K per year. At 3500 effective hours: ₪79 before an operator! + an operator ₪120 + profit = a ₪280-350 rate. 5-axis/EDM: double. The basis for every quote.

def: A quote: material + setup/quantity + machining + processes + inspection + profit.
expand: A professional structure: 1) material×BTF×price/kg, 2) setup (hours×rate)/quantity, 3) cycle time×rate, 4) outside processes (coating, HT — cost+15% markup), 5) FAI/inspection, 6) profit. Always price breaks for quantity! Ti/Inconel: lock the material price for a limited time (volatility).

def: Cycle time = Σ(volume/MRR) + tool changes + positions. The heart of costing.
expand: The quick method: volume to remove/a realistic MRR (steel: roughing 100-200 cm³/min on a VMC, finishing by area×passes). + 15-25% for: tool changes (6-15 sec), rapid moves, measurements. CAM gives an exact but optimistic time — multiply by 1.15. Experience = knowing your machine's factor.

he: Make or Buy — ייצור או רכש
def: The decision: manufacture in-house or purchase? Full cost vs. a supplier's price + strategic core.
expand: The correct calculation: internal marginal cost (if there's spare capacity — variable only!) vs. a supplier's price. Beyond money: core knowledge (don't outsource it!), confidentiality, lead time, supplier dependence. The rule: things unique to the core — in-house; standard — outsource. Full capacity changes everything.

def: Spreading fixture/mold cost over the quantity: NRE/units or a separate line.
expand: Two approaches: a separate NRE (the customer pays for the fixture and owns it — common in aerospace) or built into the price (NRE/annual quantity — the risk is yours if orders don't materialize!). A smart contract: amortization over a binding quantity, beyond it — a discount. A customer-owned fixture = state ownership clearly in writing!

def: An active metal (Zn/Al/Mg) that corrodes instead of the structure. Ships, boilers, piping.
expand: The more anodic metal sacrifices itself: zinc for steel at sea, magnesium in soil/fresh water (a higher potential), Al-Zn-In for open ocean. The maintenance rule: an anode that's disappearing = it's working! An anode still clean after a year = no electrical contact (paint underneath?). A home water heater: check every 2-3 years.

def: A current source + inert anodes — controlled protection for piping and large structures.
expand: Instead of consumable anodes: a rectifier pushes electrons into the structure through MMO/Ti anodes that don't erode. Advantages: control (a monitored -850mV CSE), kilometers of piping range, longevity. Required: test stations, continuous monitoring. Danger: overprotection = paint disbondment + hydrogen!

def: Bacteria (SRB) create a locally corrosive environment — rapid pitting in stagnant water.
expand: Sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) under deposits create local H2S — aggressive pitting even in stainless! Suspects: leftover hydrotest water, dead legs, tanks. Prevention: full drainage after hydro, biocides, flow. Diagnosis: pits beneath mounds (tubercles) + microbiological testing.

def: An extra wall thickness designed to 'be eaten': 1.5-6mm depending on service and design life.
expand: The design: the pressure-required thickness + CA = the minimum thickness on the drawing. Typical CA: 1.5mm mild, 3mm standard oil field, 6mm severe. Calculation: corrosion rate (mm/year from monitoring data) × design life. Correctly selected stainless: CA=0. Periodic UT monitoring compares to the minimum thickness — below it: replacement.

def: A reddish iron oxide film in WFI/pharmaceutical systems — stainless 'rusting'.
expand: In hot pure water (WFI, clean steam) the passive layer migrates — red/purple/black powder on 316L. Class I (migrated from a source), II (in-situ), III (black in steam). Treatment: chemical de-rouging + repassivation on a schedule. Not a structural failure — but pharma regulation requires managing it.

def: T = K×F×d: the torque that creates preload. K=0.2 dry, 0.12-0.15 lubricated.
expand: The problem: 90% of the torque goes to friction (the head+thread) — only 10% to stretching! Hence K (the nut factor) governs: dry 0.2, lubricated 0.12, moly 0.10. The same torque lubricated = 60% higher preload! Hence: the spec must state the lubrication condition. M10-8.8 dry: ~45Nm.

def: Star/cross tightening in stages: 30%-70%-100%. Flanges, cylinder heads.
expand: Sequential tightening distorts: the first side compresses and the last one lifts it! The pattern: crossing (4 bolts: 1-3-2-4), star (a round flange), center-out (a plate). Stages: 30%→70%→100% + a check pass. Gasketed flanges: doubly critical + re-torque after settling (24h hot).

def: Heating to 80-110°C expands the ring — force-free installation on a shaft with a press fit.
expand: ΔT=90°C gives an expansion of ~0.001×d — enough for an m6 fit! The tool: an induction heater with temperature control + automatic demagnetize. Forbidden: a flame (local heat!), above 120°C (structural change!), heating a sealed 2RS bearing (the grease!). Fast, safe, no damage — the professional standard.

def: F = π×d×L×p×μ: calculated from the overlap. A hydraulic press with a gauge — not a hammer!
expand: The force is proportional to the overlap and contact pressure. An abnormal rise on the press graph = a particle/scratch = stop! A 10-15° lead-in chamfer is mandatory on both sides. Lubrication: Molykote prevents galling (mandatory for stainless!). Correct installation: straight support, force through the shaft — never through the bearing body.

def: Marking matched pairs before disassembly — returning to exactly the same orientation and position.
expand: Parts that 'married': bearing caps (line-bored together — don't swap/flip!), balanced flanges, matched gears. The marking: a matched punch, paint, or matching digits. Disassembling without marking = incorrect assembly = runout, noise, failure. A golden habit: mark before you open.

def: An inkjet head glues powder layer by layer, then debind+sinter. Fast and cheap for runs.
expand: The advantage: no laser and no supports (the powder self-supports) — 10-100x faster than DMLS! The process: green printing → binder burnout → sintering (~20% shrinkage — planned in advance!). Accuracy after shrinkage: ±0.5-2%. Players: Desktop Metal, HP Metal Jet. The true competitor to MIM in production runs.

def: Laser+powder/wire in a robotic head: repairing parts, cladding, and adding to existing material!
expand: DED builds on an existing substrate — the big power: repairing expensive blades/molds (instead of scrap!), local cladding, hybrid (adding onto a lathe part). Coarser than PBF (accuracy ±0.5mm, needs machining) but a rate of kg/hour. LENS, WAAM (wire-arc = huge and cheap). Aerospace: qualified blisk repairs.

def: Metal powder: sieving, blending, cycle tracking. Ti is explosive! O2 rises with use.
expand: The powder = 30-50% of print cost, hence recycled: sieving (63μm), blending with virgin powder, and tracking O2/N2 — titanium absorbs oxygen every cycle until it's rejected! Safety: Ti/Al are explosive — ATEX, spark-free tools, no standard vacuum! Full lot documentation for aerospace.

def: As-built DMLS: Ra 6-15μm, angle-dependent! Down-skin is 2-3x worse than up-skin.
expand: Layer steps + semi-melted powder = a rough surface, and worst on overhanging surfaces (down-skin). Fatal for fatigue — hence: machine critical interfaces, or improve overall: tumbling, AFM (abrasive flow through channels!), electropolish, micro-machining. Plan: +0.5mm stock for machining.

def: A camera on a tube/fiber for internal inspection: channels, root welds, engines.
expand: Visual access without disassembly: cooling channels in molds, weld root in piping (mandatory in sanitary!), trapped chips, internal coating. Types: rigid (straight, high quality), fiber, video (articulating, with measurement!). Aircraft engines: scheduled borescope inspections = save million-dollar teardowns.

def: Measuring heights and marking on a surface plate: the central tool of the metrology room.
expand: On the plate: height measurement ±0.02 (digital ±0.01), marking lines (a carbide tip), comparisons with an indicator.
