Correct use: zero on the plate/a block, lock the arm before reading, gentle motion. A 2D height gauge (Trimos/Tesa): also diameters, distances, and functions — the poor man's CMM.

def: A set of precise pins (0.01 steps): quick hole measurement with no substitute.
expand: The true hole diameter: the largest pin that fits comfortably. Sets: 0.1-25mm in 0.01 steps, accuracy ±0.002 (Class ZZ). Also: hole spacing (a pin+micrometer), quick position checks, an improvised go/nogo. Rule: never force it — a pin stuck in a hot hole is stuck forever.

def: A diamond needle dragged over the surface, measuring Ra/Rz. Portable or lab-based.
expand: A 2μm stylus travels 0.5-5mm and calculates parameters. Correct use: perpendicular to the machining direction (lay!), a clean surface, calibrated on a standard (a Ra 3.0 specimen). The correct cutoff is critical — an instrument at 0.25 measures differently than at 0.8! Portable (MarSurf, Mitutoyo SJ) for the shop floor; lab-based with a stand = a full profile.

def: 80% of problems from 20% of causes. The chart that shows where to invest.
expand: Sorted bars + a cumulative line: the top three defects = usually 70-80% of the cost! The power: focus — don't fix everything, fix what hurts. Correct use: Pareto by cost (not just count!), then a secondary Pareto on the leading cause. The first tool in every quality investigation.

def: Mapping root causes with the 6M: man, machine, method, material, measurement, environment.
expand: The skeleton: the problem at the head, 6 main bones (6M), and brainstorming causes on each bone. The value: systematic — you don't get stuck on the first suspect. The correct follow-up: pick suspects from the fish, verify with data (not opinions!), then 5-Why on the confirmed one. A cross-functional team is mandatory.

def: Asking 'why' until the root cause — usually 5 times. Simple and lethal.
expand: Stopping too early = fixing a symptom: 'the bolt loosened' → why? Vibration → why isn't there a locking mechanism? Not on the drawing → why? No FMEA... A true root cause = one whose fix systematically prevents recurrence. A trap: 'operator fault' is almost never a root cause — why did the system allow it?

def: Automotive's problem-solving methodology: team, containment, root cause, correction, prevention.
expand: D1 team → D2 description → D3 containment (stop the bleeding!) → D4 root cause (verified!) → D5 selected correction → D6 implementation → D7 systemic prevention (FMEA, procedures) → D8 recognition. An automotive customer requires an 8D on every claim: D3 within 24 hours, closure in 30-60 days.

def: Any foreign object in the wrong place: a chip, a bolt, a tool. An FOD program = an aerospace mandate.
expand: A forgotten bolt in an engine = a catastrophe. An FOD program: tool accountability (a shadow board — a shadow for every tool!), controlled areas, documented cleaning, no personal items, a last-look check. NAS412 is the standard. Culture: any employee can stop production over FOD — no questions asked.

def: Accreditation for special aerospace processes: HT, coating, NDT, welding. Above AS9100.
expand: A special process = one that can't be fully verified by 100% inspection (coating, HT, welding, NDT, shot peening). Nadcap = a deep technical audit (not just a system!) by PRI: a checklist of hundreds of items, live job audits. Without Nadcap — no direct work from Boeing/Airbus/RTX.

def: DoD contracts: specialty metals (Ti, alloy steels) must be sourced from the US/allied nations.
expand: DFARS 252.225-7009: titanium, alloy steels, superalloys under an American defense contract — melted in an approved country (the US + qualifying countries, Israel included!). Meaning: a mill cert with documented melt source, inventory segregation. China/Russia = disqualified. Violation = losing the contract.

def: A unique number for every critical part: full traceability from birth to scrap.
expand: Life-limited and critical parts: a unique S/N + full documentation (material, processes, tests, flight hours!). Marking methods: laser (gentle!), dot peen, chemical etching — per the spec (depth, location, without harming fatigue life!). UID/DataMatrix in American defense. Wrong marking = a rejected part.

def: A small local section within a view — exposes an internal detail without a full section. Boundary: a wavy line.
expand: Instead of sectioning the whole part for one hole: a small area is 'torn out' (break-out) with a thin wavy line as the boundary. Saves views and is quick to understand. Uses: a single hole, thread depth, a local internal detail. No cutting-plane line or label needed — the wavy line tells the whole story.

def: A cross-section rotated 90° and shown on the view itself — the profile of ribs, arms, bars.
expand: The section 'rotates' into the view: you see the arm's profile (I? T? oval?) without an extra view! Revolved = on the view (within the outline or with a break); Removed = offset to the side with an A-A label. Ideal for: handles, steering-wheel spokes, profiles that vary along their length.

def: A long-dash, two-short-dash chain: alternative positions, adjacent parts, motion boundaries.
expand: Three uses: 1) an alternate position (a door open/closed, an arm at end of stroke), 2) an adjacent part for reference (not part of the drawing — just context!), 3) raw-stock outline before machining. Thin, not dimensioned, not hatched. Essential in installation drawings — shows the surroundings without drawing them.

def: Half a view = a symmetric part: a center line with a pair of parallel dashes at the ends.
expand: A fully symmetric part: draw only half with the symmetry symbol (short parallel marks at the center-line ends) — saves half the sheet! Dimensioning: to the symmetry line with a full ⌀/notation. Caution: confirm the part is truly 100% symmetric — one odd hole and the drawing misleads. Common in sheet metal and turned bodies.

def: Aerospace: OML = the outer aerodynamic surface, IML = the inner one. Sacred!
expand: The OML is set aerodynamically — don't touch it: any bump/dip = drag! Parts are built from the OML inward. IML = the structure side. In composite tooling: an OML tool = a perfect outer surface. Skin drawings: 'OML THIS SIDE'. OML deviations require aerodynamics approval.

def: The full max-min difference across one indicator rotation = runout. Also FIM.
expand: TIR/FIM (full indicator movement): mount an indicator, rotate, and the difference between the high and low reading = the runout. Note: TIR from eccentricity = double the offset! (a shaft offset 0.05 → TIR 0.1). The practical language of lathes and alignment: 'hold it to 0.02 TIR'.

def: Full notation: HBW 10/3000 (Brinell), HRC (Rockwell C), HV30 (Vickers+load).
expand: The notation says everything: HBW = Brinell carbide ball (W!, the old HBS is retired), HV30 = Vickers at 30kgf load, HRC = Rockwell diamond. Conversions are approximate only (ASTM E140)! A correct drawing note: method+value+load. '45 HRC' is clear; 'hardness 450' = missing method = an argument.

def: C/L center, F/F face-to-face, A/F across flats (hex wrench size).
expand: The shorthand language: C/L (centerline), A/F (across flats — a hex dimension for the wrench! M10 = 17 A/F), F/F (face to face — a valve's length), B.C.D/PCD (bolt circle diameter), C'BORE/C'SK, N.T.S (not to scale), TYP, REF. Command of abbreviations = fluent drawing reading.

def: A slender column collapses sideways before crushing: Pcr = π²EI/(KL)². The enemy of thin members.
expand: Failure is sudden and unrelated to strength — governed by stiffness (E and I)! K by end conditions: 2 (a cantilever!), 1 (pinned), 0.5 (fixed). Conclusions: a long compressed rod — increase the diameter, not the strength; a long hydraulic piston rod — check buckling before pressure! Slenderness>100 = Euler governs.

def: A rounded groove at a shaft shoulder: a defined radius instead of a sharp corner = improved fatigue life.
expand: DIN 509 Type E/F: a groove with a large radius at the shoulder — lets a grinding wheel 'run out' and replaces a sharp corner (Kt=3!) with a generous radius (Kt≈1.5). On dynamic shafts = mandatory. Choice: E (standard), F (with a face toward the shoulder). On a drawing: 'Undercut DIN 509-E 0.8×0.3'.

def: Constrained expansion: σ = E×α×ΔT. Constrained steel: 2.5 MPa per degree!
expand: A part that wants to expand and can't — gets stressed: steel at ΔT=100° constrained = 250MPa — above A36's yield! Hence: expansion loops in piping, oblong holes at structural connections, expansion gaps. A bimetal: two different CTEs = bending (relays) or interface stress (coatings!).

def: The point a force must pass through to avoid twisting. In a C-channel — outside the section!
expand: A load not passing through the shear center = bending + torsion together! A U/C profile: the center is outside the back — a load through the geometric center twists it. Solutions: symmetric profiles (I), closed sections (RHS — hundreds of times stiffer in torsion!), or loading through the SC. Open thin-walled beams: the crux of the issue.

def: The Rev rule: a change preserving FFF = a letter; breaking interchangeability = a new part number!
expand: Form-Fit-Function: if the new part replaces the old everywhere and vice versa — a Rev is enough. If not (a hole moved, a different interface) — a new P/N is mandatory! Otherwise: mixed stock, an incompatible field-installed part. The rule sounds simple — and most configuration failures in the world violate it.

def: The drawing hierarchy: top assembly → sub-assemblies → parts. The product map.
expand: The tree shows who calls whom: top assembly → sub-assy → details + reference lists (piping, wiring). Uses: change scope (what's affected?), FAI planning, a full delivery package. Built automatically from the BOM in PLM. An 'orphan' drawing (not in the tree) = a configuration red flag.

def: One drawing for a family of parts: dimensions as letters (A,B,C) and a variant table.
expand: A pin in 10 lengths? One drawing: length=A, and a table: -001 A=20, -002 A=25... Advantage: one document to maintain. The dash number = the identifier (P/N-003). Caution: changing a shared dimension affects the whole table — check all of them! Modern CAD: configurations/a family table.

def: An approved internal catalog: bolts, bearings, seals with company part numbers. Prevents duplication.
expand: Without a library: the same bolt under 15 different part numbers, duplicate purchasing, bloated inventory. The library: one standard item = one part number + a ready CAD model + approved suppliers. A designer picks from the library — doesn't invent one. Saves: design time, purchasing errors, and inventory. PLM enforces it automatically.

def: Teeth at a helix angle: gradual engagement = quiet and smooth. Creates an axial force!
expand: The tooth engages gradually (not all at once like spur) — a high contact ratio, low noise, high load capacity. The cost: an axial force (Fa=Ft×tanβ) requiring a suitable bearing! Typical β: 15-30°. Double helical/herringbone cancels the axial. Automotive gearboxes: always helical.

def: Transmitting rotation at 90°: straight (simple) or spiral (quiet and strong).
expand: The shafts meet (usually at 90°). Straight bevel: simple and noisy. Spiral bevel: curved teeth = overlap and quiet (like helical). Hypoid: an offset axis (automotive differentials!) — allows lowering but sliding contact = GL-5 oil mandatory. Assembly: the mounting distance is stamped in — critical!

def: Sun+planets+ring: a high ratio in a small volume, split load. Coaxial!
expand: 3-5 planets share the load = 3x the power density of a standard gearbox! Input and output on the same axis. Ratios: 3:1-10:1 per stage, stackable. Uses: robotics gearboxes, automotive automatics, wind turbines, power drills. Precise load sharing is the secret: a floating sun or precise planets.

def: A gear on a straight toothed rack: rotation ↔ linear motion. Steering, gates, CNC axes.
expand: Motion: travel per rotation = π×m×z. Advantage over a ball screw: unlimited length (join racks together!) and speed — hence CNC on large gantries and lasers. Precision: preloading a pinion pair (master-slave) eliminates backlash. Lubrication: dedicated grease or auto-lube. Car steering: a modern variable ratio.

def: t = L/(fn×n) per pass. L=length+approach, number of passes by depth.
expand: The formula: time [min] = travel length / (feed × RPM). Example: a ⌀50 shaft, L=200, roughing fn=0.3, Vc=200 → n=1273 → a pass=0.52 min. Passes: total depth/ap. + facing, grooving, threading. Quick for quotes: chip volume/MRR + 20% overhead.

def: Weight = volume × density. Round: π/4×D²×L. Always at the next stock diameter!
expand: A round bar: W[kg] = 0.00000617×D²×L (steel, mm). Quick: D²×L×6.17/10⁶. A plate: L×W×T×ρ/10⁶. The commercial rule: stock in catalog sizes (⌀55 for a ⌀50 part!) + 3-5mm length for cutoff and gripping. Al: ×0.345, stainless: ×1.02, brass: ×1.07 of steel.

def: Thread rolling: the blank diameter ≈ the pitch diameter. The material flows — not cut.
expand: In rolling the material is conserved: what's pressed at the root rises to the crest. Diameter: d2 approx = D − 0.6495×P. For M10×1.5: a ⌀9.03 blank. Precise per material (different flow behavior): the roll manufacturer's tables. A cut thread instead: the blank = the full D. Rolling's material savings: ~15-25%!

def: The shape of the distribution: negative = a load-bearing plateau (excellent!), positive = sharp peaks.
expand: Rsk<0: a surface of 'tables with channels' — load-bearing + oil retention = ideal for contact (plateau honing = Rsk -1.5!). Rsk>0: sharp peaks that wear quickly (fresh turning). The same Ra — opposite behavior! Engine cylinders, rollers: an explicit negative Rsk requirement.

def: The percentage of material at a given section depth — the Abbott-Firestone curve. Predicts wear.
expand: Virtually cutting at depth c: what % of the length is material? A full Abbott curve = a surface fingerprint: Rpk (peaks that will wear in break-in), Rk (the functional core), Rvk (the oil channels). Modern cylinder specs: the Rk-family instead of Ra alone!

def: The percentage of real contact between surfaces — determines heat, electrical, and sealing behavior.
expand: Two 'flat' surfaces actually touch at only 5-20% of the area (peaks only!). Meaning: thermal contact resistance (CPU paste!), electrical (contact clamping), and sealing (why a gasket gets crushed). Improvement: lapping (up to 90%+), manual scraping for ways (20-25 contact spots per square inch).

def: From RT to 77K: steel 0.2%, Al 0.4%, plastic 1-2%! Mandatory in cryogenic design.
expand: Most contraction happens down to 77K (below that — almost none). Consequences: a 10m Al pipe shrinks 40mm! Solutions: bellows, loops, calculated anchor points. The interface danger: a steel bolt + an Al flange = tightening loosens/tightens on cooling! Invar for long runs.

def: Below Tc: zero resistance. MRI magnets (NbTi in LHe), Maglev, accelerators.
expand: NbTi (Tc=9K): the workhorse — MRI magnets at 4.2K (LHe). Nb3Sn: stronger fields (ITER!). HTS (YBCO, Tc=93K): works in cheap LN2! — cables, fault limiters. The quench: sudden loss of superconductivity = all the energy turns to heat — critical protection systems. MRI = the world's biggest He consumer.

def: Combining tolerances in an assembly: worst case (sum) or RSS (statistical).
expand: Worst-case: Σ all the tolerances — safe but expensive (requires tightening all of them). RSS: √(Σt²) — exploits that extremes are rare; at 5 equal dimensions: 45% of WC! Condition: centered processes (a good Cpk). A systematic loop diagram: direction + sign for every link. The tool that saves assemblies that otherwise won't close.

def: If it can't be measured — it can't be manufactured: probe access, accessible datums.
expand: A dimension with no CMM access = an endless argument. Rules: physically accessible datums (not points in the air), a measurable hole depth (not beneath a shoulder), GD&T checkable with existing tools. The golden question in a design review: 'how do you check this?' — if the answer is 'a destructive section' — reconsider.

def: A multi-tooth tool in one pull: keyways, splines, internal shapes. Fast and precise.
expand: Each tooth cuts a bit more than the previous one — the full profile in a single pass (seconds!). An internal keyway: a broach + a bushing under pressure. An internal spline/hex: no economical alternative in production runs! Downsides: an expensive tool (per size!), requires a through-pass. Alternatives for one-offs: wire EDM, slotting.

def: L/D above 10: a gun drill (up to 100×D!) or BTA for large ones. Pressure coolant through the tool.
expand: Gun drill: an asymmetric point + a guide, 30-100bar coolant through the tool, chips exit through a V-groove — straightness 0.1-0.3mm per meter! BTA/ejector: ⌀16+ faster. Uses: gun barrels, mold cooling channels, crankshafts, spindles. A dedicated machine or a retrofit + high pressure.

def: A maze of grooves with no contact: zero friction and wear. Fast bearings, turbines.
expand: The seal: a series of grooves that drops pressure at each stage — not a total seal but: zero friction = zero heat = unlimited speed and infinite life! Uses: spindles (+air purge = positive outward!), turbines (honeycomb wears-in), fast gearboxes. The winning combo: labyrinth + a V-ring.

def: A magnetic fluid trapped in a field: a perfect vacuum seal for rotating shafts. Zero leakage!
expand: Nano-magnetite particles in oil, trapped in a gap by a permanent magnet — a 'liquid seal' the shaft rotates through: truly hermetic! Each stage holds ~0.2bar — stages are combined in series for full vacuum. Uses: feedthroughs into vacuum chambers (semiconductor!), hard drives, space robotics. High speed, zero maintenance.

def: Measuring the pitch diameter (d2) with 3 precision wires + a micrometer. The highest accuracy for manual measurement.
expand: 3 identical wires are laid in the thread grooves — 2 on one side, 1 on the other — and the outer distance across them is measured with a micrometer. The optimal wire: GW=0.5774×P (a 60° thread). d2 = M − 3×GW + 0.866×P. The most precise method for manual pitch diameter measurement — used to verify qualified bolts (Class 3A/3B), calibrate thread gauges, and document FAI with a numeric value (not just go/no-go). Standards: ISO 3161, ASME B1.2. Critical: the wire diameter must exactly match the pitch — a wrong wire = a systematic measurement error.

def: The standard coarse inch thread — the American default. 1/4-20 UNC = 20 TPI.
expand: UNC = coarse: a coarse pitch, resistant to dirt and damage, fast to assemble. The equivalent of 'no notation' in metric. Common sizes: #6-32, #8-32, #10-24, 1/4-20, 5/16-18, 3/8-16, 1/2-13, 5/8-11, 3/4-10. Rule: if UNF isn't written — it's UNC. Don't mix with metric — M6≠1/4-20!

def: A fine inch thread — for vibration, precise adjustment, and thin walls. 1/4-28 UNF = 28 TPI.
expand: UNF = fine: a fine pitch, a stronger core, good vibration resistance. Aerospace = 70% UNF! Common: #6-40, #8-36, #10-32, 1/4-28, 5/16-24, 3/8-24, 1/2-20. The cost: sensitive to thread damage, galling in stainless, never force it. If it jams — don't force it, Helicoil!

def: The finest pitch — for thin-walled tubing, instrumentation, and aerospace. 1/2-28 UNEF.
expand: UNEF: maximum thread density — a very large core (strength!) with fine adjustment. Uses: retaining nuts on thin tubing, optical instruments, thin-wall aerospace connections. Sizes: 1/4-32, 5/16-32, 3/8-32, 1/2-28, 9/16-24. Very sensitive — thread by hand before using a tool!

def: A thread with a defined root radius (0.15011P) — high fatigue resistance. MIL-S-8879.
expand: UNJ: a controlled root radius instead of a sharp corner = a lower stress concentration = 2x+ the fatigue life! The standard for critical aerospace bolts (NAS, MS). A special tap (UNJ tap) — not standard! Comes with a full rolled profile. In UNJF (fine) and UNJC (coarse). MIL-S-8879.

def: A non-standard diameter-pitch combination — when no standard size fits in UNC/UNF/UNEF.
expand: UNS = any combination not in the standard tables: a UNC diameter with a UNF pitch, or special diameters. Example: 0.875-20 UNS. Used in aerospace (legacy interfaces), hydraulics, and instrumentation. Always explicitly stated on the drawing with all parameters.

def: The historic British thread — a 55° angle, rounded crest and root. Replaced by BSP.
expand: BSW (1841) — the first standardized thread in the world (Joseph Whitworth). A 55° angle (not 60° like metric/UN). Still alive in: old British machines, Indian railways, old plumbing fittings. The critical difference: not compatible with BSP despite the same angle — different pitches!

def: An almost-metric thread at a 47.5° angle for fine instruments. BA0 (6mm) to BA16 (0.79mm).
expand: BA: the historic standard for British electronics and instruments. BA0=6.0mm, BA2=4.7mm, BA4=3.6mm — not a logical ratio (a logarithmic series!). Still encountered in old lab equipment, radios, and British systems. Replacement: the metric M-series. A BA2 thread ≈ M5 approximately but not compatible!

def: An asymmetric profile (7°/45°): strong in one direction. Die-casting bolts, gun barrels.
expand: Buttress: one side almost vertical (7° — load-bearing) and the other angled (45° — clearance). Maximum unidirectional axial strength! Uses: press lead screws, die-casting mold locking, pressure vessel closures, and giant bottle caps. ANSI B1.9, an American 7°/45°.

def: A square 0° profile — maximum efficiency for transmitting force. Hard to manufacture, replaced by ACME.
expand: Theoretically the best: zero radial force = 60-70% efficiency (vs. 30-40% in trapezoidal). The problem: manufacturable only by turning (not grinding/rolling), wear = uncompensated backlash, hard to fit a split-nut adjustment. Almost entirely replaced by ACME (close in efficiency, simple to manufacture).

def: A rounded profile — resistant to damage and dirt. Bottle caps, heavy equipment, railways.
expand: A thread with half-circles: no corners to damage! Maximum resistance to mechanical impact, sand, and rust. Uses: railway couplers, bottle caps, coarse casting bolts, mining equipment. Not for precision — for strength and durability in a harsh environment. DIN 405 / Edison socket.

def: A narrow groove at the thread end allowing a tap/tool to exit cleanly. DIN 76.
expand: Thread Relief (DIN 76): a groove ~2P wide and at minor-diameter depth that allows: 1) a tap to finish cleanly (no partial thread), 2) a nut to seat flush against the shoulder, 3) a stress-free root. Without it: the nut turns partway onto broken threads. Under dynamic loads: a radius at the groove bottom!

def: The active thread length between bolt and nut. 1D steel, 1.5D aluminum, 2D plastic.
expand: A minimum Le ensures the bolt breaks before the thread strips (a predictable, visible failure!). Stainless: 1.5D (work hardening weakens the thread). Gray iron: 2D. Bronze: 1.5D. An exact calc: As/Ath — but the rules of thumb work. Le doesn't include partial threads at the end!

def: Cold welding between bolt and nut (especially stainless!) — jams permanently. Prevention: lubrication!
expand: SS+SS in a thread = risk #1 for galling! The chromium oxide breaks under friction, exposed metal welds together. Prevention: anti-seize (moly/Cu), slow threading (not pneumatic!), an SS bolt+bronze/Monel nut, silver/cadmium plating. If it jams: don't force it — cut it off only. Titanium: the same story.

def: A rod threaded on both ends with no head — for flanges and frequent re-assembly.
expand: The short end is threaded into the body (a transition/light-press fit — it stays!), the long end protrudes and takes a nut. Advantage over a bolt: doesn't wear the body's thread on repeated opening (the nut absorbs the wear). Standard on pressure vessel flanges (ASTM A193 B7 + A194 2H). Hot: B16 + 4 nuts.

def: A tap with chip flutes pointing forward — pushes chips ahead of the tap. Excellent for through holes.
expand: Spiral point (gun tap): the flute cuts at a 15-30° forward angle — the chips come out through the hole! 2x faster than a straight tap, ideal for THRU holes on CNC. Limitation: not for blind holes (chips pile at the bottom!). For blind holes: a spiral flute that pulls chips upward.

def: A tap with twisted flutes — pulls chips upward. For blind holes only.
expand: Spiral flute: the spiral paths pull a long chip upward and back — mandatory for blind holes! Angles: 15° for steels (short chip), 40-52° for aluminum/stainless (long chip). Slower than a gun tap. The danger: if the chip doesn't rise — the tap jams and breaks.

def: A wax pattern → a ceramic shell → metal casting. Accuracy ±0.1mm, complex shapes, almost any alloy.
expand: The process: wax injected into a mold → a wax tree → dipping in ceramic (6-10 layers!) → wax burnout (lost wax) → casting → shell breakage. Advantages: ±0.1% tolerance, Ra 1.6-6.3μm, any alloy, zero draft. Disadvantages: wax mold NRE, slow. Aerospace: single-crystal turbine blades!

def: Injecting molten metal into a steel mold under high pressure. Large runs, high precision, Al/Zn/Mg.
expand: Hot chamber (Zn/Mg): the metal is drawn from a bath. Cold chamber (Al): manually poured (Al erodes the pump!). Pressure 100-2000 bar, fill time 10-100ms. Accuracy ±0.05mm, Ra 0.8-3.2μm. Cycle: 30 seconds. Downside: porosity (trapped gas) — not for pressure vessels without HIP! A mold: ₪50-200K, payback from 5000+ units.

def: Casting into a sand mold — the cheapest, any size and any alloy. Tolerance ±1-3mm.
expand: Sand+binder (furan, phenolic) is packed around a pattern (wood/metal/plastic). Advantages: any size (a gram to tons!), any alloy, low NRE, easy changes. Disadvantages: coarse accuracy, Ra 12-25μm, a slow rate. No-bake for large ones, green sand for runs. Every engine block, valve body, and counterweight = sand cast.

def: Resin-coated sand cured on a hot pattern — a thin, precise shell. Between sand and investment.
expand: Shell mold: a metal pattern at 250°C, resin-coated sand bonds at 6-15mm thickness, cured in an oven. Accuracy: ±0.25-0.5mm (better than sand!), Ra 3-6μm. Castings up to 10kg. Uses: crankshafts, valve bodies, gears. A fast cycle, automated. The pattern's heat = the setup.

def: A rotating mold — centrifugal force pushes metal to the walls. Pipes, bushings, cylinders.
expand: Rotation at 300-3000 RPM: the light particles (gas, slag) are pushed inward and cut away! Result: a dense casting with no porosity. Uses: iron pipes (municipal!), bronze bushings (C932), pulleys, barrel-shaft casting. True centrifugal (pipes); semi: asymmetric parts.

def: A system of channels (sprue, runner, gate) leading molten metal to the mold cavity.
expand: Sprue (a vertical funnel) → runner (a horizontal channel) → gate (the entry to the part). The design determines: fill speed (too fast=turbulence+gas), solidification direction, and shrinkage location. Removed afterward: by cutting/grinding. The gate mark always remains — place it in a non-critical area!

def: A reservoir of molten metal that compensates for shrinkage during solidification — prevents shrinkage cavities.
expand: The metal shrinks 3-7% while solidifying — without compensation, voids form (shrinkage porosity)! A riser supplies liquid metal as long as it solidifies last. Heuvers' rule: a riser thicker than the part it feeds. A blind riser (closed, more efficient) vs. open. An exothermic sleeve heats the riser and improves efficiency.

def: The material shrinks while cooling — the pattern/mold is larger than the final part. Steel: ~2%, Al: ~1.3%.
expand: Three stages: liquid (the level drops — the riser compensates), solidification (solid↔liquid — shrinkage porosity!), and solid (uniform shrinkage — the pattern allowance). Enlarge the pattern: steel +2%, gray iron +1%, Al +1.3%, brass +1.5%. Some materials expand while solidifying: bismuth, antimony, and gray iron (graphite!) — low shrinkage.

def: Voids in a casting: trapped gas (spherical) or shrinkage (branching). Weaken it. NDT for detection.
expand: Gas porosity: trapped gas bubbles — spherical, smooth. From dissolved hydrogen (Al!), mold moisture, or core gas. Shrinkage: branching voids at solidification centers/joints (last-to-freeze). Testing: RT/CT reveals internal defects, DPT only surface. HIP closes both. ASTM E446/E186/E2868 = reference atlases.

def: The joint line of the mold halves — always leaves a mark (flash). Locate it in a non-critical area.
expand: PL = where the mold opens. Consequences: flash (a metal fin) needs removal, reduced accuracy near the line, opposite draft directions on each side. In design: PL location determines draft direction, mold complexity, and core access. Die casting: the PL affects the opening direction and side actions.

def: Forging between flat hammer/anvil surfaces with no closed die — for huge, unique parts.
expand: The hammer/anvil freely shape a square/round: upsetting (shortening+widening), drawing (elongating), punching (a hole). For parts from tons to 150+ tons: ship shafts, turbine wheels, giant rings. Direction: material fibers flow = directional strength (grain flow). Multiple reheats.

def: Material is pressed into a die shaped like the part — built-in grain flow, maximum strength, production runs.
expand: Impression die: two die halves (upper/lower) with a cavity shaped like the part. Excess material exits as flash (trimmed in a further step). Advantages: grain flow follows the shape = 1.5-2x the strength of machining from bar! Disadvantages: high die NRE. Uses: connecting rods, gears, crankshafts. Flashless: no excess — precise but an expensive die.

def: The direction of metal fibers in a forging — follows the part's shape and strengthens it in the load direction.
expand: Grain flow = forging's big advantage over machining: in machining the fibers are cut (like cutting wood across the grain); in forging they flow with the shape. Result: 2x the fatigue resistance, impact strength, and wear resistance. The forging envelope on a drawing defines the flow zone.

def: Excess material pushed outside the die — trimmed in a trimming die. Ensures full fill.
expand: The flash is necessary: it's the guarantee the entire die cavity is filled! Flash line = PL — a typical 3-6mm thickness, trimmed in a dedicated press. Flashless forging: no excess — requires an exact stock volume and a complex die. Web flash (in hole areas): removed by punching. The flash mark always remains.

def: Shaping at room temperature — high accuracy, excellent finish, work hardening. Bolts!
expand: Cold heading: this is how 99% of the world's bolts and rivets are made! Wire is cut, formed into a head shape in 2-5 strikes. Accuracy ±0.05mm, Ra 0.8-1.6, no machining stock. The hardening: Sy rises 50-100%! Downside: enormous forces, limited to ductile materials. Cold extrusion: cans, cartridge cases.

def: Forging above the recrystallization temperature (1100-1250°C for steel) — low forces, complex shapes.
expand: Hot forging: the metal is soft and ductile — easy shaping at reasonable forces. Advantage: complex shapes, hard materials, any size. Disadvantage: scale (mill scale) ← 2-5mm machining stock, tolerance ±0.5-2mm, decarb. Warm forging (600-900°C): a compromise — accuracy better than hot, force lower than cold.

def: Filter + pressure regulator + lubricator — prepares clean, dry, lubricated compressed air. The entry to every system.
expand: Filter: 5-40μm (standard 25μm), removes water and dirt. Regulator: reduces from 8-10bar to a 6bar working pressure, with a gauge. Lubricator: mists pneumatic oil for valves and cylinders (not always required — dry air for clean applications). Condensate drain: automatic! A wet filter = problems.

def: A piston driven by compressed air: single-acting (spring return) or double-acting. ISO 15552/6432.
expand: Double-acting (common): air in both directions. Single-acting: air+spring (guaranteed return with no air!). Force: F=P×A (⌀50 at 6bar = 1178N). The choice: ISO 15552 (heavy, ⌀32-320) or ISO 6432 (light, ⌀8-25). Built-in cushioning = gentle deceleration at the ends. A magnet in the piston + a reed sensor = position sensing.

def: 5/2 (5 ports, 2 positions) for a double-acting cylinder. Solenoid 24VDC/220VAC or manual.
expand: 5/2: P→A+B→R (and reverse). 5/3 (3 positions): center closed/exhaust/pressure. 3/2: for a single-acting cylinder. Actuation: solenoid (fast, automation), pilot (large ones), manual (emergency). NAMUR: directly on a process valve actuator. Manifold: a valve bank on a common rail — saves piping.

def: Reduces pressure from the main line to a stable working pressure. 6 bar = the pneumatic standard.
expand: Relieving regulator: vents excess pressure when the setting is lowered (common). Non-relieving: for expensive gases — no waste. Precision regulator: ±0.01bar stability (instrumentation). Electronic: 4-20mA→precise pressure (proportional). Rule: a regulator at every point of use — don't rely on line pressure.

def: Compressed air creates vacuum via the venturi effect — simple, small, no moving parts.
expand: Compact and reliable: air through a cone → a pressure drop → suction. Vacuum down to -0.9bar. Uses: suction cups (pick&place), sheet handling, vacuum fixtures. Advantage: no moving parts, small, cheap. Disadvantage: continuous air consumption = expensive energy. A built-in digital vacuum switch = simplicity.

def: The temperature at which water condenses out of compressed air. A dryer lowers it to 3°C (refrigerant) or -40°C (desiccant).
expand: Compressed air is saturated with water (compression concentrates humidity!). In a cold pipe = condensate = rust+wear+freezing. A refrigerant dryer: cools to 3°C PDP — enough for 90%. A desiccant dryer: -40°C PDP — for painting, instrumentation, food. A membrane dryer: compact, no electricity. Rule: water in pneumatics = enemy #1.

def: The schedule determines wall thickness: Sch40=standard, Sch80=double, Sch160=high pressure. OD is fixed!
expand: ASME B36.10: every schedule of a 2" pipe shares an OD of 60.3mm — only the wall changes inward! Sch40: 3.91mm (the common one), Sch80: 5.54mm, Sch160: 8.74mm, XXH: 11.07mm. The nominal name (2 inch) ≠ any physical dimension — historical legacy! Below NPS 14: an arbitrary OD; above: OD=NPS.

def: NPS (inch) / DN (metric) — the pipe's name, not its real diameter! NPS 2 = DN 50 = OD 60.3mm.
expand: The system that confuses everyone: NPS 1/2 = OD 21.3mm (not 12.7!). The history: once ID was close to nominal, today only OD is fixed. The conversion table: NPS 1/4=DN8=OD 13.7, NPS 1/2=DN15=21.3, NPS 1=DN25=33.4, NPS 2=DN50=60.3, NPS 4=DN100=114.3. Always specify: NPS + schedule.

def: A perforated disc for a removable connection in piping — rating: 150/300/600/900/1500/2500. ASME B16.5.
expand: Flange rating: 150# (20bar@38°C), 300# (51bar), 600# (102bar)... pressure drops with temperature! Types: weld neck (the best — strong and NDT-friendly), slip-on (cheap, usually allowed up to 150#), blind (closes off), socket weld (small sizes). Raised face (RF) is common, RTJ for high pressure. Bolts: B7+2H under pressure.

def: A seal between flanges: spiral wound (common), sheet (cheap), RTJ (high pressure).
expand: Spiral wound (ASME B16.20): a coiled SS strip with PTFE/graphite — flexible, reliable, up to 600°C. A centering ring (inner+outer) prevents over-crushing. Sheet (Klinger/Garlock): compressed rubber/graphite — cheap, up to 150#. Ring type joint (RTJ): a soft metal ring in a groove — high pressures, metal-to-metal sealing.

def: The central drawing of a plant/process: all piping, valves, instrumentation, and control in symbols.
expand: P&ID = a plant's DNA: every pipe line (size, material, schedule), every valve (type, actuation, fail position), every instrument (tag number, ISA function). Standard: ISA S5.1. Reading a P&ID = a mandatory skill for every process engineer. A field change without updating the P&ID = a serious safety violation.

def: A pipe enters a socket and is welded from outside — for small diameters (up to NPS 2). A 1.5mm gap is mandatory!
expand: SW: the pipe enters the socket, pulled back 1.5mm (an expansion gap — without it: a root crack!), and fillet-welded from outside. Advantage: built-in alignment, no edge prep. Disadvantage: an internal crevice = crevice corrosion in stainless! Hence not recommended in: food, pharma, critical SS. ASME B16.11.

he: Butt Weld Fitting — חיבור ריתוך ישיר
def: Elbows, tees, and reducers welded directly to the pipe — no internal crevice. The cleanest.
expand: BW: prep+tack+weld — a smooth internal joint (a perfect TIG root + fill). ASME B16.9. Advantage: no crevice, no dead leg, a strong structure. Disadvantage: requires NDT (RT/UT), a qualified welder, and doesn't disassemble. The standard in: pressure piping, sanitary, chemical. Schedule matches the pipe!

def: External measurement at 0.01mm accuracy (digital 0.001). The classic screw-measurement tool. 0-25/25-50/50-75mm.
expand: Every technician's personal tool: a ratchet/thimble stop ensures consistent force. Calibration: every 6-12 months + a daily zero check (a standard bar for 25-50+). Limitations: diameters only (not steps!), 2 points (lobing goes unnoticed!). An inside micrometer for holes, a depth micrometer for depths. Mitutoyo/Mahr/Starrett.

def: Universal measurement: outside/inside/depth/step. Accuracy 0.02-0.03mm. The first tool people learn.
expand: Vernier: reading a vernier scale (0.02/0.05). Dial: a clock face (0.02). Digital: an LCD (0.01 display, 0.02 accuracy). Range 150/200/300mm. Rules of use: gentle closing (don't force it!), perpendicular to the part, a straight-on reading. Limitations: not accurate enough for fits — that needs a micrometer. Digital ones offer SPC output.

def: A spring-loaded needle measures displacement: 0.01 or 0.001mm. TIR, runout, alignment. The lathe's tool!
expand: Plunger type (full rotation, 0-10mm) and lever type (angled contact, 0.2-0.8mm — for tight areas). Uses: shaft runout, aligning a 4-jaw chuck, flatness checks on granite, sweeping during setup. On a magnetic base = anywhere. Calibration: a gauge block stack. Tip: tap lightly and check the zero return — hysteresis = a calibration flag!

def: Measures internal hole diameter at 0.01mm accuracy — two expanding contacts + an indicator. Calibrated against a ring.
expand: Three legs or two+an indicator: insert, rock to find the minimum (=diameter!), and read. Calibration: a ring gauge or an outside micrometer. Ranges: 18-35, 35-60, 50-100mm... Common error: not finding the minimum = an oversized reading. A 3-point bore mic: direct and fast, but expensive.

def: Go/NoGo for shafts: a set jaw spacing — pass/fail with no numeric reading.
expand: Two jaws (or a stepped pair): go at max and no-go at min. The shaft must pass at go and stop at no-go. Advantage: 10x faster than a micrometer, no operator error! Adjustable (two anvils + an adjustment micrometer) or fixed. For production runs only — periodic calibration is critical.

def: A flat reference surface (granite, 1-3μm) — the basis for every height and flatness measurement.
expand: Granite > cast iron (no burrs, doesn't rust, doesn't distort with heat). Grades: AA (lab, 1μm), A (inspection, 2μm), B (production, 4μm). Maintenance: clean and dry, covered when not in use, annual calibration (a repeat check). Forbidden: sharp tools, impacts, hot parts. On the plate: a height gauge, V-blocks, gauge blocks.

def: A precise bar + two rollers: building precise angles from gauge blocks. sin(α)=h/L.
expand: Roller distance: 100 or 200mm. To build 30°: h=100×sin30°=50.000mm (a gauge block stack). Accuracy: ±5 arc-seconds! Limitation: above 45° sensitivity drops (cosine). Use: aligning a part for machining at a precise angle, checking a taper, calibrating a digital angle gauge.

en: Gauge Block / Slip Gauge / Jo Block
def: Polished steel/carbide blocks: dimensions accurate to ±0.05-0.5μm. The universal calibration basis.
expand: They stick to each other (wringing) via molecular force — building any dimension from a set of 87-112 blocks. Grades: K (reference, ±0.05μm), 0 (calibration), 1 (inspection), 2 (production). Materials: hardened steel (HRC 64), carbide (doesn't wear), ceramic (doesn't rust). The basis of the whole traceable measurement chain.

def: A fiber/CO₂ laser cuts sheet up to 25mm steel, 15mm SS, 20mm Al. Accuracy ±0.1mm, Ra 3-6μm.
expand: A fiber laser (1μm) has replaced CO₂: 3x faster on thin sheet, less maintenance. Vc: steel 1mm→40m/min, 10mm→2m/min. HAZ: 0.1-0.5mm. Advantages: accuracy, flexibility (a DXF file→a cut), no tooling. Disadvantage: limited thickness, high reflectivity (Cu/Al are hard on CO₂). Nitrogen for SS (clean), oxygen for steel (fast).

def: Water at 4000bar + garnet particles cut any material up to 200mm. Zero HAZ! ±0.1mm.
expand: Pure waterjet: rubber, plastic, food. Abrasive waterjet: metal, glass, stone, composites — anything! The absolute advantage: zero heat-affected zone = no microstructure change, no distortion, no temper color on SS. Disadvantage: slow on thick material, a taper in the cut (fixed with 5-axis), wet and noisy. Omax, Flow.

def: A 20,000°C plasma arc cuts conductive metal up to 50mm. Fast but coarse. A large HAZ.
expand: The middle ground: faster than laser at thickness, coarser than it. Kerf: 2-4mm (laser 0.2-0.5). HAZ: 3-8mm. Uses: rough cutting, CNC plasma for structural profiles, weld prep. HyPerformance Plasma (Hypertherm): Ra 3-6μm, accuracy ±0.5mm — close to laser at thickness. Limited to conductors — not plastic/glass.

def: Bending on a press brake: V-die+punch. Minimum bend radius = the material thickness.
expand: The K-factor rule: the neutral material isn't at the center — K=0.33 for a sharp bend, 0.5 for a generous one. Bend allowance: BA = (π/180)×α×(R+K×t). Springback: the material bounces back 2-5° — compensated by over-bending. Steel 1mm: R_min=1mm, Al: R_min=0.5t. Rolling (grain) direction matters — bend perpendicular to it!

def: Drawing sheet into a cup/cone shape in a die — cans, sinks, automotive parts. D/d>2 = deep drawing.
expand: A blank (a sheet disc) → a punch pushes into a die → the sheet stretches into a cup shape. Rule of thumb: a maximum draw ratio of 2:1 per pass (a second pass requires annealing!). A blank holder prevents wrinkling. Materials: DC04 steel, 304 SS, Al 1050/3003. Runs: hundreds of thousands. The tool for making shells, drums, cans.

def: Cutting shapes from sheet on a press — blanking (the part) / punching (the hole). A progressive die for runs.
expand: Blanking: the product is what falls out; punching: the product is what remains. Clearance: 5-10% of thickness per side (governs the cut quality). Progressive die: several stations in sequence — cutting+bending+forming on every stroke. Fine blanking: 1% clearance + a counter-punch = a 100% smooth, straight cut — for flat gears!

def: Pushing metal through a die — endless profiles. Al the most common. Free cross-section!
expand: A heated billet is pushed through a die → a continuous profile. Al: 85% of extrusions (450°C, low force). Profiles: T-slot, heat sinks, frames, tracks. Accuracy: ±0.1-0.3mm/25mm. Die cost: ₪5-20K — worthwhile from 500kg. Design: uniform thickness, corner radii, hollow with a bridge die. 6063 for finish, 6061 for structure.

def: Removing material with acid through a mask — for thin sheet, zero burr, zero stress.
expand: Photo Chemical Machining: a light-sensitive film → exposure → acid dissolves the exposed area. Advantages: zero burr, zero stress, any shape, fast for prototyping (tooling = film!). Limitations: thickness ≤2mm, undercut (acid digs sideways = etch factor), a minimum 1:1 ratio. Uses: shims, meshes, EMI shields, flexures.

def: A rotating tool stirs material with no melting — a solid-state joint. Perfect for aluminum!
expand: A tool with a pin spinning at 1000+ RPM enters the joint and 'stirs' the material — with no melting! Result: a tiny HAZ, zero porosity, no filler metal, minimal distortion. Requires: a heavy CNC machine + backing. Dominates: SpaceX tanks, EV car bodies, ships. Perfect for Al; Ti/SS possible with a PCBN tool.

def: A lead screw with ball rolling elements — friction of 0.01 (vs. 0.3 for a standard screw!). The CNC axis standard.
expand: Balls roll in a gothic groove between the screw and the nut — 90%+ efficiency (ACME: 30-50%). Result: high speed, accuracy (C3=±0.008mm/300mm, C5=±0.018), preload for zero backlash. Mandatory on CNC. Backlash: a single preloaded nut or a double nut. Lubrication: Li/EP grease. Manufacturers: THK, NSK, PMI, Hiwin.

def: A rail + a carriage with ball/roller rolling elements — smooth, rigid motion. Every CNC machine.
expand: A block (carriage) rides a ground rail: balls for light/medium load, rollers for heavy. Preload: Z0 (standard), ZA (light), ZB (medium) — determines rigidity and friction. Class: C (standard), H (precision), P (high), SP (ultra). Rail length is unlimited (joinable!). Lubrication: grease from a nipple, weekly/monthly. Hiwin, THK, Bosch-Rexroth.

def: An AC motor+encoder = precise control of position, speed, and torque. The heart of CNC and robotics.
expand: AC servo (PMSM): permanent magnets + an encoder (absolute/incremental) → the drive closes a loop. Advantage: high torque at low RPM, fast response (<1ms), position accuracy ±1 pulse. Vs. a stepper: doesn't lose steps under load! Manufacturers: Fanuc, Siemens, Yaskawa, Mitsubishi. Tuning: gain+bandwidth.

def: A motor that rotates in precise steps (1.8°=200/revolution) — simple and cheap. 3D printers, small CNC.
expand: Open loop: no encoder — trusts that a command = execution (until a step is lost under load — and then everything is offset!). Micro-stepping: 1/16 step = 3200/revolution. NEMA 17/23/34 by size. Advantage: cheap, reliable, holding torque. Disadvantage: torque drops with speed, unsuited to dynamic loads. A closed-loop stepper = the best of both worlds.

def: An angular position sensor: incremental (pulses) or absolute (a fixed value). Feedback for a servo.
expand: Incremental: A+B+Z (pulses, direction, zero) — needs homing. Absolute: every position = a unique value, even after power off! Resolution: 2048-131072 PPR. Optical (accurate), magnetic (durable, cheap). A CNC spindle: an encoder on the spindle for position (C-axis, rigid tap). A linear encoder: a glass scale — 0.5-5μm resolution.

def: Connecting two shafts: rigid (precise), jaw/spider (damping), bellows (flexible+precise), Oldham (offset).
expand: Rigid: precise but requires perfect alignment — otherwise a load on the bearings! Jaw (spider): an elastomer star absorbs shock and compensates 0.1mm+1°. Bellows: high torsional rigidity + angular flexibility = ball screw+servo. Oldham: absorbs a large radial offset. Disc coupling: aerospace/CNC — high torque, zero backlash. The choice: by torque, speed, allowed misalignment.

def: The science of friction, wear, and lubrication — the field that saves billions in wear.
expand: 30% of the world's energy goes to friction, 3% of GDP to wear! Tribology = understanding the interface: micro-contacts between surfaces, lubrication regimes (boundary→mixed→hydrodynamic), wear mechanisms (adhesive, abrasive, fatigue, corrosive). Applications: oil selection, mating material, coating, roughness.

def: F_friction = μ × F_normal. Steel/steel dry: 0.6. Lubricated: 0.1-0.15. PTFE: 0.04.
expand: Static (μs, for starting motion) > dynamic (μk, while moving). Values: steel/steel dry 0.6-0.8, lubricated 0.1-0.15; Al/steel 0.47; PTFE/anything 0.04-0.1; rubber/concrete 0.6-0.8. Rule: μ isn't constant — depends on Ra, speed, heat, fluid. Galling = μ→∞ (welds together!).

def: Boundary (contact!), mixed (partial), hydrodynamic (floating on a film). The Stribeck curve.
expand: The Stribeck curve (μ vs. speed×viscosity/load): boundary: metal-metal contact, EP additives protect; mixed: partially on film; hydrodynamic (full film): zero contact, μ=0.001-0.01! A shock/stop = a return to boundary — that's where the damage happens! A hydrodynamic bearing: works only in full film.

def: Microscopic welding between surfaces — jamming. SS, Ti, Al are sensitive. Prevention: different materials + lubrication.
expand: Contact under load tears the oxide layer → fresh metal welds together ← tearing ← a destroyed surface. The bad pairs: SS/SS, Ti/Ti, Al/Al. Prevention: 1) different materials (SS+bronze), 2) a coating (nitriding, hard chrome), 3) anti-seize (moly/copper paste), 4) the right Ra (too coarse=asperities, too smooth=a vacuum effect).

def: Pressure×velocity product = a bearing material's performance metric: PV [MPa·m/s]. Above the limit = thermal failure.
expand: The limit: the heat generated (∝P×V) = the heat dissipated. PV_max: bronze bearing 1.8, PTFE 0.06, PTFE+bronze 0.5, PEEK+CF 3.5 MPa·m/s. Design: P=F/A_projected, V=π×d×n/60000. Below PV_max: the material lives. Above it: heating→softening→welding. The key parameter in bushing selection.

def: Dividing a model into thousands of small elements and solving stress/strain equations in each. ANSYS, SolidWorks Sim.
expand: Mesh: Tet4 (fast, less accurate) ← Tet10 (standard) ← Hex8/20 (the best). Convergence: refine the mesh until the result stops changing (±5%). Boundary conditions: the most critical — a wrong fixed support = a pretty, wrong result! Result: a Von Mises map, deformation, SF. The tool verifies — it doesn't replace understanding!

def: Dividing the geometry into elements: Tet (triangular-based) or Hex (rectangular-based). Size and quality govern.
expand: Mesh quality = result quality. Metrics: aspect ratio <5 (ideal 1), Jacobian >0.3, skewness <0.8. Local refinement (mesh refinement): at stress concentrations — holes, radii, section changes. Singularity: a sharp corner = infinite stress (not real!) — add a radius or ignore the edge.

def: Anchors (fixed/pinned/roller) and loads (force/pressure/moment) — define the problem. An error here = everything is wrong.
expand: Fixed: 6 DOF constrained (rare in reality — over-constrained!). Pin: 3 translations constrained, 3 rotations free. Roller/symmetry: one direction constrained. Always start with: how is the part actually held? An FBD ← BC. Oversimplifying (fixed instead of bolted) = stresses too low = dangerous!

def: fn = (1/2π)√(k/m). When the excitation frequency = fn → resonance → destructive amplification! A modal analysis finds it.
expand: Every structure = a system of springs and masses with natural frequencies. Mode 1 (the lowest) = the critical one. Rule: fn > 1.4×the excitation frequency (spindle RPM/60, a cyclic force). A modal analysis in FEA: finds fn + the mode shape (where the vibration is maximum). Changing fn: raise stiffness or lower mass. CNC chatter = resonance!

def: The part's coordinate system (G54-G59) — the location of the part's zero point on the machine.
expand: G54 = the primary system (the common one). G55-G59 = 5 more (multi-part, tombstone). G54.1 P1-P48 = extended (Fanuc). Setting it: an edge finder, a probe, or an indicator → feeds the work offset. An error in the WCS = the whole part is offset! Mandatory: a first check dry run (Z+50mm) before cutting.

def: A probe that goes in the spindle and measures the part on the machine — automatic WCS, in-process measurement.
expand: Renishaw OMP/RMP: the spindle picks up the probe, touches the part, and the controller captures the position. Uses: 1) automatic WCS setup (saves 5-15 min of setup!), 2) mid-operation measurement (a hole ← check ← continue), 3) checking stock before machining (adaptive). A tool setting probe: measures tool length automatically. ROI: 2-6 months.

def: A vertical block with 4 faces for mounting parts — multiplies HMC output. 4 setups in one rotation.
expand: A cast/welded block with T-slot or grid holes on every face — on an HMC (a horizontal machine with a rotary table) 4 parts are machined per rotation! While the spindle machines side 1, the operator loads side 3. 16 parts on a tombstone = continuous production. Modular: Jergens, Kurt.

def: Aluminum/soft-steel jaws machined to the part's shape — perfect grip with no marks.
expand: You buy soft jaw blanks, mount them to the chuck, and turn the internal profile exactly to the part's size (or an intermediate stage). Advantages: 100% contact, zero jaw marks, TIR <0.01mm. Disadvantage: dedicated to one part (or a family). Pie jaws for large parts. Machinable jaws on power chucks — the key to a repeatable Op2.

def: ER11-ER40: a collet with 8-16 slots that contract around the tool shank. Gripping range ±0.5mm.
expand: ER (DIN 6499): the most common — flexible (an ER32 holds ⌀3-20 with 10 collets), runout 5-15μm (HP: <5μm). Downside: not the best — shrink fit (1-3μm TIR) and hydraulic (3-5μm) are better for precision. Advantage: cheap, fast, can hold a square shank (a square collet). A sealed ER: coolant-through with no leak.

def: The tool shank goes in with heat — TIR <3μm, maximum rigidity, G2.5@25000 balancing. HSM mandatory.
expand: The holder is heated to 300°C (an induction heater, 10 seconds!), an h6 tool is inserted, it cools and locks. TIR: 1-3μm (the best!), rigidity: 3x an ER. The choice for: HSM, precise finishing, long tools (less deflection). Downside: requires a heating device, no immediate swap. Haimer, Schunk.

def: Rough (1-10⁻³ mbar), high (10⁻³-10⁻⁷), ultra-high (<10⁻⁷). Different uses for each level.
expand: Low/rough (1000-1 mbar): suction, packaging, drying. Medium (1-10⁻³): evaporation, PVD. High (10⁻³-10⁻⁷): SEM, thin coatings, metal AM (EBM!). UHV (<10⁻⁷): particle accelerators, semiconductors. Each level = a different pump technology, different sealing materials, and different care.

def: Release of gases from material surfaces in vacuum — the main limit to achieving high vacuum.
expand: Every material 'releases' gases absorbed at the surface: H₂O, CO₂, H₂, hydrocarbons. Plastics = the worst! Aluminum = good (after bake-out). 304L stainless with electropolish = the standard for UHV. Bake-out (150-250°C for hours) = accelerates outgassing. An RGA (residual gas analyzer) = 'sniffs' what remains.

def: KF (quick clamp, O-ring): up to 10⁻⁸ mbar. CF (ConFlat, metal-metal): UHV. VCR: pure gas.
expand: KF/NW (ISO-KF): a clamp ring + a Viton/Buna O-ring — quick, up to HV. CF (ConFlat): an SS flange with a crushed copper gasket = a metal-metal seal — UHV! Swagelok VCR: a nut + a Ni gasket — ultra-clean gas. Rule: an O-ring limits you to HV; metal = UHV. CF=the scientific standard.

def: Minimum wall thickness: steel 1mm, Al 0.8mm, plastic 0.5-1mm, die casting 0.8mm.
expand: Rules: thickness≥L/50 (against vibration), ≥3×Ra (against breakthrough), ≥tool access (milling 3×D min, L/D=3: ⌀3→a 3mm wall). Die casting: 0.8mm Al (flow), 0.5mm Zn (Zamak!). 3D print: 0.4mm FDM, 0.3mm SLA. A thin wall = clamping distortion, machining vibration, injection sink marks.

def: Minimum diameter: a carbide drill ⌀0.5mm, HSS ⌀1mm, die casting ⌀0.8mm, PCM ⌀0.1mm.
expand: The economic rule: ⌀<1mm = double the cost (a fragile tool, extra care). Maximum L/D: a standard drill 5×D, coolant-through carbide 8-10×D, a gun drill 100×D. Die casting: minimum ⌀ = wall thickness (a fragile core pin). Laser: ⌀0.1mm but tapered. EDM: ⌀0.1mm with no taper. Small and deep = always expensive.

def: Milling: corner R ≥ tool R. R=0 requires EDM! Rule: R ≥ 1mm (and in a deep pocket R ≥ 3mm).
expand: A round end mill = always a corner radius: R=D/2. A tool smaller than ⌀3 = expensive and fragile. The trick: a dog bone/T-bone relief (a circle/slot at the corner) — allows a mating part with a sharp corner to fit! A blind pocket (⌀3 at 20mm depth): L/D=7 = vibration and poor accuracy. Anything that shrinks the corner R — costs more.

def: A ground h6 pin ensuring precise alignment between two parts. Two are enough: round + diamond.
expand: Two pins define location: pin 1 (round) locates, pin 2 (diamond/slotted) sets orientation (and compensates for distance tolerance). Fit: m6/n6 in the fixed part, f7/g6 in the removable one. Material: hardened steel HRC 58+, ⌀ tolerance h6. DIN 6325 (standard), DIN 7979 (with a thread for extraction).

def: A spring ring in a groove that prevents axial movement of a shaft or bearing. DIN 471 (external), DIN 472 (internal).
expand: External (on a shaft, DIN 471): the common one — holds a bearing, gear, pulley. Internal (in a bore, DIN 472): holds a shaft in a housing. Inverted (E-clip): no tool needed, side installation. Limitation: limited axial load (a small contact area + the groove weakens the shaft!). For heavy loads: a machined shoulder + a nut.

def: A key (DIN 6885) transmits torque between a shaft and a gear. A slot in both. Side fit is common.
expand: Parallel key: rectangular, side fit (tight sides, loose height). Size by shaft diameter: ⌀20→6×6, ⌀30→8×7, ⌀50→14×9. Woodruff: a half-moon — self-centering. Taper key: adjustable, with a gib head for extraction. Weakness: the slot weakens the shaft (Kt≈2.5!) — an alternative: a spline, a press fit, or a friction hub (locking assembly).

def: Teeth on a shaft transmitting high torque with excellent centering. Involute (an involute tooth) is common.
expand: Involute spline (SAE, DIN 5480): a profile like a gear! Centers on the pitch diameter, load spread across all teeth. Vs. a key: 3-5x the torque at the same diameter, perfect centering, and doesn't weaken like a keyway. Serration: sharp teeth — angular, not involute. Manufacture: broaching for internal, hobbing/rolling for external.

def: A headless screw that fits entirely into a hole — locks a part on a shaft with point pressure.
expand: Points: cup point (common — leaves a mark), cone point (centers in a dimple), dog point (guides into a slot), flat (no marking). Allen/hex socket. Uses: locking a pulley/gear on a shaft (temporary — a key is better!), position adjustment. Weakness: torque is transmitted by friction alone — slips under dynamic load! A nyloc tip prevents loosening.

def: A bolt with a precision cylinder (h6) between the head and the thread — used as a pivot, a guide, or a spacer.
expand: The shoulder = a perfect pivot: an exact h6 ⌀, a defined length, a load-bearing head. Uses: a pivot in links, a guide in jigs (with a bush), a precise spacer, a stroke limiter (a stripper in molds). A short thread (locking only) + a long working shoulder. Material: hardened 12.9. ISO 7379 / DIN 9841.

en: Lip Seal / Oil Seal / Radial Shaft Seal
def: A rubber seal with a spring-loaded lip — keeps oil in and dirt out. DIN 3760/3761.
expand: The most common for rotating shafts! A lip on a garter spring presses against the shaft — a dynamic contact 0.1-0.3mm wide. Materials: NBR (oil, up to 100°C), FKM (200°C), PTFE (dry). Speed: V_max = 10-15 m/s (NBR). Surface life: shaft Ra 0.2-0.5μm, hardness 55-60HRC, no scratches. Double lip: +a dust lip.

def: Two polished faces (rotating+stationary) — sealing a pump shaft under pressure. Zero designed leakage.
expand: Seal faces: SiC/WC (hard) against carbon/SiC (soft) — floating on a 0.25μm film! A spring/bellows maintains contact. Sealing: a secondary O-ring. Materials: SiC/SiC for abrasive, carbon/SiC for clean. API 682: the pump standard. A double seal+barrier fluid = zero emissions. Seal failure = the #1 cause of pump downtime.

def: A rubber ring that sits on the shaft (not in a groove!) with its lip touching a shoulder — keeps dirt out.
expand: V-Ring: mounted on the shaft, rotates with it, the lip touches a stationary housing. A dust/water seal (not pressure!). Advantage: no groove, no bore tolerance, tolerates misalignment. Complements a labyrinth: a V-ring outside + a labyrinth inside = double protection. In a JCB bucket — a V-ring protects the bearing.

def: A PTFE seal with an internal spring — for extreme temperatures (−250 to +315°C), chemicals, vacuum.
expand: A PTFE jacket + an internal V/cantilever spring: the spring pushes the PTFE into contact even with no pressure (unlike an O-ring, which needs squeeze). Universal chemistry (PTFE!), cryogenics (no rubber to crack!), vacuum (low outgassing). Lower friction than an O-ring. Bal-Seal, Parker Omniseal. Expensive — used where there's no alternative.

def: An Allen bolt with a cylindrical head — the most common in engineering. M3-M30. 8.8/10.9/12.9.
expand: The workhorse: a low head (D≈1.5d, H≈d) fits into a CBORE recess. Allen key/hex socket. Advantage over hex: a small head, high torque, a small CBORE hole. Property class 12.9 = HRC 39-44. Coating: black oxide (default), Zn, Zn-Ni. The world's most common size: M8×25 12.9.

def: A low, wide, rounded head — aesthetic, safe (no edges), lower torque than SHCS.
expand: Button head: D≈1.9d but H≈0.55d — low and smooth! Ideal for: covers, medical equipment, furniture, anywhere someone touches it. The problem: a small hex socket = a lower maximum torque (the corner rounds out!). Don't use it instead of SHCS under structural load. 10.9 is common.

en: Flat Head Socket Cap Screw Countersunk
def: A 90° conical head (ISO) that fits into a CSK — a flush surface after assembly.
expand: Countersunk 90°: the head sinks into the material, a flat surface. Mandatory: a CSK at a matching angle (ISO=90°, American=82° — don't mix them!). Pull-out force: the conical head self-locks — self-centering. Downside: countersinking weakens the part, limited torque (a small Allen). For panels, covers, and anywhere flush is mandatory.

def: A standard hex nut — height ≈ 0.8d. 8/10/12. Nyloc = DIN 985, flange = DIN 6923.
expand: The basic nut: A/F (wrench size) = ISO 898 Part 2. Family: DIN 985 (nyloc — self-locking), DIN 6923 (flange — spreads force, replaces a washer), DIN 439 (thin/jam nut — half height, double locking). Class 8 on 8.8, 10 on 10.9, 12 on 12.9. Marking: the class is stamped on the face.

def: A flat washer spreads force and protects the surface. 200HV (7090) or 100HV (7089).
expand: 7089: standard (100HV, soft — deforms under heavy tightening). 7090: hardened (200HV) — the engineering choice. 7093: large (OD×2). 7094: extra-large. Size: ID=d+0.5-1mm, OD=2d-3d. When mandatory: over an elongated hole, on Al/plastic (prevents sinking), under a spring lock washer. When unnecessary: a flange nut/bolt already spreads force.

en: Thin / Low Head Socket Cap Screw
def: Head height half that of DIN 912 — for tight areas. Lower maximum torque!
expand: H≈0.6d (vs. d in DIN 912): fits into narrow clearances. A centering pilot in the head helps alignment. Class 8.8 (not 12.9 — the low head won't hold!). Uses: machine covers, height limiters, anywhere height is critical. Rule: if there's room — DIN 912 is preferable (stronger and more stable).

def: The flange standard NPS 1/2-24: rating 150-2500, dimensions, materials, and gaskets.
expand: Defines: dimensions (OD, bolt circle, holes), pressure-temperature rating (150# at 38°C=20bar, at 300°C=10bar!), materials (A105 steel, A182 F316 SS). Facing: RF (raised face, 1.6mm), FF (flat face — for cast iron!), RTJ (ring type joint). Above NPS 24: ASME B16.47.

def: A hardened SS: Sy=1000MPa + corrosion resistance like 304. Aerospace, medical, valves.
expand: 17-4 PH (630): 17% chromium + 4% nickel + 4% copper. Solution annealed: HRC 33. After aging (H900=482°C): HRC 44! Corrosion resistance between 304 and 410 — good, not perfect. Machining: like 4140 in the SA condition (before hardening). AM-qualified (DMLS). Common: valves, shafts, turbine parts, and threaded fittings.

def: Copper + 2% Be: HRC 40 + conductivity. Non-sparking tools, springs, electrodes, molds.
expand: BeCu C17200: the strongest of the coppers (Sy=1000MPa hardened!), thermally (105 W/mK) and electrically conductive. Uses: non-sparking tools (fuel/oil facilities), contact springs (connectors), spot-welding electrodes, plastic injection molds (heat spreading!). Warning: Be dust is highly toxic — masks/extraction required during machining!

def: Copper + tin + phosphorus: wear resistance + flexibility. Springs, gears, bushings.
expand: C510 (5% Sn): contact springs, diaphragms, plain bearings. C544 (4% Pb+Sn): free-machining = lathe bushings. Advantages: excellent wear resistance (worm gears!), fatigue resistance, conductivity, anti-galling against steel. Limitation: more expensive than brass, weaker than steel. The sacrificial surface: the bronze wears — and absorbs the defects.

def: A cold-work tool steel: 12% chromium, HRC 58-62, excellent wear resistance. Knives, molds, punches.
expand: D2: high-carbon high-chromium — almost stainless (11.5% Cr, missing only 1.5% for full passivity). One of the best wear-resistance grades thanks to large carbides. Hardening: air (air-hardening) = minimal distortion! Machining: in the annealed state HB 220 — relatively easy. After HT: grinding/EDM only. The tool for cutting dies, rollers, gauges.

def: A hot-work tool steel: HRC 44-52. Die-casting molds, forging, extrusion.
expand: H13: 5% Cr + 1.3% Mo + 1% V + 0.4% C — excellent at heat (withstands 500°C+ without softening!). Uses: Al die-casting dies (100K+ shots!), hot forging, extrusion, DMLS tools (AM-approved). Nitriding improves: HV 1000+ at the surface. The steel that holds up the entire casting industry.

def: 18% Ni + Co + Mo + Ti: Sy 1700-2400MPa with no carbon! Excellent welding, near-zero HT distortion.
expand: Maraging = martensite + aging: a soft martensite (machinable!) hardened at 480°C (no quench = no distortion!). Enormous strength + high KIC + easy welding (no carbon!). Uses: die-casting molds (1M shots!), aircraft landing gear, uranium centrifuges, missile heads. Very expensive — used only when the unique combination is needed.

def: 8 rules for identifying abnormal patterns in a control chart: crossing ±3σ, 7 rising, 2/3 crossing ±2σ, etc.
expand: Beyond 'a point outside the limit': rule 1 (crossing 3σ), rule 2 (9 on the same side), rule 3 (6 rising/falling), rule 4 (14 alternating), rule 5 (2/3 crossing 2σ), rule 6 (4/5 crossing 1σ), rule 7 (15 within 1σ — stratification), rule 8 (8 outside 1σ). Every violation = a special cause → investigate!

def: An MSA study: 10 parts × 3 inspectors × 3 trials = equipment variation (EV) + inspector variation (AV).
expand: The ANOVA method (more precise than X̄-R): breaks down variation into EV, AV, and interaction. Results: %GRR (of tolerance) <10% excellent, 10-30% conditional, >30% unacceptable. ndc (number of distinct categories) ≥5 = the system distinguishes well enough. Before any Cpk study — GRR first! Otherwise you're measuring noise.

def: OEE = availability × performance × quality. World class ≥ 85%. The central operational metric.
expand: A=running/planned (downtime: setup, breakdowns, material). P=actual/ideal rate (micro-stops, slowdowns). Q=good/total (scrap, rework). Example: 90%×85%×99% = 75.7% — typical! The six big losses: breakdowns, setup, micro-stops, speed, defects, startup. TPM = total productive maintenance = the method to improve it.

def: A rivet with a pull-out stem — access from one side only! Sheet, plastic, signage. Not structural.
expand: Drill → insert the rivet → squeeze the gun → the stem pulls the rear head, expands it ← locks → the stem breaks off. Materials: Al/Al (common), steel/steel (strong), SS/SS (corrosion), Al/steel (galvanic). Limitation: low shear strength (not structural!), a broken stem inside (FOD?). A structural blind rivet (Huck): structural — the stem stays.

def: A split pin inserted into a hole in a bolt/pin and bent — prevents loosening visibly.
expand: Passes through a hole in a shaft/bolt, the legs bend = a positive lock. The classic use: a clevis pin + a cotter pin. In a castellated nut: tightened to torque, the cotter pin prevents it from spinning back (no exact torque needed — hand-tight + a pin is enough!). Single use — never reuse an old pin.

def: Stresses 'frozen' in a part with no external load: welding, machining, HT, cold rolling. Released = distortion!
expand: Sources: welding (tension in the HAZ area), machining (compression at the surface), hardening (martensite expands), cold rolling (tension at the back). The consequence: asymmetric machining distortion (a long slot in a CR blank = a banana!). Fixes: stress relief, normalizing, vibratory SR, symmetric machining. Shot peening = deliberate compressive stress (good!).

def: Atomic hydrogen penetrates hardened steel → a sudden, delayed fracture. Acid cleaning/plating → bake!
expand: The mechanism: atomic H migrates to stress concentrations and accumulates → a brittle fracture with no warning, hours to days after loading! Sources: acid cleaning (pickling), galvanic plating, corrosion, wet welding. Sensitivity: HRC 39+ (hardened steels!). Prevention: baking at 190°C×8-24h within 4 hours of exposure. ASTM F519 tests for it.

def: CE = C + Mn/6 + (Cr+Mo+V)/5 + (Ni+Cu)/15. CE<0.4 free welding. CE>0.6 = preheat mandatory!
expand: Carbon equivalent predicts HAZ cracking risk: a high CE = brittle martensite on cooling. CE<0.35: free welding (A36/S235). 0.35-0.45: preheat 100-150°C. >0.45: preheat 200°C+, low-H (E7018/MIG). 4140: CE≈0.65 — preheat 250°C+, PWHT mandatory. The first formula a welding inspector checks.

def: The effective cross-sectional area for bolt strength calculation: As = π/4 × ((d2+d3)/2)². M10: As=58mm².
expand: As: the average between the pitch diameter and minor — where the bolt actually breaks. A table worth remembering: M6=20.1, M8=36.6, M10=58.0, M12=84.3, M16=157, M20=245 mm². Breaking force: F=As×Rm. M10-8.8: 58×800=46,400N=4.7 tons! Tightening torque: T=K×F×d (K=0.2 dry).

def: The X.Y code on a bolt head: X×100=UTS[MPa], Sy=X×Y×10. 8.8: UTS=800, Sy=640.
expand: Decoding: 4.6 (soft, Sy=240), 5.8 (medium), 8.8 (the structural standard, Sy=640 — stamped '8.8'), 10.9 (hardened, Sy=940), 12.9 (maximum, Sy=1080 — beware HE!). Inch: SAE grade 2/5/8. Stainless: A2-70 (Sy=450) — weaker than 8.8! Don't swap 1:1. The marking is stamped on the head — always check.

def: Measures distances at 0.5ppm accuracy (0.5μm per meter!) — CNC axis calibration, ball screws, bolt wear.
expand: A He-Ne laser (632.8nm) + a retroreflector: counting waves = distance. Accuracy: 0.5ppm (0.05μm at 100mm!). Uses: linear calibration of CNC axes (ISO 230-2), backlash measurement, ball screw pitch error, error compensation (an error map → the CNC controller). Renishaw XL-80 / Agilent. Annual calibration = a precise machine.

def: Projects a magnified shadow (10-100×) of a part onto a screen — compares against a template/DXF. Profiles, threads.
expand: A light source → the part → magnifying lenses → a screen with an overlay (a drawing/DXF). Measurement: an X-Y table with encoders. Uses: thread profile (angle, pitch, shape), O-ring cross-sections, sealing strips, tool edges. Digital: a camera + software (Keyence IM, OGP) = automatic in 3 seconds! Replaces the traditional comparator.

def: A probe (touch/scanning/laser) maps points in 3D — the only tool for true GD&T. Accuracy 1-3μm.
expand: Bridge CMM (the lab standard), articulated arm (portable, ±30μm), portable scanner (a point cloud). Software: PC-DMIS, Calypso, Polyworks. Important: 20°C±1°, a skilled operator, a verified measurement program. MPE = 1.5+L/333 μm (Zeiss Contura). Best fit alignment vs. datum alignment — know when to use which!

def: A wrench with a torque limit: click (mechanical, ±4%), digital (±2%), dial (visual). Annual calibration!
expand: Click (the common one): set → tighten → a 'click' = target reached. Don't continue! Digital: a display+peak hold — accurate and documented. Beam/dial: simple with no calibration needed (the spring doesn't fatigue). Ranges: 1-25Nm (small), 20-100 (medium), 100-500 (large). Calibration: ISO 6789 annually. Storage: always reset to the lowest value!

def: A set of thin blades (0.02-1.0mm) for measuring gaps: backlash, clearance, coarse flatness.
expand: Insert a blade → slides free = too large → the next one, thicker = jams = the size is in between. Uses: gear backlash, engine valve clearance, coarse flatness (on a plate), bearing clearance. Tip: go/no-go with two blades (the thin one passes, the thick one doesn't). Never bend it — it deforms and won't straighten. Brass ones for sensitive areas.

def: A set of R-shaped templates — pressed against a corner to check for a light gap. R1-R25 typical.
expand: The simple check: an R template on the corner, light = doesn't match, dark = the right R. Convex (an outer corner) and concave (an inner corner) — separate sets! Accuracy: ±10-20% (a visual comparison). For precision: a CMM, an optical comparator, or a digital radius gauge. On a drawing: R with TYP = check several representative spots.

def: A precision level (0.02mm/m) for leveling a granite table — without leveling, every height measurement is wrong!
expand: Spirit level accuracy: 0.01-0.02mm/m (10-20 arcsec). The plate sits on 3 points (prevents twisting from a fourth leg!). Check: level in two directions, adjust the plate's feet. Every six months — a flatness check by a calibration technician (a repeat method or an autocollimator). An unleveled plate = a lying height gauge.

def: A digital height gauge with a built-in computer: heights, distances, diameters, internal dimensions. ±0.01mm.
expand: Trimos/Tesa/Mitutoyo: on the plate — the arm moves, the probe touches, the computer calculates. Functions: min/max (finds a peak/trough = a diameter!), 2-point (a distance), ID/OD, preset, SPC output. With a granite anvil = Ra measurement, with a V-block = runout measurement. The small metrology room's CMM.

def: Angle measurement at 0.1 arc-second accuracy (0.5μm/m!) — machine alignment, way flatness.
expand: Emits parallel light → reflects off the surface → returns → the shift measures the angle. Accuracy: 0.1-1 arcsec. Uses: rotary table calibration (a polygon mirror), machine way flatness (mirror walk), straightness, parallelism. Taylor Hobson, Möller Wedel. The tool of high-level CNC machine installers.

def: Hardness measurement: Rockwell (fast, HRC), Brinell (coarse), Vickers (universal), Leeb (portable).
expand: Rockwell: fast (10 seconds!), direct. Bench-top for a metrology room, portable for the field. Vickers: micro-hardness (HV0.05 for coatings!) up to macro. Brinell: castings, forgings. Leeb/UCI: portable — rebound or ultrasonic, measurement on large parts that don't fit in a machine. Calibration: a certified test block.

def: An 87/112-block set: every dimension 0.5-100mm. Grade 0 for calibration, grade 1 for inspection, grade 2 for production.
expand: An 87-piece metric set: 1.001-1.009 (9), 1.01-1.49 (49), 0.5-9.5 (19), 10-100 (10). Building any dimension from 3-4 blocks: 37.625 = 1.005+6.12+30.5. Wringing: cleaning ← contact ← sliding — molecular force holds them! Storage: a thin oil, no direct fingers, a padded case. A rusted block = rejected.

def: A DTI on a rotating part/tool: TIR = the maximum deviation. Aligning a 4-jaw chuck, a shaft in a V-block.
expand: The everyday use: 1) aligning a part in a 4-jaw chuck (TIR <0.02 after adjustment), 2) checking runout on a finished shaft (on centers or a V-block), 3) checking a tool in the spindle, 4) an annual spindle runout check. TIR = max−min = double the deviation! Rule: allowed TIR = 50% of the drawing's runout tolerance.

def: NPT with no sealant — the threads compress for a mechanical seal. Fuels, gases, high pressure.
expand: NPTF (Dryseal): the root and crest are flatter than NPT — they compress and seal metal-to-metal! No Teflon = clean = fuel, oxygen (oil+O₂=fire!). Tightening: 1-2 turns past hand-tight. ANSI B1.20.3. More expensive and precise than NPT — used only when sealant is forbidden.

def: A straight (not tapered) pipe thread — for a mechanical connection only, not sealing. Sealed with an O-ring.
expand: NPSM: the same pitch and 60° as NPT but straight — doesn't seal! Used as a mechanical joint + an O-ring at the shoulder (SAE J1926 — the common O-ring boss in hydraulics). Advantage: can be disassembled and reassembled without degradation (unlike NPT, which is destroyed by repeated opening).

def: JIS B0203: similar to BSP but slightly different — not compatible! Common on older Japanese equipment.
expand: JIS: a Japanese pipe thread — a 55° profile like BSP, but a slightly different pitch diameter and tolerances! Compatible with BSP in 80% of cases but leaks in 20% (mainly small sizes). Identification: older Komatsu, Hitachi, Daikin equipment. Testing: separate BSP+JIS thread gauges.

def: A set of serrated blades for measuring thread pitch — metric (0.25-6mm) and inch (8-56 TPI).
expand: Two sets: metric (0.25, 0.3, 0.35... 6mm) and inch (8, 10, 11... 56 TPI). Use: press against the thread, if there's light = a mismatch. Step 1 in thread identification: pitch gauge → a caliper diameter → a table. A common mistake: M10×1.5 looks like 3/8-16 UNC — a pitch gauge reveals it instantly!

def: A set of precision wires for measuring the pitch diameter with the 3-wire method. Best wire = 0.577×P.
expand: 3-wire method: 2 wires on one side + 1 on the other → a micrometer measures across them → calculating d2. Best wire: d_w=0.577×P (60°). Formula: d2=M−3×d_w+0.866×P. Example M10×1.5: best wire 0.866mm, M=10.531 → d2=9.026. Accuracy: ±0.003mm. For verifying thread gauges and detailed FAI.

def: A polystyrene pattern burned away during casting — no split, no cores, free shapes.
expand: EPS (foam!) is cut/glued into a shape → coated in a ceramic layer → buried in vibrated sand → metal is poured and vaporizes the foam! Advantages: no PL, no flash, free geometry, low NRE (CNC EPS). Disadvantages: defects from foam gases, coarse Ra. Uses: GM engine blocks, custom and prototype parts.

def: Metal powder + a plastic binder → injection → debind → sintering. Small, complex parts in production runs.
expand: MIM: die casting's complexity in excellent metal materials (17-4PH, Ti, WC-Co!). Parts 0.5-100g, tolerance ±0.3-0.5%, density 96-99%. Shrinkage during sintering: ~20% (uniform and planned). Mold cost: like plastic. Uses: watches, firearms (triggers!), medical, connectors. Competitor: binder jetting.

def: Molten metal is pressed in a closed die at 50-150MPa — zero porosity, properties like forging.
expand: Combining casting+forging: liquid/semi-solid metal is pressed ← solidification under pressure ← zero gas, zero shrinkage, fine grain. Result: mechanical properties like forging! Uses: pistons (Al-Si), sports car wheels, suspension parts. More expensive than die casting — only when perfect density is needed.

def: A hot ring rolled between rollers — the diameter grows, the wall thins. Bearing rings, flanges, gears.
expand: Starting from upset+punch (a small thick ring) → a radial roll expands it, an axial roll maintains height. OD up to 8 meters! Advantage: circumferential grain flow = excellent strength, near net shape, seamless (no welding!). Uses: bearing rings, flanges, gear blanks, turbine rings. Materials: any steel, Ti, Ni-alloy.

def: Compressing a tube/rod around a die with fast rotating strikes — cable termination, pointing.
expand: 4 hammers rotate and strike 1000+ times/minute — compressing the material around an internal die (or none). Uses: steel cable termination (a swage ferrule), pointing a rod's end, compressing a tube onto a sleeve, hydraulic piping connections (Parker). Advantage: a strong joint with no welding, low heat.

def: A local valve that vents air directly to atmosphere — double or more the cylinder speed.
expand: In a standard exhaust: the air returns through all the piping + the valve. A QEV on the cylinder: senses a pressure drop ← opens a direct outlet ← double the speed! Normally closed: doesn't leak under pressure. Uses: fast cylinders, pneumatic punches, a fast gripper. Downside: uncontrolled — cushioning only with a flow control.

def: Chokes in one direction, free in the other — controls cylinder speed. Meter-out is common.
