expand: One-way: an adjustable throttle screw + a check valve = choking in one direction only. Meter-out (exhaust throttling): smooth control — the compressed air acts as a cushion! Meter-in (inlet throttling): less stable — a varying load = varying speed. Rule: meter-out for cylinders, meter-in for motors. ⌀4-12mm tubing.

def: Grips parts: parallel (parallel jaws) or angular (scissor). 2/3 fingers.
expand: Parallel: jaws move in parallel — a consistent grip at any diameter (on a robot!). Angular: rotate — high force but a changing distance. 3-finger: self-centering (cylindrical parts). Sizing: gripping force (N) × friction coefficient ÷ SF 3-4 ≥ part weight. Custom soft jaws. Schunk PGN, SMC MHZ, Festo DHPS.

he: Tube vs Pipe — צינור מול צנרת
def: Tube: measured by OD×wall (real dimensions!). Pipe: measured by NPS (an arbitrary nominal!). Don't mix them.
expand: TUBE (ASTM A269/A213): OD×wall = what's measured. A 25×2 tube = OD 25.00, wall 2.00, ID 21.00. PIPE (ASTM A106/A312): NPS 1" = OD 33.40 (not 25.4!). Tube: instrumentation, hydraulics, heat exchangers. Pipe: industrial, water, gas. Fittings aren't interchangeable!

def: A weldless pipe connection: 2 ferrules are compressed onto the tube and seal it. Swagelok = the generic name.
expand: Tightening: 1¼ turns on first assembly, ¼ more on every re-assembly. The front ferrule bites, the back ferrule locks. Up to 420bar in stainless! Uses: instrumentation, analytical, gas, labs. Advantage: fast, disassembles, needs no welding. Disadvantage: expensive at large diameters, sensitive to misalignment. Parker A-LOK, Ham-Let = competitors.

def: Removes condensate and air from a steam system — while keeping steam in. 3 main types.
expand: Mechanical (float/bucket): a float opens a valve as the water level rises — continuous and efficient. Thermodynamic (disc): simple, compact, cheap — chatters. Thermostatic (bimetallic): responds to temperature. Failure: 15-30% of steam traps fail (stuck open=wasted energy, stuck closed=water hammer!). An annual survey = enormous savings.

def: A Ni-Cr-Fe superalloy: Sy=1035MPa at 650°C! Turbine blades, space, nuclear. Very hard to machine.
expand: 718: 53%Ni+19%Cr+18%Fe+5%Nb+3%Mo. Precipitation hardened (γ'+γ") at 720°C. Sy=1035 at RT, 860 at 650°C! Machining: Vc=20-40 m/min (carbide), high torques, tools wear fast. DMLS/EBW qualified. Uses: turbine discs, combustion liners, hot bolts, subsea. ~$40/kg.

def: Ni-Mo-Cr: near-total chemical resistance — acids, bases, chlorides. The chemist's alloy.
expand: C-276: 57%Ni+16%Mo+15%Cr — resistant to: HCl, H₂SO₄, FeCl₃, wet Cl₂, hot seawater. The alloy chosen when 'nothing else works'! Machining: similar to 316 (relatively easy for a superalloy). Welding: excellent (like 316L). Price: ~$70/kg. Uses: scrubbers, FGD, chlor-alkali, pharmaceuticals.

def: 67%Ni + 30%Cu: excellent seawater resistance + hydrofluoric acid. Marine, chemical, oil.
expand: Monel 400: seawater resistance superior to 316L (no pitting!), resistant to HF (hydrofluoric acid — which SS can't tolerate!). UTS=550MPa. Hardening: cold work only. Welding: good (ERNiCu-7). Uses: seawater pumps, seawater heat exchangers, chemical valves. K-500: aged-hardened to HRC 30 — for marine bearings.

def: Fe-25Ni-15Cr: hot bolts up to 700°C. Cheaper than Inconel. AMS 5731/5737.
expand: A286: Sy=585 at RT, 540 at 650°C. Weldable — welds well. Machining: hard (work hardening). Main use: bolts and nuts for high temperature (jet engine casings!), turbine wheels, afterburners. Hardening: solution treat 980°C + aging 720°C. Cheaper than 718 and sufficient up to 700°C.

def: Ni-Cr-Co-Mo: turbine wheels up to 750°C. Sy=795MPa. Excellent creep resistance.
expand: Waspaloy: 58%Ni+19%Cr+13%Co+4%Mo+3%Ti+1.4%Al. Stronger than 718 at high temperature (above 650°C). Uses: turbine discs, spacers, compressor cases. Forged+solution+aged. Machining: Vc=15-25 m/min (harder than 718!). Modern alternative: AD730/René 65. Expensive: ~$80/kg.

def: An engineering plastic: rigid, strong, low friction. Gears, bushings, guides. Excellent machining!
expand: POM (Delrin = DuPont): Sy=70MPa, E=3.1GPa, μ=0.2 (no lubrication needed!). Resistant to solvents, fuels, water. Not UV resistant. Homopolymer (Delrin — stronger) vs. copolymer (Celcon — more chemically resistant). Uses: plastic gears, sliding bushings, sliding rails, clock mechanisms. Excellent machinability: easily achieves Ra 0.4!

def: Strong, rigid, wear resistant. Absorbs water 2-8%! = dimensional change. Gears, bushings, cables.
expand: PA66 (stronger, 260°C Tm) vs. PA6 (rigid, cheap). Sy=70-85MPa. The problem: water absorption 2-8% = dimensions grow 0.3-2%! Design for the conditioned (wet) dimensions. GF30 (glass fiber): Sy×2, less absorption, but anisotropic. Uses: gears (quiet!), cable ties, bushings, connectors. Injection = cheap; machining = prototype.

def: The cheap plastic with the lowest wear! Artificial joints, rails, chutes.
expand: UHMWPE: MW>3.5M — extremely long chains = 10x lower wear than HDPE! Self-lubricating, impact resistant, non-stick, FDA. Downsides: creep (never bolt it tight!), not injectable (only compression/machining). Uses: hip joints, mining wear plates, conveyor buckets, dump truck liners.

def: Rotary vane (rough), turbo (high), ion (UHV). A Roots blower boosts. Each range = a different pump.
expand: Rotary vane: oil, 10⁻³ mbar (the common one). Scroll/diaphragm: dry, clean. Roots: a booster ×10. Turbo-molecular: 10⁻¹⁰ (blades at 80,000 RPM!). Cryo-pump: adsorption on a cold surface. Ion: UHV with no moving parts. A chain: rough+turbo = 10⁻⁸ easily. Every semiconductor fab = a vacuum room.

def: Unit: mbar·L/s. Good sealing: <10⁻⁶. A He leak test detects down to 10⁻¹². A leak differs from outgassing!
expand: Leak rate = the volume of gas passing through a defect per unit time. The distinction: a real leak (a hole/crack — findable and fixable) vs. a virtual leak (trapped gas slowly releasing — a blind hole, an unwrung O-ring). He sniffer: fast but less sensitive. He vacuum: slow but 10⁻¹². Standard: every vacuum system needs a leak rate spec.

def: A fillet (rounding) spreads stress — for fatigue. A chamfer (an angled cut) is cheap and fast — for breaking sharpness.
expand: Fillet: reduces Kt from 3 to 1.5 (R=0.2×d good, 0.5×d excellent). Mandatory on dynamic shafts! Chamfer: breaks sharpness (C0.3-C0.5), a lead-in for assembly, easy to manufacture (a 45° end mill/chamfering). Rule: internal = fillet (stress); external = chamfer (assembly). Chamfer+fillet = two tools = cost.

def: A coiled SS strip with PTFE/graphite — the standard gasket for 150-2500# pressure flanges.
expand: Inner ring (SS): prevents inward buckling. Filler (PTFE/graphite/mica): seals. Outer ring (CS): centering + compression limiting (25-35% depending on the manufacturer). Graphite: up to 450°C+; PTFE: up to 260°C, chemical. Reconnecting: a new gasket every time it's opened! ASME B16.20. Flexitallic, Garlock = brands.

def: A C-shaped metal ring compressed to seal — high pressure, extreme temperature, vacuum.
expand: Inconel/SS/Ti in a C shape (or E for double springiness): compressed 15-25% ← springback maintains contact. Temperature: −269 to +900°C! Pressure: thousands of bar. Uses: jet engines, nuclear, UHV vacuum, extreme pressure vessels. Silver/gold plating improves sealing. The gasket that works when rubber fails.

en: Hex Head Bolt ISO 4014 Full Thread
def: 4014: partial thread + a smooth shank. 4017: fully threaded. The most common classic bolt.
expand: Hex bolt: the basic fastener — an external wrench, A/F=ISO 898-1. 4014: a smooth shank+thread = shear on a ground body (a bearing type). 4017: fully threaded = economical, but shear strength is on the minor ⌀! On a drawing: 'ISO 4017 M10×40-8.8'. DIN 931/933 are the old equivalents. Property class is stamped on the head.

en: Low Head Socket Cap Screw DIN 7984
def: Head height 60% of DIN 912 — for limited clearance. 8.8/10.9. A small Allen = limited torque!
expand: Head H≈0.6d (vs. d in DIN 912). Uses: machine covers, height limiters, fixtures — anywhere height is critical but structural load is low. Class 8.8 or 10.9 (not 12.9 — the small Allen can't transmit enough torque!). DIN 6912 = a similar version with a centering pilot.

def: A precise h6 cylinder + an Allen head + a short thread. A pivot, guide, spacer. 12.9.
expand: ISO 7379: an h6 shoulder ⌀ (precise!), a defined length, an SHCS head, a short M-1 thread (an ⌀8 shoulder = an M6 thread). Class 12.9 (hardened!). Uses: a pivot in links, a guide in jigs (with an H7 bush), a stripper bolt in molds. Shoulder ⌀: 3-20mm. A ready-made off-the-shelf pivot.

def: A rectangular key for transmitting torque between shaft and gear. Size by shaft ⌀: ⌀20→6×6, ⌀30→8×7.
expand: DIN 6885: type A (rounded ends — the common one), B (straight ends), C (one rounded end). Fit: a P9 key in the shaft (press), JS9 in the gear (free fit). Height: half in the shaft, half in the gear (side fit = tight sides, free height). Calculation: L ≥ 2T/(d×τ_allow×h). The shaft's weakness: Kt≈2.5 at the keyway base!

def: The process piping code: design, materials, assembly, testing. Hydrotest 1.5×design. NDT by fluid service.
expand: The code of the chemical and oil industry: defines allowable stresses (S×E×W), tests (hydro 1.5P, pneumatic 1.1P), and NDT per fluid category (D=normal, M=toxic, K=cryogenic). Visual=100%, RT/UT per category and joint factor. PWHT by thickness and material. In Israel: ASME B31.3 is the most common in the chemical industry.

def: Isolating a body + drawing all the forces + solving equilibrium. Step 1 in every analysis. ΣF=0, ΣM=0.
expand: The step you can't skip: 1) isolate a body, 2) draw weight, external forces, support reactions, 3) ΣFx=0, ΣFy=0, ΣM=0. An error in the FBD = an error in everything that follows. Also in FEA: boundary conditions = the model's FBD. Rule: if you're not sure — draw the FBD.

def: A graphical representation of a stress state: finds principal stresses, maximum shear, and direction.
expand: X axis=σ, Y axis=τ. Center (σ_avg, 0), radius R=√((σ_diff/2)²+τ²). σ1,2=center±R. τ_max=R. The angle: 2θ_p = atan(2τ/σ_diff). Uses: understanding a combined stress state (bending+torsion in a shaft), crack direction, material optimization. In industry: FEA does this — but Mohr teaches understanding.

def: Pcr = π²EI/(KL)². K=1 (pinned), K=0.5 (fixed), K=2 (cantilever). Slenderness ratio: KL/r.
expand: When the slenderness ratio KL/r > ~100 (steel) = a stiffness failure (Euler), not a strength one! Doubling the length = a quarter of the capacity. Doubling the diameter (I∝d⁴) = 16x the capacity. A hydraulic piston, a column, a long compressed bolt — always check buckling! The Johnson formula for intermediate range (KL/r < 100).

def: Minimum clearance for tools: an Allen M8 = 20mm, a screwdriver = 50mm, a hand = 100mm. Design for access!
expand: The rule designers forget: is there room for a tool? An Allen M8 needs a 20mm radius. A screwdriver: 100mm length + 30mm of rotation. A torque wrench: 300mm. If there's no access = assembly is impossible (discovered at prototype). The DFA rule: mark tool bodies in CAD (SolidWorks clearance check). Check access before release!

def: A split washer — prevents loosening? Debated. DIN 127. Common but not recommended.
expand: DIN 127 (split lock washer): common but studies (the Junker Test) show it doesn't prevent vibration loosening! The sharp edges dig in = surface damage. The good alternatives: Nord-Lock (wedge), a nyloc nut, Loctite, safety wire. A spring washer at class 10.9/12.9 = forbidden (breakage!). Still common in general use.

def: A pair of washers with wedge teeth — a guaranteed positive lock. Junker Test approved. The DIN 127 replacement.
expand: Two washers with teeth facing each other: on tightening the teeth lock; on loosening — the wedges lift the nut (the angle > the thread angle = self-locking!). Passes the Junker Test DIN 65151. Reusable! Works with 10.9/12.9. The cost: 5-10x DIN 127 — worth every penny in vibration applications.

def: A bolt/nut with a built-in disc that replaces a washer — spreads force, saves a part, fast.
expand: DIN 6921 (flange bolt), DIN 6923 (flange nut): the disc spreads pressure over a large area (like an integrated washer) = no separate washer needed! Savings: one fewer part in the BOM. Serrated flange: teeth = some locking. Common in automotive: 90% flange bolts. Downside: a taller head.

def: A tapered bushing that locks a pulley/gear onto a shaft — bolt tightening, easy disassembly.
expand: The taper (1:16): tightening the bolts compresses the bushing onto the shaft ← a guaranteed press fit! Disassembly: thread bolts into the opposing holes ← pushes it out. Advantage: fast install/remove with no press, no key (friction transmits torque). Standard sizes: 1008-5050. Fenner/Martin = brands.

def: Flow and heat transfer simulation: ANSYS Fluent, OpenFOAM, SolidWorks Flow. Mesh matters a lot!
expand: CFD solves Navier-Stokes: velocity, pressure, temperature at every point. Uses: heat sink design, aerodynamics, valve flow, combustion. Mesh: the boundary layer matters! A correct y+ (1 for k-ω, 30-300 for k-ε). CFD is less accurate than FEA — verify with a prototype! But saves 80% of experiments.

def: Finding a structure's natural frequencies and mode shapes. The first step in any vibration analysis.
expand: In FEA: an eigenvalue problem → frequencies + mode shapes. Mode 1 = the lowest frequency, the easiest to excite. Rule: fn_1 > 1.4×the excitation frequency. Experimental: a tap test + FFT (an impact hammer + an accelerometer). Uses: preventing resonance in spindles, bridges, frames. Adding mass lowers fn; adding stiffness raises it.

def: Cp = (USL−LSL)/6σ. How many times the spread fits within the tolerance, ignoring centering. Cp=1.33 required.
expand: Cp measures the potential: how 'wide' the process is relative to the tolerance. Cp=1: the spread exactly fills the tolerance (2,700 PPM on each side!). Cp=2: half the tolerance is used = excellent. The problem: Cp ignores centering — Cp=2 with an off-center mean = defects! Hence Cpk = the worse side = the real metric.

def: X̄-R: average+range of subgroups (3-5). I-MR: an individual point+moving range. UCL/LCL = ±3σ.
expand: X̄-R: sample 3-5 units → average (controls centering), range (controls spread). I-MR: when only one sample is possible (expensive, destructive, a continuous process). Limits from the first 25+ subgroups. An out-of-limit point = a special cause → stop and investigate. A pattern (7 rising, 7 above) = a trend/shift. Tools: Minitab, InfinityQS.

def: 4 original rules for identifying an out-of-control state: 1 crossing 3σ, 2/3 crossing 2σ, 4/5 crossing 1σ, 8 on the same side.
expand: The original rules (1956): rule 1 (a point outside 3σ — obvious!), rule 2 (2 of 3 crossing 2σ — a shift?), rule 3 (4 of 5 crossing 1σ — drift), rule 4 (8 in a row on the same side — bias). Nelson expanded to 8. Balanced: not overly sensitive (false alarms) and not missing signals (missed signals).

def: A metallic paste (Cu/Ni/MoS₂) on threads — prevents galling, seizing, and galvanic corrosion.
expand: Copper-based: up to 980°C (exhaust bolts). Nickel: stainless and food (no Cu). Moly: nuclear (no metals). K-factor: anti-seize lowers it to 0.12-0.15 (from 0.2 dry) — the same torque = 50% higher preload! Mandatory: SS+SS, exhaust, spark plugs, any joint not opened for a year+. Not on hardened 12.9 bolts (HE risk).

def: Flanges must be aligned to ±1mm and parallel to ±1°/m before tightening — otherwise the gasket fails.
expand: ASME PCC-1: alignment (centering ±1.5mm), parallelism (±0.13mm/100mm), gap (uniform ±0.8mm), rotation (aligned holes). Tools: flange alignment pins, a laser, a feeler gauge. Bolt-up: a star pattern, 30%→70%→100%+a check pass. Hot re-torque: after the first 24 hours of operation!

def: An anaerobic adhesive: 222 (purple, weak), 243 (blue, medium — the standard), 271 (red, strong). Cures inside the thread.
expand: Mechanism: anaerobic = cures with no oxygen (inside the thread). 222: M2-M6, removable by hand. 243: the general one — removable with a tool, oil resistant, active surface (doesn't require perfect cleaning). 271/277: red — removable only with 250°C heat! 290 (green): wicking = penetrates an assembled thread. Mandatory: clean, oil-free surfaces = half the job.

def: Bonding as a structural connection: epoxy (strong), acrylic (fast), PU (flexible), cyanoacrylate (instant).
expand: 2-part epoxy (Hysol EA9394): shear 25-40MPa — like a rivet! Time: 24h RT, 1h@65°C. Acrylic (Plexus): on dirty surfaces! PU (Sikaflex): flexible, replaces welding in sheet metal. Design: a large contact area (shear, not peel!), Ra 0.8-3.2 (anchoring), surface prep is critical. Bond: τ=F/A, peel=forbidden! Overlap > 25×t.

def: A defined overlap: the shaft is larger than the hole. Assembly: a hydraulic press or heating/cooling. H7/p6 light, H7/s6 heavy.
expand: Insertion force: F=π×d×L×p×μ (p from the Lamé pressure, μ=0.1-0.15 lubricated). Bore heating: ΔT=interference/(α×d)+20°C. Pin cooling: LN₂ (−196°C) → free insertion! The force-displacement graph on the press: must be smooth and rising — a jump = a particle/scratch. A centering mark: a 10-15° lead-in chamfer on both parts is mandatory.

def: Two-stage tightening: snug torque (50-70%) then an angle turn (30-180°). More precise than torque alone.
expand: Stage 1: snug (a constant torque bringing full contact). Stage 2: a measured angle (30-360° depending on the joint). The advantage: the angle directly controls stretch — indifferent to friction! The same preload within ±5% (vs. ±25% with torque-only). Uses: cylinder heads, critical flanges, structural bolts. Tool: an electronic torque-angle wrench.

def: A 5-character code uniquely identifying a defense supplier worldwide. Appears in drawing title blocks.
expand: Commercial and Government Entity: the unique identity of every defense supplier/manufacturer. Israel: 5 letters/digits from the DSPO. US: 5 letters/digits from DLIS. Appears in: drawing title blocks, CoCs, purchase orders, ITAR documentation. Without a CAGE = you don't exist in the defense system. Free to register!

def: When a change takes effect: from serial number X, from date Y, or from lot Z. A critical field in an ECO.
expand: Effectivity = the boundary between old and new: S/N 001-050 = Rev A, S/N 051+ = Rev B. Block effectivity: an entire lot. Date effectivity: from a release date. Existing inventory: use-as-is (fine as is), rework (fix it), scrap (discard). Configuration management lives on effectivity — without it you can't know what's on the aircraft.

def: Deviation: advance approval for an exception (before production). Waiver: after-the-fact approval (a part already made as an exception).
expand: Deviation: 'we know we won't meet X — may we?' → an engineering analysis → approval for a defined batch. Waiver: 'an exception came out — what do we do?' → an MRB → use-as-is/rework/scrap. Both: quantity/time limited, documented, and don't change the drawing! Repeated use = an ECO. A deviation that becomes permanent = a management problem.

def: FAA/EASA approval for a change to an approved aircraft design — installing equipment, structural changes, upgrades.
expand: STC = the legal way to change an aircraft's type certificate: an avionics upgrade, an engine change, adding a tank, cabin interior. The data: a drawing package + a stress analysis + flight testing (sometimes) + instructions for continued airworthiness. A DER approves it. In Israel: an Israeli STC via the CAAI, or a recognized foreign STC.

def: 641 (medium) / 648 (strong) — fills the gap between a shaft/housing and a bearing. Replaces a press fit.
expand: Retaining: an anaerobic that fills up to a 0.25mm gap ← transmits force by friction+adhesive. 641: medium, removable with heat — for worn clearance fits. 648: very strong, transmits torque — when the shaft is h7 instead of m6 (worn). 620: resists 230°C. 250°C heat = releases it. Not a substitute for the correct fit — a professional patch!

def: Silicone rubber that cures in air — a formed-in-place gasket. −60 to +315°C. Oil resistant.
expand: Room temperature vulcanizing: apply → close → cures in 24h. Red (hi-temp 315°C), blue (instrumentation, 260°C), black (oil, 232°C), clear (general, 200°C). Uses: a non-standard gasket, supplemental sealing for a hard gasket, electrical potting. MIL-A-46146 aerospace-grade. Thickness: 0.5-3mm. Forbidden: oxygen, spring/mechanical contact.

def: Copper (up to 980°C), nickel (stainless/food), moly (nuclear/vacuum), ceramic (1400°C).
expand: The base: oil/grease + metal particles (protecting the threads). Copper: the classic — exhaust bolts, turbines. Nickel: when Cu is forbidden (SS sensitization, food). Moly: when metals are forbidden (nuclear). Ceramic (BN): extreme temperature, vacuum. Remember: anti-seize lowers the K-factor ← the same torque = higher preload!

def: An emulsion (5-10% oil in water) is common. Synthetic (no oil). Neat oil (pure oil — grinding, tapping).
expand: Soluble oil (emulsion): the common one — cooling+lubrication as a compromise. Semi-synthetic: less oil, less smoke. Synthetic: water+additives — maximum cooling, no oil (modern CNC). Neat oil: maximum lubrication — grinding, tapping, deep hole. Concentration: 5-10% (a refractometer!). pH 8.5-9.5. Bacteria = odor = illness — a weekly check!

def: An adhesive that cures with no air inside a thread: 222 weak, 243 medium, 271/277 strong. Loctite = the brand.
expand: An anaerobic family: cures only in the absence of O₂ + metal contact (ions). Speed: steel 5-10 min fixed, 24h full cure. SS/Al: slow — an activator (primer T/N) speeds it up! Active materials: primer T (7471) = seconds to set. Strong removal (271): 250°C heat+a tool. Storage: a fridge = years; heat = months.

def: Stamping a diamond/straight pattern onto a cylindrical surface — a hand grip, a press fit in plastic.
expand: A grooved wheel is pressed onto the rotating part — cold forming (no chips!). Diamond (crossed): grip. Straight: a press fit (inserted into plastic!). Pitch: fine (instruments), medium (general), coarse (industrial). On CNC: G96 constant speed + 0.5mm/pass infeed. The OD grows! Design a smaller starting diameter.

def: Metal plating with electrical current: Ni, Cr, Zn, Au, Ag. Thickness 5-50μm. Not uniform on complex geometry!
expand: The part = the cathode in a metal salt bath. Advantage: a range of metals, shiny, conductive. Disadvantage: uneven thickness! Corners/edges get more (current density), recesses get less. Hence: a rack (hung) for large parts, a barrel (tumbled) for small ones. Decorative chrome: Ni+Cr (only 0.25μm Cr!). Hard chrome: 25-250μm industrial chrome.

def: Chrome 25-250μm, HV 850-1050. Excellent wear resistance. Pistons, cylinders, molds. Cr6+ is carcinogenic!
expand: The classic wear coating: HV 850-1000, low friction (micro-cracks retain oil!). Uses: hydraulic pistons, printing rollers, molds. The problem: Cr6+ (carcinogenic!) — restricted by REACH. Substitutes: HVOF WC-Co (aerospace has already switched!), electroless Ni+bake, PEO. Hydrogen embrittlement: baking at 190°C×3h is mandatory!

def: 5-25μm electrolytic zinc + a chromate passivation. Common for bolts and sheet. 96-200h salt spray.
expand: Galvanic protection: the zinc corrodes instead of the steel! Passivation: clear (blue/clear — 72h SST), yellow (Cr6+ — 200h, banned by RoHS), black (decorative). Cr3+ trivalent: RoHS-OK, 96-120h. Thickness: 5μm for bolts, 8-12 general, 25 outdoor. Limit: above 250°C the zinc breaks down. HE: baking mandatory above HRC 32.

def: Calculating accumulated tolerances in an assembly: WC (sum), RSS (statistical), Monte Carlo (precise).
expand: 1D stack: a linear chain — gap = Σnominals ± Σtolerances (WC) or ±√(Σt²) (RSS). 2D/3D: includes angles and GD&T (complex!). Monte Carlo: simulating 10,000 assemblies — a full probability map. Tools: Sigmetrix CETOL, 3DCS, Excel (for 1D). The rule: if the stack doesn't close — either widen tolerances (cheap) or add a shim/adjustment (flexible).

def: A thin strip (0.05-2mm) for adjusting a gap/alignment. SS/Al/brass/plastic. A peelable shim = separate layers.
expand: The solution for a stack that doesn't close: a shim fitted at assembly. Solid (pre-calculated), peelable (0.05 layers — peel off until it fits), liquid (Loctite — cures to a size). Uses: machine alignment (a dial+shim), TRB bearing preload, gear clearance, a fixture height gauge. Shim thickness = the gap check — documented!

def: A flat seal between two surfaces in a bolted joint: rubber, PTFE, graphite, metal. Static only.
expand: Sheet gasket (Klinger/Garlock): cut from a sheet by a template. Materials: NBR (oil), EPDM (water), PTFE (chemical), compressed fiber (AF — general), graphite (heat 500°C+). Metal gaskets: RTJ, spiral wound, C-ring (pressure/heat). Rule: a lower-stress gasket needs a smoother surface finish (Ra 3.2 for spiral, Ra 0.8 for metal).

def: An aerospace tube fitting: a sleeve bites into the tube on tightening. No flare, re-assembles repeatedly.
expand: MS33656 / AN818+AN819: a body+nut+sleeve — the first tightening bites the sleeve into the tube (a pre-set on a bench!). Repeated connections: 3-5 openings allowed. Pressure: 3000-6000 PSI. Material: SS, Ti, Al. Advantage: a large contact area, vibration-tolerant, field-disassemblable. Parker Ermeto = the civilian standard.

def: Climb: chip thick→thin, good finish, preferred on CNC. Conventional: thin→thick, safer manually.
expand: Climb: the tool enters at maximum thickness and exits at zero — good Ra, less heat, force pushes onto the table (reduces backlash issues on CNC). Conventional: enters at zero and grows — initial rubbing (heat!), a pulling force = safer on old machines with backlash. Rule: CNC=climb always (except on thin walls).

en: Chip Load per Tooth / Feed per Tooth
def: fz = F/(n×Z). The chip thickness per tooth. Below the minimum = rubbing ← heat ← a broken tool!
expand: A minimum fz is critical: below it the tool rubs instead of cutting → heat → work hardening → breakage. Rules: Al fz=0.05-0.2mm, steel 0.05-0.15, SS 0.03-0.1. Chip thinning: in partial side milling (ae<50%D) the chip is thin — compensate by raising fz! Formula: fz_adjusted = fz × D/√(D×ae − ae²).

def: Coolant through the spindle and tool ← fluid/air reaches the cutting edge directly. 20-70 bar.
expand: The fluid reaches exactly the cutting zone through holes in the tool (⌀0.5-2mm). Advantages: chip clearance from deep holes, effective cooling (tool life 2-3x longer!), L/D>5 possible. Pressure: 20bar (general), 40-70 (SS/Ti deep hole). MQL (minimum quantity lubricant): an oil mist 5-50ml/h — green and economical. Mandatory on modern CNC.

def: A tool for cutting internal threads: hand (straight flutes), machine (spiral), form (no chips!).
expand: Hand tap set: taper+plug+bottoming (not on CNC!). Machine tap: spiral point (THRU) / spiral flute (blind). Form tap (roll tap): compresses rather than cuts = no chips, a strong thread! Only in ductile materials (Al, Cu, soft steel). Thread mill: one tool for every size — if it breaks: easy to remove! The cheapest bolt = a thread mill.

def: 50% austenite + 50% ferrite = double the strength of 316L + excellent pitting resistance. Chemical, marine.
expand: 2205 (UNS S31803): Sy=450MPa (316L: 170!). PREN=35 (316L: 24) = excellent pitting resistance. Lean duplex (2304): economical. Super duplex (2507, PREN=43): hot seawater! Machining: hard (work hardening), Vc=60-80 for carbide. Welding: possible with care (controlled heat input!). The 316L replacement for severe applications.

def: The high-end engineering plastic: 260°C continuous, chemical, medical. Replaces metal! Very expensive.
expand: PEEK: Sy=100MPa (competes with Al!), E=4GPa, Tm=343°C, near-total chemical resistance (except concentrated H₂SO₄). Uses: medical implants (biocompatible!), oil-field seals (250°C+H₂S), bearings (CF-PEEK = PV 300MPa·m/min!), electrical insulation. Cost: $100-200/kg. Machining: like Al, but sharp tools needed!

def: WC + brazed cobalt: HV 1500+, E=600GPa. Cutting tools, wear molds, valves.
expand: Grades: K (WC+Co 6%: hard, for cutting CI/Al), P (WC+TiC+Co: for steel), M (general). HV 1300-1800 = 3x hardened steel! E=600GPa (3x steel). Brittle — no impact! Submicron grain: hard+strong. Uses: inserts, drills, wear dies, valve balls. Binder: Co (common), Ni (corrosion).

def: Ni-Cr-Mo-Nb: corrosion resistance + excellent fatigue resistance. Excellent welding. Marine, chemical, aerospace.
expand: 625: 62%Ni+22%Cr+9%Mo+3.5%Nb. Solution strengthened (not precipitation = free welding!). Sy=414 at RT, up to 815°C. Pitting+crevice resistance better than C-276 at medium temperatures. Uses: bellows, expansion joints, exhaust (F1!), weld overlay on CS. Filler metal: ERNiCrMo-3 — the most popular filler for welding Ni-alloys.

def: 15%Cr + 5%Ni + 3%Cu: like 17-4PH but better under transverse loading (VAR). Aerospace, medical.
expand: 15-5 PH = a VAR (vacuum arc remelted) version of 17-4 PH: high cleanliness, uniform grain direction, less delta ferrite. H900: HRC 44, Sy=1170MPa. AMS 5659. Forging grade: stronger than 17-4 in the transverse direction. Hardening: identical to 17-4 (SA+aging). Choice: 15-5 for aerospace/medical (cleanliness), 17-4 for industrial (cheaper).

def: An air-hardening tool steel: HRC 57-62, stronger than D2, less wear resistant. Knives, punches.
expand: A2: 5%Cr+1%Mo+0.95%C — air-hardening = minimal distortion when hardened! Toughness > D2, wear < D2. The good compromise: strong enough and not too brittle. Uses: punches (D2 would shatter!), knives, die inserts, shear blades. Machining: annealed at HB 200. After HT: grinding only. The 'all-purpose' tool steel.

def: A document defining every welding parameter: process, filler, gas, current, speed, preheat. WPS→PQR→WPQ.
expand: WPS: the 'recipe' (ASME IX / ISO 15614). PQR (procedure qualification record): proof the WPS works — a sample weld + mechanical tests + a macro. WPQ/WPQR: the welder's own qualification. Essential variables: a change in material/thickness/process = a new PQR! The only allowed weld = a weld per an approved WPS.

def: Heating to 600-750°C after welding — reduces residual stress, tempers the HAZ. ASME VIII mandatory above a certain thickness.
expand: Stress relief: 600-650°C for carbon steel (ASME VIII: mandatory above 38mm!). Tempering: 700-750°C for Cr-Mo (P11, P22). Heating/cooling rate: ≤200°C/h (prevents new stress!). Holding time: an hour per inch of thickness. Local PWHT: a heating blanket (when the part doesn't fit a furnace) — a band width ≥3×thickness on each side.

def: A hydraulic pressure reservoir: a gas (N₂) bladder absorbs shocks, compensates for leaks, and supplies peak flow.
expand: Bladder: the common one — compressed N₂ in a rubber bladder, oil around it. Piston: for large volumes. Diaphragm: small ones. Pre-charge: 80-90% of minimum working pressure. Uses: absorbing pressure shocks (water hammer), spring preload, emergency motion (pump shutdown), thermal expansion compensation. EN 14359 / ASME VIII.

def: A hydraulic valve with precise analog control of flow and pressure. 4-20mA / ±10V. Moog = the name.
expand: Servo valve (2-stage): flapper-nozzle or jet pipe → a spool → flow proportional to the input. Accuracy: <1% full scale, response <10ms. Proportional valve: simpler, 5-50ms — enough for most. Direct drive: no intermediate stage, fast. Uses: hydraulic CNC, a precision press, a flight simulator. Filtration: NAS 1638 Class 6 = mandatory (3μm)!

def: A piston driven by oil: tie-rod (disassembles), mill type (solid — strong). ISO 6020/6022. Up to 350bar.
expand: Tie-rod (ISO 6020/2): 4 bolts hold it = disassemblable and repairable. Mill type (NFPA): a welded solid body = strong, for harsh environments (rolling mills!). Telescopic: 2-6 stages — dump trucks. Cushioning: hydraulic deceleration at the ends. Seals: piston seal + rod seal + wiper + guide ring.

def: A conical disc that flexes under load — high force in a small deflection. Stacked in series/parallel.
expand: Belleville (DIN 2093): a very high spring constant (a large force in a small movement!). Stacking: parallel (same direction) = force × n; series (alternating) = deflection × n. Uses: bearing preload, bolt preload (maintains clamp force!), safety mechanisms (over-pressure). 3 groups: A (fine), B (medium), C (coarse). Material: 51CrV4 / Inconel.

def: A flattened, wound-flat spring — half the height of a regular spring! Bearings, clutches, covers. Smalley.
expand: A ring with 2-20+ waves: force up to 500N at 2-3mm height (a regular spring: 5-10mm!). Advantage: saves 50% height = smaller housings. Uses: bearing preload (instead of Belleville), seals (preload), clutches, push-on connectors. Material: SS 17-7PH, CS. Smalley = the brand (edgewound — no cut!). Tolerance: ±10% force.

def: The gap between meshing teeth: AGMA 7-8 = 0.05-0.1mm. Zero backlash = a split gear or spring-loaded.
expand: Backlash is needed: compensates for thermal expansion, tolerance, and lubrication. Too much: lost motion, noise. Too little: seizing under heat! Backlash = fn(module, AGMA class, center distance tolerance). Anti-backlash: a split gear + spring, a preloaded double gear. On CNC: backlash compensation in the controller compensates — but not perfectly.

def: m = d/Z = P/π. The tooth size. m=1 a 3.14mm tooth, m=3 a 9.42mm tooth. Metric! Inch: DP = 25.4/m.
expand: Module sets the tooth size: root, addendum, dedendum — all a function of m. m=0.5 (watches), m=1-3 (industrial), m=5-25 (mining, ships). Two gears must share the same module (and pressure angle!) to mesh. Calculation: d = m×Z (pitch ⌀), Z = the tooth count. Center distance = (Z₁+Z₂)×m/2.

def: A pre-applied axial force on a bearing — eliminates play, increases stiffness, improves accuracy. A spacer/spring/nut anchor.
expand: Preload eliminates internal clearance = maximum stiffness + minimum runout. Methods: a lock nut (precise, adjustable), a spacer/shim (defined, reliable), a spring (thermally compensating — in spindles!). Over-preload = heating → failure! Optimal: 3-5% of C0r (dynamic load). DB (back-to-back): rigid; DF (face-to-face): forgiving. TRB: a defined endplay (0.025-0.125mm).

def: Thin, long rollers (L/D>3) — high radial load in minimal height. A drawn cup is common.
expand: Needle bearing: a ⌀2-5 × L10-30mm roller. A small OD = a small housing! Drawn cup (HK/BK): a thin metal shell — cheap. Full complement (no cage): maximum load, low speed. Cage type: medium speed. Uses: connecting rods (engines!), rocker arms, gearboxes. Downside: sensitive to alignment, no axial load allowed.

def: B7 (4140 Q&T, Sy=724): the standard bolt for pressure vessels + flanges. Nut: A194 2H.
expand: B7: Cr-Mo Q&T, −29 to 400°C (above that: B7M or B16). B7M: low hardness (HRC<22) — for sour gas environments (NACE MR0175). B8 (304), B8M (316): strain hardened — for corrosion. B16 (4140+V): up to 500°C. Sizes: 1/2"-4" ×any length. Always with a matching A194! The spec every piping engineer lives with.

def: Basic structural steel: Sy=250MPa. Cheap, weldable, available. 90% of structures worldwide.
expand: A36 (American) ≈ S235JR (European) ≈ SS400 (Japanese): carbon 0.2-0.26%, Sy≈250MPa, UTS 400-550. Welding: free (CE<0.35). Uses: I/H/L profiles, structural piping, platforms, frames. Hot rolled: black mill scale. Cold rolled: smooth, precise, more expensive. The cheapest steel still called steel.

en: ASME Boiler Pressure Vessel Code Section VIII
def: The pressure vessel design and manufacturing code. Div 1: standard (design by rule). Div 2: FEA (design by analysis).
expand: Div 1: a 'cookbook' — formulas for wall thickness, joints, openings. Div 2: allows higher stress (with FEA). U-stamp: a mark confirming the vessel meets code. An authorized inspector (AI): mandatory — without their signature, there's no vessel. Hydrotest: 1.3×MAWP. Materials: only from Section II. In Israel: ASME VIII Div 1 is the most common.

def: Tolerances for unspecified dimensions: f (fine), m (medium), c (coarse). ±0.1-±0.5mm depending on size.
expand: Part 1 (linear): f: 0.5-3mm→±0.05, 3-6→±0.05, 6-30→±0.1, 30-120→±0.15. m: 0.5-3→±0.1... Part 2 (geometric): H/K/L. The title block note: 'ISO 2768-mK'. Saves noting tolerance on every dimension! But: doesn't replace an explicit callout on critical dimensions. Rule: if unspecified — ISO 2768 applies.

def: SF = Sy/σ_actual. SF=2 general, 3 fatigue, 4 chains/cranes, 1.5 aerospace (with FEA).
expand: SF>1 = safe (theoretically). SF=2: pressure vessels, structures. SF=3: fatigue, dynamic loads. SF=4-5: cranes, chains (human lives + wear). SF=1.5: aerospace (every gram matters, FEA+test). SF=1.25: pneumatic devices (energy-storing). Rule: a low SF requires an accurate model + NDT + testing. A high SF allows less precision.

def: The stress below which steel lives 'forever' (>10⁷ cycles). Se ≈ 0.5×UTS. Aluminum: no limit!
expand: Steel: Se ≈ 0.5×Sut (up to Sut=1400). Above 1400: Se=700 (flattens). Corrections: ka(finish), kb(size), kc(load), kd(temperature), ke(reliability). The S-N diagram: high cycle (>10³, elastic) vs. low cycle (<10³, plastic). Aluminum/titanium: no endurance limit — every stress accumulates damage! Design: a Goodman/Soderberg diagram.

def: Kt = σ_max/σ_nominal. A hole: Kt≈3, a keyway: Kt≈2.5, a fillet R/d=0.1: Kt≈2. A radius = the fix!
expand: Kt depends on geometry alone (not material!). Kf (fatigue): Kf = 1+q×(Kt−1), q=0-1 (notch sensitivity). A stronger material = a higher q (more sensitive!). A corner radius reduces Kt dramatically: R/d=0.05→Kt=3, R/d=0.2→Kt=1.6. FEA finds Kt automatically — but a singularity at a sharp corner = an error!

def: A carbide blade with 2-8 edges: arrives ← locks ← works ← rotates ← discarded. ISO coding.
expand: ISO coding: CNMG 120408 = C(shape: 80° rhombic), N(clearance: 0°), M(tolerance: ±0.13), G(hole+chip breaker), 12(edge 12mm), 04(thickness 4.76), 08(radius 0.8mm). Grade: a CVD coating (TiCN+Al₂O₃) for steel, PVD (TiAlN) for SS/Ti. Chipbreaker: light/medium/heavy. Every manufacturer = a full catalog!

def: Flat, ball nose (3D), corner radius (strength!), roughing (short chip).
expand: Flat: pockets, slots, shoulders — the basic one. Ball nose: 3D contouring (molds, aerodynamic parts). Corner radius: an R at the edge = 2-3x the strength of sharp, good Ra, tool life ×2. Roughing (corncob): serrated teeth → a short chip, less vibration, high MRR. Variable helix: less vibration! 2F (slotting), 3F (Al), 4F (steel).

def: A magnet + fluorescent powder detects cracks on and near the surface in ferromagnetic materials (steel, iron).
expand: The principle: a magnetic field 'leaks' from a crack → iron particles accumulate = a mark! Wet fluorescent (UV, the most sensitive): a 0.5mm crack. Dry (field): coarser, cheaper. A yoke (AC/DC): AC for surface, DC for more depth. Ferromagnetic only (not austenitic SS, not Al!). In SS/Al: DPT or ET instead.

def: A liquid penetrates cracks → wiping → a developer pulls it out ← a red/fluorescent mark. Surface only. Any material!
expand: 3 stages: 1) penetrant (red visible or fluorescent): penetrates cracks by capillary action. 2) excess removal: a towel/solvent/water — don't wash out of the crack! 3) developer (white): draws the penetrant out of the crack ← a red/green mark. Dwell time: 10-30 min. Sensitivity: fluorescent > visible. Works on any material — but surface only!

def: Minimum order quantity: casting 100+, forging 500+, die casting 5000+. Setup cost governs!
expand: The economics: setup cost / quantity. CNC: MOQ=1 (setup 30-60 min). Sheet metal: MOQ=10-50 (programming+setup). Casting: MOQ=100-500 (pattern/core). Die casting: MOQ=5000+ (a $15-60K die!). Forging: MOQ=500+ (a $6-30K die). Extrusion: MOQ=500kg (a $1.5-5K die). MIM: MOQ=5000+. Rule: a net-shape process = a high MOQ, machining = MOQ=1.

def: A document package to a supplier: a drawing, material spec, quantity, schedule, quality requirements. The basis for every order.
expand: A good RFQ = an accurate quote. A missing RFQ = surprises. What to include: a drawing (PDF+STEP), a material spec (AMS/ASTM), quantity+a blanket, the required LT, QC requirements (FAI, CoC, NDT), packaging, shipping. Tip: at least 3 quotes. The lowest ≠ the best — check capability!

def: The physical body that represents the Datum: a surface plate = A, a V-block = B, a pin = C. Not the part — the fixture!
expand: Datum feature = on the part (the surface). Datum = a perfect theoretical plane/axis. Datum feature simulator = the physical body (a plate, an axis, a pin) that produces the datum from the part. The rule: the highest points of the part touch the simulator = the datum. A fixture = a collection of datum feature simulators representing a DRF.

def: HRC (a diamond cone, 150kg) for hard materials: 20-70. HRB (a 1/16" ball, 100kg) for soft ones: 20-100. Fast!
expand: The most common test: a minor load (10kg) → a major load → release → the remaining indentation depth = the hardness number. HRC: hardened steels, tools, bearings (HRC 58-64). HRB: soft steels, aluminum, brass (HRB 60-95). 15N/30N/45N: superficial — for thin coatings. Portable: Leeb/UCI — rebound, accurate ±2 HRC.

def: Thread tolerance class: class 2A/2B (75% of uses), 3A/3B (aerospace). Metric: 6g/6H (standard), 4h6h/4H5H (precision).
expand: Inch: 1A/1B (loose), 2A/2B (standard — a regular go/no-go), 3A/3B (tight — aerospace, no plating!). Metric: 6g/6H (standard = ISO 286), 5g6g/5H6H (medium), 4h6h/4H5H (precision). A=external, B=internal. Plating: causes growth — design 2A before plating, or an over-size tap. Thread gauge: go passes, no-go doesn't.

def: Design for assembly: fewer parts, poka-yoke, tool access, one direction. Boothroyd-Dewhurst.
expand: Principles: 1) minimum parts (consolidate ← 3D print/casting), 2) self-locating (parts locate themselves), 3) one assembly direction (top-down = cheapest), 4) poka-yoke (won't fit backward), 5) tool access (100mm minimum). DFA index = theoretical assembly time / ideal. The Boothroyd method: analyzes every part — can it be eliminated? Combined? Simplified?

def: A systematic analysis of possible design failures: what could fail, how severe, how likely. RPN = S×O×D.
expand: DFMEA (AIAG/VDA): function → failure mode → effect → severity (1-10) × occurrence (1-10) × detection (1-10) = RPN. High → a corrective action. AIAG/VDA 2019: Action Priority (AP) = H/M/L (instead of raw RPN). DFMEA (design) → PFMEA (process). Mandatory under IATF 16949 (automotive), AS9100 (aerospace). The tool for preventing problems before they happen.

def: Straight teeth parallel to the axis — the simplest. Noisy at high RPM. Load on a single tooth.
expand: The basic gear: simple manufacture (hobbing/shaping), cheap, no axial force. Downside: sudden contact (a whole tooth engages at once) = noise+shock. Contact ratio 1.2-1.8. Recommended speed: Vp<20m/s. Uses: industrial gearboxes, watches, printers, teaching. Above 1000 RPM = switch to helical.

def: Teeth on the inside of a ring — planetary gears, harmonic drives. Compact.
expand: Ring gear: the teeth face inward — the pinion rotates inside it. Advantage: compact, small radial forces (convex meets concave = wide contact!). Manufacture: shaping (not hobbing!), wire EDM, broaching. Uses: planetary gearboxes (ring+sun+planets), harmonic drives, slewing rings. Minimum teeth: Z_ring − Z_pinion ≥ 10.

def: Teeth on the face (not the circumference) — turns 90° with a spur gear. Simpler than bevel.
expand: Face gear: teeth on the flat surface — a standard spur gear meshes from below at 90°. Advantage: a standard pinion!, simpler manufacture than bevel, tolerates axial misalignment. Downside: limited load, a low contact ratio. Uses: helicopter engines (the Apache AH-64!), clock mechanisms, kitchen tools.

def: A spherical bearing with no rolling — spherical sliding surfaces. Compensates for misalignment. A rod end is common.
expand: An inner ball in a spherical outer cup: angular motion ±15-25° + rotation. No rolling = static/slow loads only. Lubrication: grease from a nipple (mandatory!), or a PTFE liner (maintenance-free). Rod end (Heim joint): a ball+thread = a jointed connection. Uses: cylinders, links, steering, aerospace. Aurora, SKF, INA.

def: A ball bearing for linear motion on a ground shaft — LM8UU, LM12UU. A shaft h5, a housing H7.
expand: Balls roll on a ground shaft (HRC 60+) and return through channels. Open type: side loading. Closed: standard. Flanged: with a flange for mounting. Super: double the ball rows = double the load. Thomson, THK, Hiwin. Limitation: radial load only (no moment!) — hence two parallel shafts + 4 bearings = rigidity. 3D printers: LM8UU is the standard.

def: Nickel 20-40μm + chrome 0.25μm — a shiny appearance. Faucets, car wheels, fixtures.
expand: The difference from hard chrome: decorative = thick nickel (protective!) + thin chrome (shiny). Stack: a copper strike → semi-bright Ni → bright Ni → 0.25μm Cr. The chrome = only appearance and scratch resistance! Protection = the nickel. Triple chrome: adding microporous Ni — corrosion resistance ×5. Satin/brushed: a matte texture. PVD = the greener alternative.

def: A family of coatings: plasma, HVOF, arc, flame. Thickness 0.1-2mm, any material on any substrate.
expand: HVOF (WC-Co/CrC): dense, hard, the alternative to hard chrome in aerospace. Plasma (Al₂O₃, YSZ): ceramic coatings, thermal barriers. Arc (Zn/Al): structural corrosion protection (bridges!). Wire flame: Babbitt on plain bearings. Common thread: molten/semi-molten particles sprayed onto the substrate ← a mechanical (not chemical!) layer. A bond coat (NiCr) always goes first.

def: mm/year (metric) or mpy (inch). <0.05 excellent, 0.05-0.5 good, >1.0 unacceptable.
expand: CR = (W×87600)/(ρ×A×t) [mm/y]. Field coupons: installed in the process, pulled and weighed. Ultrasonic: annual thickness measurement (corrosion mapping). ER probes: real-time. Corrosion allowance in design: CA = CR × design life. Steel in seawater: 0.1 mm/y = 2mm over 20 years. SS in piping: CR<0.01 — hence CA=0!

def: Two methods: SACP (sacrificial Zn/Mg/Al anodes) or ICCP (impressed current). Protects piping and structures.
expand: SACP: a Zn/Mg anode on a ship's hull/a tank — corrodes instead of the steel. Simple, no electricity, limited by size. ICCP: a rectifier + a Ti/MMO anode → controls the potential (−850mV CSE). For kilometers of piping, huge tanks, continuous. In Israel: gas piping requires CP. Rule: periodic testing + documentation!

def: 14 symbols: 4 form (⏤□○⌭), 3 orientation (∥⊥∠), 2 location (⊕◎), 2 profile (⌒⌓), 2 runout (↗⇗), 1 symmetry.
expand: Form (no datum): straightness ⏤, flatness □, circularity ○, cylindricity ⌭. Orientation (a datum!): parallelism ∥, perpendicularity ⊥, angularity ∠. Location (a datum!): true position ⊕, concentricity ◎ (removed in 2018). Profile: line ⌒, surface ⌓. Runout (a datum!): circular ↗, total ⇗. Symmetry (removed in 2018). Profile = the most flexible!

def: A two-row FCF: the top row = pattern location against datums, the bottom row = relation between holes only.
expand: Composite position (the most common!): row 1 (PLTZF — pattern location): ⊕⌀0.5 A B C = the pattern's location relative to the DRF. Row 2 (FRTZF — feature relating): ⊕⌀0.2 A = the relation between holes in the pattern relative to A alone. Meaning: the pattern can drift ±0.5 — but within it the holes stay tight ±0.2!

def: Metal powder pressed in a die + sintered. Near net shape, density 85-95%. Gears, bushings, filters.
expand: Press+sinter: powder (Fe, Cu, SS) in a die → 300-800MPa → sintering at 70-90% Tm. Density: 6.4-7.2 g/cm³ (solid steel 7.85). Advantage: near net shape, complex geometry, self-lubricating (porous!). Uses: gears (automotive! 1M/month), bushings (oil-soaked), filters. HIP = 100% density. Competitor: MIM (small parts), binder jetting.

def: Building a whole metal part by plating onto a mandrel ← removing the mandrel. No tooling! Ni, Cu.
expand: Like electroplating — but at 0.1-10mm thickness = the part itself! The mandrel (wax/Al/coated metal) is removed afterward. Accuracy: ±0.005mm. Uses: waveguides (microwave — 0.1mm walls!), molds, screens, bellows, CD stampers. Nickel electroforms: precise surface replication. Advantage: no forces = no stress = perfect dimensions.

def: An imaginary circle on which bolt holes are centered. BCD + number of holes = one designation (wheel bolts: 5×114.3).
expand: PCD (pitch circle diameter) = BCD: the ⌀ of the circle the hole centers sit on. From a measurement: PCD = d/(sin(180°/n)). Example: 4 holes, a neighbor distance of 106mm → PCD=106/sin(45°)=150mm. Automotive: 5×114.3, 4×100 etc. Position GD&T: every hole at true position on the PCD — a composite FCF is ideal!

def: A defined overlap: H7/p6 (light), H7/s6 (heavy). Assembly: a press, heating the housing, cooling the shaft.
expand: Calculation: p_contact = δ/(d×(1/E_hub × (d_o²+d²)/(d_o²−d²) + 1/E_shaft × (d²+d_i²)/(d²−d_i²))). Transmitted torque: T = μ×p×π×d²×L/2. In practice: a 15° chamfer on both, moly lubrication, straight assembly (not angled!). Cooling the shaft in LN₂ (−196°C): the shaft contracts and enters freely — the most precise method.

def: A pressure test with water: 1.5× design (ASME B31.3). The safest — an incompressible fluid = no explosion.
expand: Water filling (a vent at the high point!), gradual pressurization to 1.5×MAWP, holding 10-30 min. Check: a pressure drop = a leak (note: a 1°C temperature change ≈ a 5bar change from a small volume change!). Criteria: no leak, no permanent distortion. Pneumatic (1.1×): only when water is forbidden — stored energy = an explosion risk!

def: X-ray/gamma imaging of welds — reveals porosity, inclusions, lack of fusion. ASME V Art.2.
expand: X-ray (thin walls, a lab) or gamma (Ir-192/Co-60 — the field, thick walls). The film/detector behind the part: a defect = a density change = a mark. An IQI (penetrameter): confirms 2% sensitivity. Mandatory: a radiation-protected area! Digital RT (CR/DR): filmless, fast, documented. PAUT is replacing RT in more and more applications.

def: A motor driven by compressed air: vane (common) or piston. Explosion-proof, light, high speed.
expand: Vane motor: 4-8 vanes, 500-25000 RPM, 0.1-5kW. Advantage: no sparks (ATEX!), overload-tolerant (stalls with no damage), light (0.5 kg/kW), works wet. Downside: 20-30% efficiency (expensive air!), noisy. Uses: drills/grinders, chemical mixers, ATEX zones, clean rooms.

def: Rules: corner R ≥ tool, hole L/D ≤ 5, wall thickness ≥ 1mm, 0° draft (an advantage!), minimum setups.
expand: The rules: 1) internal corner R ≥ 1mm (R=0 = EDM!), 2) hole L/D ≤ 4 standard, ≤ 10 carbide TSC, 3) avoid undercuts, 4) wall thickness ≥ t (1mm steel, 0.8 Al), 5) design for fixturing — two parallel gripping surfaces, 6) done-in-one: plan OP1 from one side+OP2 flipped = only 2 setups.

def: Materials for H₂S (sour gas): HRC ≤ 22 for carbon steel! Stainless: duplex, 316L. Limits hardness.
expand: H₂S + water = SSC (sulfide stress cracking) + HIC (hydrogen induced cracking). The fix: hardness limitation (HRC22 = Sy~550 = a compromise!). Approved materials: CS ≤ HRC22 (PWHT mandatory!), 316L, 2205/2507 duplex, Inconel 625/825. Bolts: ASTM A193 B7M (low hardness). Any unapproved material = an H₂S cracking risk = a leak = a catastrophe.

def: The European directive for pressure equipment: categories I-IV by PS×V, materials, and approved processes. CE mark.
expand: PED classifies by: fluid group (1=hazardous, 2=standard) × PS×V or PS×DN. Categories I-IV: higher = higher requirements (NB inspection, QMS, 100% NDT). Notified body: an external auditor. Mandatory for a CE mark = entry to the European market. In Israel: pressure equipment exported to Europe = PED mandatory. Sound engineering practice: below Cat I = the manufacturer's own responsibility.

def: Straightening a bent shaft on a press: a DTI → pressure → elastic springback → repeat. Target TIR × 3 = over-press.
expand: Shafts bend from: hardening (martensite expands!), welding, asymmetric machining (stress release). The method: V-blocks + a DTI → find the high point → press 3× the deviation (springback!) → check → repeat. Hot straightening (>150°C): severe distortion. Limit: hardened steels above HRC 45 = fracture risk — temper first!

def: Heating at 550-650°C/1-2h (steel) to reduce internal stress. Also: VSR (vibration — no furnace).
expand: Thermal: 600°C × 1h/25mm → slow cooling (≤200°C/h). Reduces 80% of stresses. When: after heavy welding, between Op1 and Op2 (precision parts), after bending/straightening. VSR (vibratory): vibrating at a natural frequency — reduces stress 30-50% with no furnace (for large parts that don't fit!). Al: 200-300°C (careful with T6!).

def: Freezing rubber/plastic in LN₂ + shot blasting — removes flash/burr without harming the part.
expand: Rubber and plastic are too soft for standard burr removal — but at −196°C they harden and become brittle! The technique: a rotating drum + LN₂ + polycarbonate/aluminum shot — the thin flash breaks off, the large body survives. Uses: O-rings, injection-molded parts, molded rubber. Replaces manual cleaning = a 90% labor savings.

def: Superalloys for temperatures above 600°C: Ni-base (718, 625, Waspaloy), Co-base (Stellite), Fe-base (A286).
expand: Alloys born from jet engine needs: 700-1100°C + loads + corrosion + fatigue. Ni-base: γ' precipitation (718, Waspaloy, René 88) — the turbine. Co-base: Stellite — wear at heat. Fe-base: A286 — economical. Machining: very hard (Vc=20-40, high forces, work hardening). AM: EBM/DMLS qualified for 718, 625.

def: Lean manufacturing: 8 wastes (DOWNTIME). 5S, Kanban, value stream mapping, SMED. Toyota.
expand: 8 wastes (DOWNTIME): defects, overproduction, waiting, non-utilized talent, transportation, inventory, motion, extra-processing. Tools: 5S (order), VSM (value mapping), Kanban (pull), SMED (setup reduction), poka-yoke, kaizen. The goal: only activity the customer pays for! In machine shops: 95% of lead time = waiting, not machining.

def: Sort, set, shine, standardize, sustain. The basis of all lean. If the floor is a mess — no method will work.
expand: Seiri (sort — discard the unneeded!), Seiton (set in order — a place for everything!), Seiso (shine — clean=an inspection!), Seiketsu (standardize — everyone the same way), Shitsuke (sustain — a habit). On CNC: a tool shadow board, an organized station, sorted stock. 5S = not cleanliness — it's visual control that exposes problems.

def: The goal: a setup under 10 minutes! Separating internal (machine stopped) from external (machine running).
expand: Shigeo Shingo (Toyota): 1) film the setup, 2) separate internal/external, 3) convert internal→external (prepare everything in advance!), 4) streamline the internal (a quick-change chuck, preset tools). A CNC example: external=tool prep, reading the program, staging stock. Internal=fixture change, WCS. From 45 min to 8 = 5x the flexibility!

def: An improved NPT — seals metal-to-metal with no Teflon. For fuel, oxygen, gases. ANSI B1.20.3.
expand: NPTF: the root and crest are flat — compress and seal with no sealant! Uses: O₂ lines (Teflon+O₂ under pressure = flammable!), fuels, hydraulics (if not an SAE O-ring boss). Tightening: 1-2 turns past hand-tight. More expensive than NPT — used only when required. L1/L3 gauge testing.

def: The tapered version of BSP: 1:16 at 55°. Seals in the thread. Common in Israel for piping!
expand: R (external taper) + Rp (internal cylindrical) = the common seal in Israel and Europe. 55° Whitworth — not compatible with NPT (60°)! A common mix-up: G (BSPP, straight) vs. R (BSPT, tapered). R seals in the thread+Teflon. G seals with a gasket/O-ring. Both share the same pitch — but a different purpose.

def: Cleaning with 20-40kHz waves: vacuum bubbles collapse on the surface and remove dirt. Precision parts, medical.
expand: Microscopic cavitation: sound waves create and collapse tiny bubbles — a mechanical cleaning effect in every crevice! Solution: water+detergent (Branson EC), or IPA, acetone. Uses: precision parts after machining (chips in holes!), medical, electronics, restoration. 40kHz=gentle, 20kHz=aggressive. Time: 3-15 minutes.

def: Removing burrs: manual (a knife/brush), tumbling (rubbing in a drum), thermal (TEM), electrochemical (ECM).
expand: Manual: a Noga knife/brush = cheap, slow, uneven. Tumbling/vibratory: ceramic/plastic media = all surfaces at once, uniform. Thermal (TEM): a gas explosion in a chamber — burns off burrs in 20ms (internal ones!). Cryogenic: freezing+shot = for rubber/plastic. Rule: the best burr is the one that never formed (a sharp tool, cutting direction!).

def: Adding/removing weight to eliminate rotational vibration. G2.5 (ISO 1940) = general. G1 = precision.
expand: Unbalance = mass × distance from center [g·mm]. Single-plane (a disc): one weight. Two-plane (a shaft): two planes. G grade (ISO 1940): G6.3 (motors), G2.5 (mills), G1 (grinding), G0.4 (spindles). A balancing machine: force sensors + phase → where to add how much. A CNC spindle: in-situ balancing with a vibration analyzer.

def: Electrochemical polishing: removes 5-25μm from the peaks in stainless. Ra↓50%, shiny, built-in passivation.
expand: The opposite of electroplating: the part = the anode, dissolves selectively (peaks more than valleys). Result: Ra↓30-50%, burr-free, excellent passivation (a Cr₂O₃-rich layer). Mandatory in: pharma/biotech (GMP), semiconductor, medical. SS 304/316 only (usually). ASTM B912. Doesn't fix deep scratches — only smooths.

def: An abrasive paste pushed through internal channels — polishes/deburrs where nothing else can reach. AM!
expand: Media: a viscous polymer + SiC/diamond grains pushed at 7-200bar pressure through an internal cavity. Improves: Ra from 6μm to 0.5, removes internal burrs, radiuses edges. An exploding use in AM: internal cooling channels in metal printing (DMLS) — AFM is the only thing that polishes inside! Also: nozzles, turbine blades, hydraulic manifolds.

def: Coating from gases at 800-1050°C: TiC, TiCN, multi-layer Al₂O₃. On carbide inserts. Thicker than PVD.
expand: CVD: gases react on the hot surface ← a 5-20μm layer. Multi-layer: TiN+TiCN+Al₂O₃+TiN = each contributes something! Al₂O₃: thermal insulation from the substrate. Advantage: thick, uniform, multi-layer. Disadvantage: 1000°C = distorts small tools, residual tension (less sharp). Hence: CVD for large inserts, PVD for small/sharp tools.

def: Vacuum coating at 200-500°C: TiN, TiAlN, AlCrN, DLC. 2-5μm. On end mills, inserts, medical.
expand: PVD: a target is bombarded (sputtering) or evaporated (cathodic arc) ← atoms condense on the tool at 400-500°C. Advantage: low temperature (no distortion!), residual compression (sharp!), thin = sharp edges. TiN (gold, basic), TiAlN (purple, heat), AlCrN (dry), DLC (low friction). The standard for end mills, drills, taps.

def: Grinding flat surfaces — Ra 0.1-0.8, flatness 0.005mm. After hardening. An Al₂O₃ or CBN wheel.
expand: A magnetic table holds a ferromagnetic part, a grinding wheel removes 0.005-0.02mm per pass. Reciprocating (a back-and-forth table): the common one. Rotary: round parts. Creep feed: one deep, slow pass (1-5mm) — like milling! Wheels: Al₂O₃ (soft steel), CBN (hardened — wheel life ×100!). Dressing: a diamond re-sharpens.

def: Grinding shafts (OD) and holes (ID) — IT5-IT6, Ra 0.1-0.4. Between centers or chucking.
expand: OD grinding: a part between centers (the most precise — no chucking effect!) or a chuck. ID grinding: a small wheel inside a hole — high RPM, low rigidity. Plunge (depth) vs. traverse (length). Centerless: no centers — production runs (pins, shafts, pistons). Superfinish afterward: Ra 0.025!

def: A hob (a spiral tool) rotates synchronized with the gear — cuts involute teeth. The main manufacturing process for gears.
expand: Hob: a rotating worm-shaped cutting tool synchronized with the gear (a 1:Z ratio). Cuts spur and helical (at an angle). Accuracy: DIN 6-8 (without grinding), DIN 3-5 (with grinding after). Uses: 80% of gears. Hob: HSS (M35 TiN) or carbide. CNC hobbing: 5-axis. Above module 1 — hobbing is the standard.

def: Grinding teeth after hardening — DIN 3-5 (the most precise). Profile (form) or generating (rolling).
expand: Generating (threaded wheel): a synchronized worm-shaped grinding wheel — fast, DIN 4-6. Profile (form): a tooth-shaped wheel — precise DIN 2-3, slow. Honing: an abrasive plastic wheel — a quiet DIN 5-7 finish. Hard finish mandatory: hardened gears (HRC 58-62) — hobbing can't! Klingelnberg, Gleason, Reishauer = the names.

def: Grinding shafts with no centers — thrufeed (continuous pass) or infeed (stationary). Production runs!
expand: 3 contacts: a grinding wheel (fast), a regulating wheel (slow, angled 2-8°), a support blade (V-shaped). Thrufeed: the shaft passes continuously between the wheels — thousands per hour! Infeed: a stop limits it, for stepped shafts. Accuracy: ±0.005mm, roundness <0.002. Uses: pins, shafts, pistons, rollers. The best for roundness.

def: A multi-tooth tool for enlarging and precisioning a drilled hole: H7 easily. Stock: 0.1-0.3mm. HSS/carbide.
expand: Reamer: 4-16 teeth, straight/spiral leading edges. Removes 0.1-0.3mm from the drilled hole ← H7 ± 0.01mm, Ra 0.4-1.6. HSS (hand/machine — cheap), carbide (precise, ×10 life). Chucking reamer: for CNC. Hand reamer: a square for a handle. Adjustable: diameter adjustment ±0.2mm. Rules: never insert/remove in reverse rotation (ruins the edge!). Coolant mandatory.

def: A multi-tooth tool in one pull/push: keyways, splines, internal hex. Seconds!
expand: Each tooth is 0.02-0.1mm higher than the previous — the whole shape in one pass! Pull broach: internal (keyway, spline, special shapes). Push broach: for small ones. Surface broach: external (turbine disc slots!). Accuracy: IT7, Ra 0.4-1.6. Downside: an expensive dedicated tool ($1000-50,000). ROI from 500+ parts.

def: A 60/82/90/120° conical tool creating a recess for a countersunk bolt or removing burrs. Single/3-flute.
expand: 90° ISO (flat head socket), 82° ANSI (flat head machine screw) — don't mix them! 60°: piping parts, valve seats. 120°: deburring + centering (a spot drill). 3-flute: clean, for CNC. 1-flute (zero-flute): thin sheet with no chatter. A piloted CSK: precise — the pilot enters the hole and centers. A deburring tool (Noga): a handle+rotating blade = convenient!

def: Rotating tools on a CNC lathe: milling, side drilling, threading — no transfer to a machining center!
expand: A lathe with a C-axis (an indexable spindle) + live tools (motorized in the turret): milling slots, radial drilling, hexagons, side threads — done-in-one! Y-axis: off-center milling. Sub-spindle: automatic Op2. The modern lathe = a multi-purpose machining center. Savings: 2 setups → 1, higher accuracy (no re-chucking).

def: Translates CAM tool paths into the controller's language (Fanuc/Siemens/Heidenhain). Every machine = a different post!
expand: CAM generates CL data (generic) → a post processor translates it into specific G-code. Fanuc: G43 H, Siemens: CYCLE800, Heidenhain: PLANE SPATIAL. A wrong post = wrong G-code = a collision! Requirements: correct M-codes (tool change, coolant), safe lines, program structure. A new post: test in simulation (Vericut!) before cutting metal.

def: The 3-2-1 principle: 3 points (a plane) + 2 (a line) + 1 (a point) = 6 DOF. Clamp, don't distort!
expand: 3-2-1: 3 on datum A (the table), 2 on B (an edge), 1 on C (a stop). Clamping: over support points (not in the air!), enough force with no distortion (sheet metal!). Quick-change: Jergens/Schunk zero-point = a 30-second setup! Rules: don't rely on friction for cutting loads, leave tool access, ensure chip clearance.

def: A chuck (3/4 jaws), a vise (Kurt), a collet (ER/5C), vacuum, magnetic, a dedicated fixture.
expand: 3-jaw chuck: self-centering, TIR 0.05-0.1. 4-jaw: each jaw independent, TIR<0.01. 6-jaw: thin sheet. Kurt vise: the standard VMC vise. Double station: 2 parts. ER/5C collet: shafts, rods. Vacuum: thin sheet/plastic. Magnetic: flat steel. Zero-point: Schunk Vero-S = table → fixture in 10 seconds!

def: Vericut / CAM simulation: runs the program virtually — detects collisions before the machine gets destroyed!
expand: CAM simulation (backplot): tool paths — catches gross errors. Machine simulation (a full machine model): catches fixture/turret/spindle collisions. Vericut (the standard): actual G-code + a machine model + stock = full verification. Auto-diff: compares the machined part to CAD. Mandatory in: 5-axis, expensive parts, new machines. 30 minutes of simulation = saves a week of repairs.

def: A spindle-mounted probe measures the part between operations: WCS update, dimension checks, adaptive machining.
expand: Renishaw OMP60/RMP600: infrared/radio → the controller. O9xxx (Fanuc) / L97xx (Siemens) cycles. Uses: 1) auto WCS setting (saves 5-15 min/setup), 2) checking a dimension after roughing (adjust finishing!), 3) verifying FAI on the machine, 4) adaptive: measuring stock and updating the program. A tool setter: measures tool length automatically = zero H-offset errors.

def: An MSA study: 10 parts × 3 inspectors × 3 trials. %GRR<10% excellent, >30% unacceptable.
expand: The question: how much of the spread is the measurement system and not the process? The ANOVA method breaks it down: EV (equipment), AV (appraiser), interaction. ndc≥5 = distinguishes enough categories. Before Cpk — GRR first! An instrument with GRR 40% is measuring noise, not parts. The AIAG MSA Manual, 4th Edition.

def: A statistical method for testing the effect of several factors simultaneously: full factorial, fractional, Taguchi.
expand: Instead of one-factor-at-a-time (OFAT — slow and misses interactions!): DOE varies several factors simultaneously in a planned pattern. Full factorial 2³ = 8 experiments (3 factors × 2 levels). Fractional: half (2³⁻¹=4). Taguchi: economical but less information. The goal: identify what really matters and by how much — and lock it in. A Black Belt's most powerful tool.

def: Involute teeth on a shaft — transmits high torque with excellent centering. DIN 5480, SAE.
expand: Involute spline: a profile like a gear = standard tools! Centering on: sides (uniform force), major ⌀ (precise), minor ⌀ (worn). Class: 4-7 (4=tight, 7=loose). External manufacture: hobbing/rolling. Internal: broaching/shaping. Vs. a keyway: torque ×3-5, no Kt in the shaft, built-in centering. DIN 5480: m, Z, P.A.

def: Wear mechanisms: adhesive (galling), abrasive (scraping), fatigue (pitting), corrosive (combined).
expand: 4 wear mechanisms: 1) adhesive: micro-welding ← tearing (SS+SS!). 2) abrasive: hard particles gouge (sand, chips). 3) surface fatigue: cyclic contact ← pitting (gears, bearings). 4) corrosive/tribochemical: chemistry+mechanics. Usually: a combination! The fix by mechanism: coating/material (adhesive), filtration (abrasive), lubrication (fatigue), material selection (corrosive).

def: A process producing a shape close to final: BTF 1.1-2. Investment cast, MIM, PM, precision forge, AM.
expand: NNS = minimal material removal = minimal cost and waste! Comparison: hogging out from a block (BTF=10-20, 90% chips!), NNS (BTF=1.1-2, 10% chips). Processes: investment casting (±0.1mm), MIM (<100g), PM (gears), precision forging (crankshafts), AM (complex). ROI: high tooling NRE — worthwhile from 100-5000 units depending on the process.

def: Forging at ±0.1-0.5mm tolerance — almost no machining needed. Flashless, near net shape.
expand: Precision forging: a precise die + controlled force = an almost finished part. BTF 1.1-1.5 (vs. 3-5 standard!). Flashless: no flash = no trimming. Isothermal forging (Ti, Ni): a die as hot as the part — uniform flow. Uses: turbine blades, racing connecting rods, gears. Die NRE ×3-5 of standard — ROI at 1000+ parts.

def: Casting into a metal mold under gravity — accuracy and quality between sand and die casting. Al/Cu.
expand: Gravity permanent mold: metal is poured (not injected!) into a steel/iron mold. Advantage: fine grain (cools fast), Ra 3-6μm, tolerance ±0.5mm. Vs. sand: 3x more accurate; vs. die cast: no porosity (no pressure = no trapped gas!). Tilt-pour: controlled filling. 5,000-50,000 parts per mold. Al automotive OEM wheels.

def: Parts + abrasive media in a rotating/vibrating drum — burr removal, smoothing, cleaning. Production runs!
expand: Media: ceramic (aggressive, deburr+radiusing), plastic (gentle, pre-plate), steel (burnishing=shiny). Compound: water+chemical (cleaning+rust prevention). Time: 30 min-8 hours. Batch (a drum) vs. continuous (a flow). Advantage: uniform, automatic, cheap. Disadvantage: non-selective — all surfaces affected. CNC parts after machining: 1-2 hours ceramic = burr-free.

def: Brazing in a vacuum furnace: filler metal melts and flows by capillary action with no flux. Excellent for stainless, Ti, superalloys.
expand: Vacuum 10⁻⁴-10⁻⁵ mbar + heating above the braze's liquidus (BNi, BAg, BCu) → the filler flows by capillary action, filling the gap (0.025-0.125mm!). Advantages: clean (no flux/residue!), multiple joints simultaneously, minimal distortion. Uses: plate-fin heat exchangers, turbine nozzles, carbide tools. AMS 2675.

def: An analog sensor for measuring linear displacement ±0.1μm. No friction, no wear, infinite life!
expand: 3 coils + a moving iron core: an AC voltage output proportional to displacement. Range: ±0.5 to ±500mm. Accuracy: 0.1μm! Infinite life (no contact, no wear). Uses: position measurement in cylinders, continuous thickness gauging, CMM, test machines. Spring-return: a digital indicator = an LVDT+display. Contactless (eddy current): for rotating metals.

def: An instrument for measuring friction coefficient and wear: pin-on-disc, ball-on-flat, block-on-ring. ASTM G99.
expand: Pin-on-disc (ASTM G99): a pin is pressed onto a rotating disc — measures friction force+wear over time. Ball-on-flat: reciprocating — simulates a piston. Block-on-ring: sliding — plain bearings. Falex: EP additives. Result: μ(t) + a wear rate [mm³/Nm]. Uses: coating development, oil selection, material comparison. Tribology's instrument.
